messages.content: How does the hospital accommodate different dietary and religious needs?

LHSC offers a variety of therapeutic, allergy-based, and religious-based diets. That includes vegan, vegetarian (with various inclusions), halal, kosher, and pork-free options, as well as accommodation for priority allergens like eggs, milk, mustard, and nuts. You'll choose from a menu each day based on your prescribed diet. If your dietary needs aren't being met, talk to your nurse and they can involve a dietitian.
What is the Pat Relations Office and when should I contact them?

The Patient Relations Office is LHSC's point of contact for questions, concerns, or feedback about your care experience. Before reaching out to them, try resolving any issue directly with your care team — they can often address concerns on the spot. If that doesn't work, you can contact Patient Relations by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, by phone at extension 52036 (519-685-8500), or through the online contact form on the LHSC website. They're available Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. If you had a positive experience, the Great Moments Recognition Program lets you recognize a staff member who made a difference.
I feel like the staff forgets about me. I've been waiting forever.

Waiting without updates is incredibly frustrating, and you're right to feel that way. Hospital staff are often juggling multiple patients, but that doesn't mean your needs should be overlooked. Here's what you can do: press the call button and ask for an update, or ask your parent to go to the nurses' station. You can also ask for a specific timeline — 'When will someone come to check on me?' — so you're not just waiting in a void. If you consistently feel overlooked, you can speak to the charge nurse or reach out to the Patient Relations office. You deserve attentive care, and advocating for yourself is not rude — it's appropriate.
What happens when I'm discharged?

Your care team will go over everything with you and your family: medications (purpose, dosage, timing, side effects), any dietary changes, activity restrictions, follow-up appointments, and what to watch for at home. You'll receive written instructions. If you need equipment or home care services, those need to be assessed by an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator before you leave. If your stay was longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is needed. Make sure you understand everything before you leave — and don't be afraid to ask questions.
Why can only two people visit at a time? I want all my friends here.

Visitor limits exist to protect patients — including you — from overcrowding and infection, and to respect the privacy of other patients who share the space. I know it's frustrating when you want your crew around you. The current policy allows two care partners at the bedside at a time for inpatients. You could set up a rotation so different friends come at different times. Video calling is also an option for larger group hangouts. If you want to make the case for a specific exception, talk to your nurse — in some situations, flexibility is possible. The intent isn't to isolate you, it's to keep the environment safe.
I don't want medical students practicing on me.

That's a valid concern, and you have the right to understand who is involved in your care. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, so medical students and residents are part of the environment. However, they always work under the supervision of experienced physicians. You can ask at any point who is doing what, and you're within your rights to request that certain procedures be performed by a senior team member. Your care team should explain who everyone is and what their role is. If you're uncomfortable with someone's involvement, speak up or have your parent advocate for you. Patient comfort is part of good care.
What infection prevention protocols should I be aware of?

Hand hygiene is the top priority. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) dispensers are located throughout the hospital, and you should clean your hands before entering a patient room, when leaving, and at the end of any visit. If a patient requires additional infection control precautions, you'll see a sign posted at the room or bed space entry. This might mean wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection — staff will walk you through it. Other practical rules: don't visit if you're sick, don't sit on hospital beds or put feet on bedded chairs, don't use patient washrooms if you're a visitor, and don't touch supplies on carts — ask staff instead. Keeping personal items minimal also helps the cleaning team maintain hygiene.
Can I use my phone in the hospital?

Absolutely. The hospital encourages patients to use their own cell phones to make calls and keep in touch with people. There's WiFi for internet access, and patient telephones are also available for free local and toll-free calls. So staying connected with friends and family shouldn't be a problem.
I complained to the nurse and now I feel bad. Am I being difficult?

Advocating for your own needs isn't being difficult — it's being a good patient. Nurses prefer patients who speak up about what's wrong because it helps them provide better care. If you told a nurse about pain, discomfort, a need that wasn't being met, or something that was bothering you — that's exactly what you should do. Don't confuse assertiveness with rudeness. As long as you're respectful, communicating your needs is welcomed, not resented. If you're still feeling bad about it, you could simply say to your nurse, 'Thanks for listening to me earlier.' But you truly have nothing to apologize for.
What sounds should I expect in the hospital?

Hospitals have a distinct soundscape. Monitors produce steady beeping that corresponds to heart rates and oxygen levels. Infusion pumps attached to IVs make periodic sounds, especially when a bag is running low or there's an occlusion. You'll hear overhead announcements, doors opening and closing, footsteps in the hallway, and occasional alarms. In units like the PCCU, the density of monitoring equipment means the ambient beeping is more constant. At night, the hospital quiets down but doesn't go silent — nurses still move through the halls and check on patients. If any alarm sound worries you, ask your nurse what it means.
What's the difference between an RN and an RPN?

Both Registered Nurses (RNs) and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs) provide direct patient care at Children's Hospital — things like administering medication, monitoring your condition, and coordinating your care. The main difference is in their education and scope of practice. RNs complete a four-year university degree and may manage more complex clinical situations, while RPNs complete a shorter diploma program and often work alongside RNs. Both are licensed, knowledgeable, and integral to your care team. The nursing team works closely with each other and with your physicians to make sure your needs are met.
I'm trans. Is there anyone at this hospital who gets that?

Yes. Children's Hospital has the Gender Pathways Service, or GPS. It's a multidisciplinary service providing gender-affirming care to gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents 17 and under. The team follows North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. You can learn more or reach out to them directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca. If you want, your care team can also help connect you. You deserve to feel respected and understood during your care.
They just told me I have to stay longer than expected. I can't do this.

Hearing that your stay has been extended when you were mentally counting down the days is crushing. That disappointment is entirely valid. Take a moment to feel it. Then, when you're ready, ask your doctor specifically why the stay was extended and what the new timeline looks like. Having concrete information helps more than vague uncertainty. You've already gotten through every day up to this point — that's proof you can keep going. Reach out to friends, ask for activities, talk to a counsellor if the news hit hard. You can do this. Not because it's easy, but because you've been doing it all along.
Is smoking allowed anywhere on the property?

No. LHSC is completely smoke-free — all buildings, grounds, and parking lots. This includes cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, and cannabis. The only exemption is for the traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous Peoples, for which a designated space is provided.
Someone talked to my family about bereavement support. Who was that?

That was likely a Spiritual Care Specialist or a social worker. Bereavement care at LHSC is provided by both of those services. The hospital also holds an annual 'Remembering the Children' memorial event each fall — a non-religious event that acknowledges all infants and children who have passed away at LHSC over the year. Your nurse can provide a 'Consent to be Contacted' form if your family is interested in attending. These services exist to provide compassionate support during an incredibly difficult time.
I haven't had a proper shower in days and I feel disgusting.

Feeling clean is a basic need, and not being able to shower normally can really get to you. Depending on your situation — IVs, bandages, mobility — there are workarounds. Your nurse can help you figure out the best option, whether that's a modified shower, a bed bath, or waterproof coverings for certain equipment. The sleeping areas in some units share bathrooms with showers. Ask about what's possible. If you need toiletries like shampoo, deodorant, or a toothbrush, the Paediatric Family Resource Centre or the pharmacy may have them. You don't have to just deal with it — tell your nurse, and they'll help.
What should I know about medication management during my stay?

Bring a complete list of all medications you're currently taking — prescriptions, over-the-counter drugs, herbal supplements, vitamins, creams, inhalers, eye drops, everything. Include your pharmacy's phone number. Important: don't take any medications from home unless explicitly approved by your hospital care team, because your in-hospital medications are managed separately. While admitted, the hospital supplies your prescribed medications. Before discharge, you'll receive an updated medication list — make sure it's shared with your family doctor and home pharmacy. If you have questions about side effects or interactions, a pharmacist is available through your nurse.
Why do some rooms require you to wear a gown, gloves, and mask before entering?

Those are additional infection control precautions, also called isolation precautions. They're in place when a patient has an infection that could spread to others or when a patient's immune system is so compromised that they need extra protection from outside germs. The specific gear depends on the type of precaution — contact precautions typically require gloves and a gown, droplet precautions add a mask, and airborne precautions may require an N95 respirator. Always check with staff before entering a room with a precaution sign.
Where can I grab food?

On the Go featuring Tim Hortons is on the second floor of Zone B in the main atrium — open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. (closed weekends and holidays). Vending machines and ATMs are near the Zone B elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors. If you're an inpatient on B6, there are pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks. A full list of food options is on the LHSC website.
Can my friends visit whenever they want?

Visiting times aren't fixed hospital-wide — they vary by unit and depend on your condition and care needs. Check with the unit staff about optimal visiting times. Visitors shouldn't come if they've been sick in the past week, and visiting may be interrupted or restricted for your care, privacy, or safety. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., visitors should be in your room and staff should be aware of their presence.
Why does everyone keep checking my armband? It's getting annoying.

I get it — it can feel repetitive. But armband checks are one of the most critical safety protocols in the hospital. Before any medication, test, procedure, or transport, staff verify your identity by checking your armband — which has your name, date of birth, hospital ID, and a barcode. It's a standard practice designed to prevent medical errors, like giving the wrong medication or performing the wrong procedure on the wrong patient. These errors are rare precisely because of this kind of verification. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red bracelet that alerts every member of your care team.
How does fall prevention work here?

When you're admitted, your nurse will do a fall risk assessment and go over fall prevention strategies with you and your family. Even if you're usually steady on your feet, being in a hospital — with unfamiliar surroundings, medications that might make you drowsy, and periods of bed rest — can increase fall risk. Practical steps include wearing slip-proof socks or slippers whenever you get up, keeping bed rails raised when you're in bed, keeping the floor clear of clutter, and asking for help before getting out of bed if you've been sedated or feel unsteady. If any staff leave items that create a trip hazard, flag it.
What's the deal with poinsettias?

Poinsettias are completely banned from LHSC. They contain a compound similar to what's found in rubber latex, which can cause a severe allergic reaction through touch or even inhalation. So especially during the holidays, make sure nobody sends or brings poinsettias to the hospital.
What is shared decision-making?

Shared Decision Making is a structured approach at LHSC where you and your caregivers work together with healthcare providers and a Decision Coach to make important choices about your care. It integrates the best medical evidence with your personal values and preferences. It means you're not just being told what's going to happen — you're part of the process. If you're facing a significant treatment decision and want more control over the direction, ask your care team about Shared Decision Making or visit the LHSC website for more information.
I'm so angry. Why do I have to deal with this? None of my friends do.

That anger is completely justified. There's nothing fair about dealing with a health issue when your peers don't have to, and you don't have to pretend you're okay with it. Feeling angry doesn't make you ungrateful or difficult — it makes you human. What matters is having somewhere to channel it. Some people find it helps to write it down, talk to someone, or even just name the feeling out loud. If the anger starts to feel overwhelming or constant, the hospital has psychologists and social workers who work specifically with teens. You don't have to process this alone, and you don't have to be positive all the time.
I got a red bracelet in addition to my regular one. Why?

The red bracelet is an allergy alert bracelet. It's placed on patients who have known allergies — whether to medications, foods, or environmental factors — so that every member of your care team is immediately aware. It serves as a visual, always-present reminder alongside the allergy information in your chart. Your nurse will have documented your allergies when you were admitted, and the red bracelet ensures that even someone seeing you for the first time — like a new nurse or technician — knows to check before administering anything.
How can I get around the hospital?

You can download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map, use the wayfinding kiosks on-site, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays. Information Desks are open 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby are available weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.
What infection control rules should I know about?

Key rules: wash or sanitize your hands frequently, don't visit if you're feeling unwell or have been sick in the past week, don't sit on hospital beds or chairs covered with sheets, don't use patient washrooms if you're a visitor, and don't touch supplies on the carts — ask staff instead. Some patients may require extra precautions like gowns, gloves, or masks. If you see a sign posted outside a room, check with the nurses' station before entering.
Is there a weapons detection system?

Yes, in the Emergency Departments. LHSC has a weapons detection system at ED entrances. Everyone entering the ED has to pass through it each time. It uses non-invasive technology — you walk through without stopping or removing personal items. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. If you need accommodations, speak to the security guard at the ED entrance before going through.
Can I eat food people bring me from outside?

Check with your care team first. Depending on your condition, you might be on a specific diet or restricted from certain foods. If they clear it, your family can store outside food in the family fridge — just label it with your name and date. The hospital isn't responsible for anything that goes missing from the fridge.
What time are meals served?

Breakfast is delivered between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m., and dinner between 4:45 and 5:45 p.m. If you want something between meals, the B6 inpatient unit has pantries (B6-149 and B6-231) stocked with drinks and light snacks. There are also vending machines near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors. Always check with your care team before eating, especially before tests or procedures.
What's Alex's Butterfly Garden?

It's an outdoor garden in D Zone, Level 2, created by the Hart Family in partnership with the Children's Health Foundation. It was built in honour of perinatal and infant loss and offers a tranquil environment with benches and a water fountain. It's open to children, families, and staff as a space for quiet reflection and fresh air. You can find it on MazeMap or ask for directions.
What about parking?

Parking is available 24/7 across several lots. The closest to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, a garage off Baseline Road. It's $4 for the first hour, $2 per half hour after that, with a daily max of $12 (no in-and-out). Multi-day passes are available from the parking office: 7-day for $45, 14-day for $65, or 30-day for $75. You can pay with Visa, Mastercard, or cash. The parking office is in P8, ground floor, Room 105.
I know my family can't really afford all this. It stresses me out.

Financial stress on top of health stress is a heavy burden, and it's mature of you to be aware of it. But I don't want this worry consuming your energy when you should be focused on healing. Here's what you should know: a lot of care at Children's Hospital is covered by OHIP, and there are social workers on staff whose job is specifically to help families navigate financial resources, insurance questions, and community support programs. There's also a legal support program called PBLO that offers free legal help to families. Encourage your parent to talk to a social worker — they can help far more than most people expect.
What is a care partner vs. a visitor?

A care partner is someone more directly involved in supporting your care — like a parent or primary caregiver. Inpatients can have up to two care partners at the bedside at once, while outpatients are limited to one. Care partners currently don't need to register. Visitors are friends, extended family, etc. who come to see you. All visitors must follow infection control rules and check optimal visiting times with unit staff.
I can't eat what I want. They've got me on some special diet and it's terrible.

Hospital diets can be really restrictive, and when food is one of the few comforts you have, losing that is rough. Your diet is prescribed by your doctor for a medical reason, so it's important to follow it even when it's frustrating. That said, the hospital offers a range of dietary options — including halal, kosher, vegetarian, and options for allergies — so there may be more choices than you realize. Talk to your care team or a dietitian about what you can eat. Your family can also bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit, as long as your care team approves. Hang in there.
What's Bravery Beads? Someone offered it to me but I feel like I'm too old for beads.

That's a fair reaction. Bravery Beads is a voluntary program at Children's Hospital designed for patients of all ages dealing with long-term or chronic illness or injury. Each bead represents a specific element of your care or treatment — procedures, milestones, challenges. For some patients, including teens, it becomes a tangible record of what they've been through. It's not really about the beads themselves — it's about documenting your journey. Some people find it meaningful, others don't, and both are completely valid. No pressure either way.
My mom hasn't slept properly in days. She won't leave my side.

Your awareness of your mom's wellbeing shows real maturity. Parents of hospitalized kids often push themselves to the point of exhaustion. You could try having an honest conversation: 'Mom, I'm okay here. The nurses are watching me. Please go rest.' Your care team can also encourage her. The hospital has sleeping accommodations — fold-out chairs and sleep rooms near some units — and the Ronald McDonald House nearby provides a place for families to rest. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre and a sanctuary space in Zone C for quiet reflection. Taking care of herself isn't leaving you — it's making sure she can be there for you long-term.
What are the hand hygiene rules?

Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to prevent infections in the hospital. You should clean your hands before entering a patient room, when leaving, and at the end of any visit. Alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method when hands aren't visibly soiled. If they are, use soap and water. Hand sanitizer dispensers are throughout the hospital. It applies to everyone — patients, families, staff.
What if I'm asked to participate in a research study?

Research participation is always voluntary. During your stay, a physician or research team member might ask if you'd like to join a study. All studies conducted at LHSC are reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and a Research Ethics Board. You'll receive a detailed Letter of Information about the study. Take your time, ask as many questions as you need, and review it thoroughly. Saying no will not affect your care in any way. If you have concerns, you can contact the Quality Assurance and Education Team at researchqualityandeducation@lhsc.on.ca.
What's the difference between a nurse practitioner and a nurse?

At Children's Hospital, Registered Nurses (RNs) and Registered Practical Nurses (RPNs) provide direct bedside care — monitoring your condition, administering medications, coordinating appointments, and educating you about your diagnosis. Nurse Practitioners (NPs) function more like resident doctors in terms of their scope. They partner with the medical team and work closely with attending physicians to plan and manage your care. NPs can assess patients, order tests, and adjust treatment plans. Both are critical parts of your care team, but their roles and level of clinical decision-making differ.
How does the room numbering work?

Room numbers follow the format like B2-503. The letter (B) is the zone, the number right after it (2) is the floor, and the last numbers (503) are the room itself. So B2-503 means room 503 on the 2nd floor of Zone B. It's pretty straightforward once you know the system. You can also use the MazeMap app to navigate.
Why do nurses change every 12 hours?

Nursing shifts at Children's Hospital run roughly 12 hours, with handovers at around 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (shift changes happen between 6:45 and 7:30 a.m./p.m.). This structure ensures nurses are alert and performing at their best — patient safety research shows that fatigue increases the risk of errors. The trade-off is continuity, which is why the bedside shift report is so important. It ensures all your information transfers accurately between nurses.
What does 'therapeutic' mean when they talk about therapeutic clowns or therapy dogs?

In a medical context, 'therapeutic' means it's intentionally designed to promote healing, comfort, or wellbeing. A therapeutic clown like Ollie isn't just entertaining — they're trained to normalize the hospital experience, reduce anxiety, and give kids a sense of play and normalcy. Therapy dogs are certified animals whose visits are structured to improve a patient's emotional state and support rehabilitation. It's the difference between something that's fun and something that's been specifically designed and studied for its health benefits.
How does a nasogastric (NG) tube work?

A nasogastric tube is a thin, flexible tube that's inserted through your nose, down the back of your throat, and into your stomach. It's used to deliver nutrition, fluids, or medication when you're unable to eat by mouth, or to remove stomach contents. The insertion can be uncomfortable — you'll feel a sensation in the back of your throat and may have a gag reflex. Once it's in place, the discomfort typically settles. The tube is secured with tape on your nose. Swallowing may feel slightly different with it in. If the tube causes ongoing pain or falls out, tell your nurse. Removal is usually quick and takes just a few seconds.
What's the point of a blood pressure reading?

Blood pressure measures the force your blood exerts against your arterial walls. The two numbers you see — systolic (the higher one) and diastolic (the lower one) — represent the pressure when your heart contracts and when it relaxes between beats, respectively. Monitoring it helps your team detect things like dehydration, blood loss, infection response, or cardiac issues. In a hospital setting, it's checked frequently because changes can be an early warning sign that something needs attention.
What's the difference between an X-ray, CT scan, MRI, and ultrasound?

They all image the inside of your body but use different technology. X-rays use ionizing radiation and are best for bones and detecting fluid in lungs — quick and simple. CT scans also use X-rays but take cross-sectional slices, giving much more detail for soft tissue, organs, and blood vessels. MRIs use magnetic fields and radio waves — no radiation — and excel at soft tissue detail like the brain, spinal cord, and joints. Ultrasound uses sound waves and is great for real-time imaging, like watching blood flow or examining organs. Each has trade-offs in terms of detail, time, cost, and radiation exposure.
What does an ultrasound feel like?

An ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to create real-time images of internal organs and structures. A technician applies warm gel to your skin over the area being examined, then moves a handheld probe (called a transducer) across the gel. The probe sends sound waves into your body that bounce back to create images on a screen. You won't feel the sound waves — just the pressure of the probe and the slipperiness of the gel. It's completely painless and doesn't involve any radiation. The gel gets wiped off afterward. Depending on the area, you may be asked to fast or drink extra water beforehand to improve image quality.
How does the hospital protect patient privacy in shared rooms?

Privacy curtains between beds can be drawn at any time. Staff are trained to protect confidentiality — they won't discuss your medical details where other patients can overhear. Your health information is only shared with your parents or legal guardians. Visiting can be restricted to protect the privacy of other patients. If you're uncomfortable with anything privacy-related in a shared room, raise it with your nurse — they can take steps to address it, or you can contact the privacy office at 519-685-8500 ext. 32996.
What's the deal with the smoke-free policy?

LHSC is completely smoke-free in compliance with the Smoke-Free Ontario Act. That means all buildings, all grounds, and all parking lots — including smoking inside cars on hospital property. The policy covers cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, pipes, and any other substance that can be smoked, including marijuana. The one exception is the traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous peoples for cultural or spiritual purposes — there's a designated space for that.
Are my parents going to get a huge bill for this?

Most medical care at Children's Hospital is covered by OHIP, which means there's no bill for the core medical services. However, some things — like certain supplies, devices, or medications — may have costs that aren't fully covered. The Business Office in Zone D handles billing questions, and a social worker can help your family understand what's covered and what financial support programs might be available. There's also the PBLO legal service that helps low-income families navigate these issues. Don't carry this financial worry yourself. Encourage your parent to talk to a social worker, and let your focus stay on getting better.
Sometimes I think about whether things will ever go back to normal.

That question sits with a lot of patients, especially during a long stay or a significant health event. 'Normal' might look a little different when you come out the other side — and that's okay. Some changes might actually surprise you in good ways. You might discover strength you didn't know you had, or shift what you value. And a lot of things WILL go back to how they were — friendships, interests, goals. The core of who you are isn't going anywhere. If this question is keeping you up at night, it's worth exploring with a counsellor. Not because the answer is bad, but because having someone help you think through it can make it feel less heavy.
What does the PCCU team look like and who will I see there?

The Paediatric Critical Care Unit (PCCU) is staffed by a specialized team trained to care for the most critically ill or injured children. You'll see intensivists (doctors who specialize in critical care), critical care nurses who provide very close monitoring, respiratory therapists, and potentially other specialists depending on your condition. The nurse-to-patient ratio is typically much lower than on a general unit, meaning your nurse is focused on fewer patients. Two family sleep spaces are available at the bedside, plus a quiet room and a sleep room nearby. The team communicates closely with families about what's happening, and you should feel empowered to ask questions.
What are the visiting hours and rules?

Visiting at Children's Hospital is flexible and based on each patient's condition and care needs, so there aren't rigid universal hours. However, there are some consistent guidelines. You're allowed up to two care partners at the bedside at one time for inpatients, or one for outpatient visits. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., anyone staying with you should remain in your room and let unit staff know when they arrive and leave. All visitors should wash their hands or use hand sanitizer before and after visiting, and anyone who's been sick in the past week should stay home. Specific units may have additional restrictions, so check with staff on your unit for the details.
I had so many plans. Now I don't know what's going to happen.

Having your plans disrupted by something beyond your control is deeply unsettling. You've invested in a vision of your future, and now there's uncertainty. That grief for the life you had mapped out is valid. But uncertainty doesn't mean your plans are gone — they might just need to be adjusted or delayed. Once you have more clarity on your health, you can start rebuilding. For now, try to focus on what you can control today. If the uncertainty is paralyzing you, talk to someone about it — a counsellor, social worker, or trusted adult. Planning can resume. Right now, just get through today.
What is the Transitions in Care team?

The Transitions in Care team supports paediatric patients and families through key transition points. The two big ones are: transitioning from paediatric to adult care as you age out of Children's Hospital services, and transitioning between school and hospital. These shifts can be complicated — new providers, different systems, and a lot of unknowns. The team helps coordinate and smooth out these processes so you're not navigating them alone. Ask your care team if you'd like to connect with them.
Can I stream Netflix or Disney+ here?

Yes. The hospital's patient entertainment site lets you log in to your own streaming accounts. You can also watch live Rogers TV for free. The hospital has WiFi, so as long as you have your login credentials, you should be able to stream content on your phone, tablet, or a laptop available through Child Life Services.
Where's the closest coffee or food I can buy?

'On the Go featuring Tim Hortons' is right on the second floor of Zone B in the main atrium. It's open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. but closed on weekends and holidays. Vending machines with snacks and drinks are near the elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors of Zone B, and there are ATMs there too. A full list of on-site food options is on the LHSC website.
Why do they need to take my blood so often?

Blood tests give your care team a snapshot of what's happening inside your body — things like blood cell counts, electrolyte levels, organ function markers, and inflammation indicators. If your condition is changing or you're on certain medications, they need to monitor these values regularly to adjust your treatment plan. Each draw is usually a small amount, and it's tracked carefully. If the frequency is bothering you, it's worth asking your team to explain exactly why each one is needed.
What is music therapy like?

Music therapy at Children's Hospital is provided by an accredited music therapist who uses music-based activities to support your health and wellbeing. Sessions are tailored to your needs and can focus on pain management, relaxation, emotional expression, or rehabilitation. You don't need any musical ability to participate. Activities might include listening, singing, playing simple instruments, songwriting, or guided imagery with music. Research supports music therapy's effectiveness for pain reduction and anxiety management. It's available regardless of your age, diagnosis, or disability. To access it, ask your care team.
What accessibility features does the hospital have?

LHSC is committed to accessibility under the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA). The hospital has drop-off points at main entrances, wheelchairs available inside entrances, accessible parking throughout, amplified phones for hearing-impaired patients, relay services, sign language interpretation, and free interpretation services for spoken languages. Entrance points are wheelchair-accessible, and you can request documents in alternative formats. If you need specific accommodations, tell your care team — they're required to work with you to find a solution.
What accessibility accommodations are available?

LHSC is committed to accessibility under the AODA and Ontario Human Rights Code. Most hospital zones have vehicle drop-off points at main doors. Wheelchairs are available inside entrances, or staff can assist in locating one. For deaf, deafened, or hard-of-hearing patients, amplified phones, relay services, sign language interpretation, and deaf-blind translation are all available — just notify staff. The hospital provides documents in accessible formats on request. Free interpretation services cover both spoken languages and sign language. Accessible parking is available throughout visitor lots and garages. If you have specific access needs, communicate them early to your care team.
I feel like nobody on my care team actually listens to me.

Feeling unheard by the people responsible for your care is really frustrating, and you shouldn't have to accept it. You have the right to be listened to and included in decisions about your own health. Here are some things you can try: ask to speak directly with your attending physician, not just the residents. Write down your concerns so you don't forget them in the moment. You can also ask your parent to advocate alongside you. If things don't improve, the Patient Relations office is available to help — you can reach them at extension 52036. Your experience of your own body matters, and good medical care includes hearing the patient.
Why is there security at the hospital?

Security exists to keep everyone — patients, families, and staff — safe. They patrol the building, manage after-hours access (the B Tower entrance locks at 8:30 p.m. and is controlled by security after that), respond to emergencies, and can escort you to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House if needed. You can reach security dispatch at extension 52281. The emergency response extension is 55555. They're a resource, not something to be worried about.
I hate how I look right now. The hospital gown, the IV, everything.

Feeling uncomfortable with how you look in this context is really valid. Hospital gowns aren't exactly designed for self-expression. When you're not in an active procedure, you can absolutely wear your own clothes — ask your nurse when that's okay. Having your own comfy hoodie or pyjamas can make a surprising difference to how you feel. The IV and medical equipment are temporary tools, not part of who you are. If body image is something that weighs on you beyond just the hospital aesthetic, there are psychologists and social workers here you can talk to confidentially. You don't have to tough it out alone.
I know I should be grateful I'm getting help, but I mostly just feel angry and sad.

Gratitude and pain aren't mutually exclusive. You can appreciate the care you're receiving and still be angry about needing it. You can be thankful for your nurses and still hate being in the hospital. Those aren't contradictions — they're the full, honest range of human emotion. Nobody benefits from you suppressing the hard feelings in favour of performed gratitude. Feel what you feel. The staff here don't need you to be grateful — they need you to be honest so they can actually help you. And when you're ready, it's okay to hold both the anger and the appreciation at the same time. That's not confusing — that's real.
What is the weapons detection system in the Emergency Department?

When you enter the Emergency Department at Children's Hospital, you'll pass through a weapons detection system. It uses advanced, non-invasive technology — you just walk through without stopping or emptying your pockets. It's designed to maintain a safe environment for everyone. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. If you need specific accommodations, you can speak to the security guard at the ED entrance before going through. The system scans everyone, including minors accompanied by a parent or guardian.
Why do they measure my urine output?

Urine output is a straightforward but important clinical indicator. It tells your care team a lot about your kidney function, hydration status, and how your body is processing fluids and medications. If output drops below expected levels, it can signal dehydration, kidney stress, or fluid retention. If it increases significantly, that could indicate a response to diuretics or other changes. It's one of those simple measurements that gives your team a real-time window into how your body is functioning.
What is the Indigenous Healing Space?

The Indigenous Healing Space is located in room E1-204 and is open to all, with priority given to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous Peoples seeking care at LHSC and their families. It provides a culturally safe space for healing practices. There's also a Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant at Children's Hospital who supports mental health and cultural wellness for Indigenous kids, bridging traditional ways of knowing with Western approaches to care. To learn more about accessing the space or connecting with the consultant, speak with your care team.
Can I have a say in my own care? It feels like everything is decided for me.

You absolutely can and should have a say. Children's Hospital sees families — including you — as partners in care. You're encouraged to ask questions, request explanations of any treatments, tests, or medications, and express your preferences. The Shared Decision Making program at LHSC exists specifically to ensure patients and caregivers collaborate with health-care providers on important choices. If you feel like your voice isn't being heard, tell your nurse, ask to speak with a social worker, or contact Patient Relations. Being a teenager in a hospital doesn't mean you lose your agency.
They said recovery will take months. I don't know how I'm going to do this.

A months-long recovery feels like an impossible stretch when you're standing at the beginning of it. But you don't have to do all those months today. You only have to do today. Then tomorrow. Recovery isn't a straight line — there will be setbacks and breakthroughs, and the early days are usually the hardest. As time goes on, you'll develop a routine and start seeing progress that motivates you. Your care team will be with you for this, including physiotherapists, psychologists, and social workers. Lean on your support system. You've already handled things you didn't think you could. This is no different.
There's someone in the lounge who said they volunteer here. Why do people volunteer at a hospital?

People volunteer at Children's Hospital for a range of reasons — some are students gaining health-care experience, others are community members who want to give back, and some are former patients or family members who want to support others going through what they went through. Volunteers help at information desks, guide stations, playrooms, and special events. They're at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. They're not part of your medical team, but they contribute to the overall experience by providing guidance, companionship, and support. It takes real commitment to volunteer your time in a hospital setting.
What are visiting hours at Children's Hospital?

There aren't strict hospital-wide visiting hours. Visiting times are based on the individual patient's condition, care needs, and wishes, so they can vary between patients and units. Check with the unit staff about the best times. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., family members should stay in the patient's room and let staff know when they're coming and going.
What is a Child Life Specialist and how can they help me as a teen?

Child Life Specialists are trained professionals who focus on helping patients cope with the psychological and emotional aspects of hospitalization. They're not just for little kids. For teens, they can help prepare you for procedures by explaining exactly what will happen and what you'll feel, teach coping and relaxation strategies, provide distraction during uncomfortable procedures, and advocate for your needs with the medical team. They can also connect you with resources like Upopolis, art therapy, or music therapy. If you're anxious about a procedure or just need someone to talk to who isn't a doctor, ask for a Child Life Specialist.
Someone mentioned a psychologist vs a social worker. What's the difference?

Both support your mental and emotional well-being, but their training and focus differ. Psychologists at Children's Hospital have specialized graduate-level training in clinical psychology. They do formal assessments — like evaluating your thinking and learning skills if a medical condition affects them — and provide structured therapeutic interventions like cognitive-behavioural therapy. Social workers focus more broadly on connecting you and your family with support systems, advocacy, financial resources, discharge planning, and community services. Think of the psychologist as more clinically focused on your mental health, while the social worker addresses the wider picture of how your family navigates the system.
What's the deal with the therapy dogs? How does that actually work?

Children's Hospital partners with St. John Ambulance to run a therapy dog program on several units. The dogs are specifically trained and certified for hospital environments — they're calm, gentle, and screened for health and temperament. Visits are scheduled by the program and the care team, and a trained handler always accompanies the dog. There's research showing that interaction with therapy animals can reduce stress, lower blood pressure, and improve mood. Family pets aren't allowed for infection control reasons, but these therapy dogs go through a rigorous vetting process. Ask your care team if a visit is coming up on your unit.
What happens to my school work while I'm in hospital?

The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital supports patients moving between school and hospital. They can help coordinate with your school so you don't fall behind. Before discharge, you or your family should talk to your teachers and possibly the principal about homework assignments and accommodations for your return. Your social worker can also help with communication. If your stay is long, ask your care team about educational support options — the goal is to make the transition back to school as smooth as possible.
What is the fragrance-free policy?

LHSC maintains a fragrance-free environment across all its facilities. This means patients, visitors, and staff are asked not to use or bring any scented products — perfume, cologne, body spray, scented lotions, or other fragranced items. The reason is medical: fragrances can trigger allergic reactions, migraines, and respiratory distress in sensitive individuals, including immunocompromised patients. Use unscented versions of personal care products during your stay and remind anyone who plans to visit to do the same.
Why do they keep asking me to confirm my name and birthday?

It's a standardized patient safety protocol. Before any medication, test, or procedure, staff verify your identity by checking your name and date of birth against your armband. It might feel repetitive, but it's one of the most effective ways to prevent medical errors. If something ever seems off — like a wrong name or medication — speak up. They want you to.
Can I leave my room and walk around?

That depends on your care plan. Some patients are free to move around the unit or visit common areas like the activity rooms or the family lounge (Culliton Family Lounge, B6-110). Others may have restrictions depending on their condition, IV lines, or infection control precautions. Always check with your nurse first. If you have an IV, you can usually bring the pole with you — it's on wheels. If you want to visit areas outside your unit, you'll definitely need to clear it with your team.
I'm waiting for test results and I'm terrified of what they'll say.

Waiting for results is its own kind of torture — the uncertainty is often worse than the answer. Your brain is probably running through every worst-case scenario right now, and that's a normal stress response, not a prediction. Whatever the results show, your medical team will have a plan. You won't be left alone with bad news and no direction. If you're spiraling, try a grounding technique: name five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch. It won't erase the anxiety, but it can turn the volume down. And when the results come, make sure you ask every question you have. You deserve full information.
My parents are missing work and spending money on parking because of me. I feel terrible.

That guilt is a sign of how empathetic you are, but I want you to hear this clearly: you are not a burden. Your parents are here because you matter more to them than work schedules or parking fees. That said, there are things that might ease your mind — the hospital has parking passes that can reduce costs, and there are social workers on staff who can help families navigate financial resources. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre can help with that too. If this guilt is weighing on you, it might help to actually talk to your parents about it. They'd probably want to know how you're feeling.
What does the Patient Relations Office actually do?

The Patient Relations Office at LHSC is the formal channel for questions, concerns, and feedback about care experiences. Their Patient Relations Specialists serve as a neutral point of contact between you and the hospital. They're reachable at extension 52036 or 58230, by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, or through an online contact form on the LHSC website. They check messages between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. on weekdays. They recommend starting with your care team first if you have a concern, but if that doesn't resolve things, they're the next step. You also have the option of submitting feedback in French.
Can I leave the unit during my stay?

That depends on your condition and care plan. Always check with your nurse before leaving the unit. If you're on infection precautions, you may need to stay in your room. On the B6 inpatient unit, which is locked, you'll need your confidential code to re-enter. Let your care team know whenever you leave so they know where you are.
What happens if my condition worsens while I'm at the hospital?

If your condition deteriorates, your care team will escalate your level of care accordingly. This might mean more frequent monitoring, additional tests, changes in medication, or transfer to a higher-acuity unit like the PCCU. In urgent situations, rapid response protocols kick in — a team with specialized skills will come to your bedside quickly. As a patient, the most important thing you can do is speak up immediately if something feels wrong — sudden changes in pain level, difficulty breathing, dizziness, chest tightness, or anything unusual. Don't wait for the next scheduled check. Use the call button, and trust your instincts.
What's the point of the information desk volunteers?

The information desk volunteers and guide volunteers at Children's Hospital help patients and families navigate the building — which can be pretty confusing. Information desks are open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers are stationed at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays. They can help you read room numbers (which follow a specific format like B2-503 — Zone B, Floor 2, Room 503), direct you to services, or just point you the right way. When you're stressed and in an unfamiliar building, having a friendly person who knows the layout can make a real difference.
What is the role of a resident doctor?

Residents are doctors who have completed medical school and are now doing specialized training. At Children's Hospital, they work under the supervision of an attending physician. They'll be involved in assessing your condition, contributing to your treatment plan, and providing day-to-day care. Residents may be the ones who examine you during rounds or follow up on test results. They're fully qualified physicians who are gaining additional expertise in a specific area. If a resident talks to you about your care, their recommendations have been or will be reviewed by the supervising physician.
I overheard another family getting bad news and now I can't stop thinking about it.

Overhearing something like that in a hospital is jarring, and it's natural for it to shake you. Hospitals hold both hope and heartbreak, and being surrounded by other families' journeys can affect you emotionally even when it has nothing to do with your own situation. What you heard about that family doesn't change anything about your health. If it's weighing on you, talk to someone — your nurse, a parent, or a psychologist here. Processing other people's pain while dealing with your own is a lot. Be gentle with yourself.
What's the security team's role here? They're not just standing around, right?

Definitely not. Security at Children's Hospital has a pretty significant role. They control access to the building — the main B Tower entrance locks at 8:30 p.m. and caregivers need to check in with security after hours. They operate the weapons detection system at the Emergency Department. They patrol the hospital grounds. They can escort you or your family to the parking lot or Ronald McDonald House after dark. Certain zones and floors are locked 24/7, and security manages access to those areas. If there's an emergency, the Emergency Response extension is 55555. For non-emergencies, security dispatch is at extension 52281.
I'm in pain all the time and I'm tired of telling people about it.

Pain fatigue — being tired of your own pain and tired of reporting it — is a real thing, and I'm sorry you're experiencing it. But please keep communicating with your care team about your pain levels. They can't help if they don't know, and you deserve proper pain management. The Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital means they're committed to addressing your pain with evidence-based strategies. There's also the Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care team, which specializes in exactly this. You shouldn't have to just endure it. Ask your nurse specifically about a pain management referral if what you're getting isn't working.
I'm questioning a lot of things right now — like whether any of this means anything.

Big life experiences like this have a way of shaking up what you thought you knew. Questioning meaning, purpose, and beliefs is not a crisis — it's a sign that you're thinking deeply about your experience. You don't have to have answers right now. If you'd like to explore these questions, Children's Hospital has a Spiritual Care service that works with people of all beliefs and backgrounds — including people who aren't sure what they believe. The sanctuary space on the third floor in Zone C is open 24/7 for quiet reflection. This kind of introspection can actually lead to real growth, even when it feels uncomfortable. Take your time with it.
What kind of music therapy is offered here?

An accredited music therapist at Children's Hospital uses music-based activities to support patients across all areas of health and wellbeing — that can include pain management, rehabilitation, emotional processing, and stress reduction. Sessions are tailored to you: it might involve listening, playing instruments, songwriting, or other musical activities. You don't need any musical skill or experience. Music therapy is available for patients of any age, illness, or disability. Ask your care team or a Child Life Specialist to arrange a session.
What if I want to recognize a staff member who was great?

LHSC has a Great Moments Recognition Program for exactly that. You can fill out the form on the LHSC website to recognize a staff member, physician, volunteer, learner, or patient partner who made a difference. They'll receive a letter of appreciation and a small item of recognition. If you don't remember their exact name, share as many details as you can to help identify them.
What shouldn't I bring to the hospital?

Leave these at home: latex balloons (they can trigger severe allergies), perfume or any scented products (the hospital is fragrance-free), baby walkers, small items that could be a choking hazard for younger patients, and personal electrical equipment. The hospital takes these rules seriously to protect all patients.
What's the PCCU?

PCCU stands for Paediatric Critical Care Unit. It's the intensive care unit for children — where patients who need the closest monitoring and most intensive medical intervention are treated. It has specialized equipment and a high nurse-to-patient ratio. Visiting policies there may be different from other units, and the environment is more controlled. If someone you know is in the PCCU, the unit can be reached at 519-685-8500, extension 52824.
I feel like they treat every patient the same. I'm not just a chart.

You're right — you're not just a chart, and personalized care matters. Hospital systems can feel standardized, and that can make you feel like you're on an assembly line. Speak up about your preferences, your values, your concerns. Share your interests with your care team — it helps them see you as a person. If you feel like your care lacks a personal touch, mention it to your primary nurse or a social worker. You can also share specific preferences during conversations or bedside shift changes. The best care happens when the team knows who they're caring for, not just what they're treating.
How is Children's Hospital laid out? It's confusing.

Totally understandable — it's a big building. Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site at 800 Commissioners Road East in London. Room numbers tell you exactly where you are: the first letter is the zone, the next number is the floor. So B6-261 means Zone B, floor 6, room 261. There's an app called MazeMap you can download that has a full interactive map, and you can scan QR codes near elevator bays to pull up maps too. Information desks are also staffed Monday–Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
What's an occupational therapist and how is that different from a physiotherapist?

While they overlap in some ways, occupational therapists (OTs) and physiotherapists (PTs) focus on different things. A PT works on movement, strength, and mobility — think walking, balance, and physical recovery. An OT focuses on your ability to perform daily activities — getting dressed, using your hands effectively, managing self-care tasks, and adapting to any limitations. At Children's Hospital, if your condition affects how you function in day-to-day life, an OT will work with you on strategies and tools to maximize your independence.
How does the hospital handle a patient's personal food storage?

On the B6 inpatient unit, there's a family refrigerator with a freezer in the pantry rooms (B6-149 and B6-231) for storing personal food items. All items must be labeled with your name and dated. The hospital is not responsible for food that goes missing from the fridge. In the PCCU, there's a small fridge in the waiting room for temporary storage. In the NICU, check with a healthcare provider about specific food storage locations. If you're bringing food from home, keep it organized, labeled, and within your family's designated space.
Why are visiting hours not the same on every unit?

Different units have different patient needs and care intensities. For example, the NICU and PCCU have stricter access because those patients are more vulnerable. Visiting policies are based on the condition and care needs of each patient, privacy considerations for other patients, and infection control requirements — especially during outbreaks, when only essential care partners are permitted. The flexibility is intentional so each unit can prioritize what's best for the patients on it.
What time do nurse shift changes happen?

Nursing shift changes happen twice a day, from 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. It's harder to get through to the unit by phone during these times. The bedside shift change report takes about three to five minutes, and you're welcome to be part of it.
What is a chest X-ray like?

For a chest X-ray, you'll typically stand in front of a flat panel and be asked to position yourself with your chest pressed against it. The technologist will position you, then step behind a protective screen. You'll be asked to take a deep breath and hold it for a few seconds while the image is captured — holding your breath keeps your lungs fully expanded for a clearer picture. You might hear a brief click or buzz. The whole thing takes maybe two minutes. It's painless, and the radiation exposure is minimal. If you need to stay in bed, the X-ray can sometimes be done portably right in your room.
Where is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?

It's on the 1st floor of Zone B, room B1-006. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; Tuesday and Thursday from 8:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.; and Saturday and Sunday from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. by appointment only. They offer peer support, help with forms, and information about children's health from a lived-experience perspective.
What's the deal with the smoke-free policy?

LHSC is entirely smoke-free in compliance with the Smoke-Free Ontario Act. This covers all buildings, grounds, and parking lots — including smoking inside vehicles on hospital property. The policy applies to cigarettes, e-cigarettes, cigars, pipes, and any other substance that can be smoked, including cannabis. There is one exemption: Indigenous Peoples may use tobacco for traditional, cultural, or spiritual purposes in a designated space provided by the hospital. If you're a smoker or vaper and anticipate cravings during a longer stay, talk to your care team about management strategies.
They said I need a lumbar puncture and I'm freaking out.

I understand the fear — the name alone sounds intense. It's okay to be scared. What might help is knowing what to expect: your doctor will numb the area first so you shouldn't feel the procedure itself, though you might feel pressure. You'll need to stay very still, and the care team will help you get into the right position. It's usually over in 15 to 30 minutes. Talk to your doctor or nurse about exactly what to expect step by step, and ask about any comfort measures they can provide. Preparation is the best weapon against fear. And tell them you're scared — they want to know so they can support you through it.
What services are available to help me cope emotionally?

Children's Hospital has several programs designed to support your emotional wellbeing. Child Life Specialists help with preparation for procedures and coping strategies. The Art Therapy program lets you express thoughts and feelings through creative activities. Music Therapy, led by an accredited therapist, supports areas like pain control, relaxation, and rehabilitation — no musical skill required. The Heroes' Circle teaches breathing, relaxation, and martial arts techniques. Paediatric Psychology Services offer assessment and treatment for challenges in adjusting to illness, plus coping strategies for managing symptoms. And if you want to connect with peers, Upopolis is a secure online network for patients ages 8–18. If you're struggling, let your care team know — they can connect you with the right support.
How does the hospital handle pain management for teens?

Children's Hospital follows the Comfort Promise, which is their commitment to evidence-based pain and anxiety management. For needle procedures, that includes topical anaesthetics, comfort positioning (upright and supportive, not restraining), and distraction techniques. Beyond needles, your care team assesses and manages pain as part of your overall care plan. You should always communicate openly about your pain levels — there's no benefit to toughing it out, and untreated pain can actually slow recovery. Ask your team about what options are available for your specific situation.
What are the afterhours entrance procedures?

The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily. After hours, entry is controlled by Security. Care partners will need to check in with the security guard to gain access. The parking garage entrance remains open 24 hours, but you'll still need to check in with Security after hours. Zone D Level 2 and 3 entrances are locked from 8:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m., and Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked 24/7. If you're arriving late, plan to enter through the garage or the B Tower entrance where a security guard will be posted.
How does the hospital handle allergies?

If you have allergies, you'll be given a red allergy bracelet so every member of your care team can see it immediately. Your allergies will also be documented in your medical record. The food services team can accommodate allergy-specific diets — including priority allergens like eggs, milk, mustard, nuts, and more. The nursing staff and pharmacists check for drug allergies before administering any medication. If you develop a new allergy or sensitivity during your stay, tell your nurse right away.
What is a CT scan like?

A CT scan uses X-ray technology to create cross-sectional images of your body. You lie flat on a motorized table that slides through a large, donut-shaped ring. The ring rotates around you while capturing images — you won't feel anything from the scan itself. You'll need to stay still, and you might be asked to briefly hold your breath. In some cases, you may receive contrast dye through an IV, which can cause a warm or flushed feeling and a metallic taste — that's temporary and normal. The whole process is usually quick, often under 15 minutes. The detailed images help your care team assess internal structures that standard X-rays can't capture as clearly.
I'm terrified of going under anaesthesia. What if something goes wrong?

Fear of anaesthesia is extremely common, and the fact that you're thinking about it means you're processing things — that's healthy. Here's what might help: the anaesthesiologist is a specialist whose entire job is keeping you safe while you're asleep. They monitor your heart, breathing, oxygen, and blood pressure the entire time. Modern anaesthesia is very safe. Before the procedure, you'll meet the anaesthesia team, and you can ask every question you have. Children's Hospital also offers the PPI program, which may allow a parent to be with you during induction. Talk to your care team about your fear — they've supported thousands of patients through this and they can help calm your specific worries.
What can I expect about my emotional response to hospitalization?

Being hospitalized as a teenager can bring up a range of emotions — anxiety, frustration, boredom, sadness, anger, or feeling like you've lost control over your life. All of these are normal responses to an abnormal situation. The loss of your regular routine, separation from friends, and dealing with pain or uncertainty can compound the emotional load. Children's Hospital has resources to help: Child Life Specialists, Psychology Services, Social Work, Art Therapy, Music Therapy, and Spiritual Care. If you're feeling overwhelmed, talk to someone — your nurse, a social worker, or a trusted family member. You don't have to manage it alone, and asking for help is a sign of strength.
I'm worried about getting addicted to the pain medication they're giving me.

That's a really thoughtful and mature concern. Addiction risk is something your care team takes seriously, and they monitor medication use carefully. Pain medication given in a supervised hospital setting for acute pain is very different from unsupervised use. If you have concerns, talk directly with your doctor or the pharmacist. They can explain what you're taking, how long you'll be on it, and what the transition plan looks like. You should never be in unnecessary pain because of fear of addiction, and you should never have unnecessary medication either. Your care team will work with you to find the right balance. Always speak up about your concerns.
What's the purpose of the weapons detection system at the ER?

LHSC has introduced a weapons detection system at their Emergency Department entrances as a security measure. Everyone entering the ED walks through it — including children, who are scanned with their parent or guardian present. The technology is non-invasive, meaning you don't have to stop, empty your pockets, or remove anything. If the system flags something, a trained security guard will check. There are accommodations available if you need them — just speak with the security guard at the entrance.
What is the Gender Pathways Service?

The Gender Pathways Service (GPS) at Children's Hospital provides gender-affirming care to gender diverse and transgender youth aged 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service that follows North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH). The service offers access to several specialties. If you'd like to learn more or access the service, you can contact them at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team to connect you.
What's the emergency response team?

The emergency response team, sometimes called a code team or rapid response team, is a group of highly trained health-care professionals who respond to medical emergencies within the hospital. If a patient's condition deteriorates rapidly, staff can activate the emergency response using extension 55555. The team typically includes physicians, nurses, and respiratory therapists who arrive quickly to stabilize the patient. You might hear overhead announcements or see rapid movement in the halls — that's the system working as designed. Security dispatch at extension 52281 handles non-medical emergencies.
What does the pharmacist do beyond just filling prescriptions?

At Children's Hospital, pharmacists are medication specialists who do a lot more than fill bottles. They review all your medications — prescription, over-the-counter, herbal, vitamins, creams, inhalers, everything — to check for interactions and appropriate dosing. They consult with your care team on medication choices. If you're on multiple medications, a pharmacist can prepare a medication calendar and review it with you and your family before discharge. They're available to answer questions about side effects, timing, and drug interactions. The pharmacy is located at B1-001, open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. You can ask your nurse to have a pharmacist come to your room anytime.
Will the hospital help me transition back to school?

Yes. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital specifically supports key transition milestones, including moving from hospital back to school. They can help you and your family communicate with your school about any accommodations or modifications you might need. Your social worker can also help coordinate this. It's a good idea to talk with your care team about school re-entry early so everything is in place before discharge.
My sister gets to live a normal life while I'm here. It's not fair.

That resentment is a natural response to an unfair situation. It doesn't make you a bad sibling. Watching someone your age live freely while you're confined to a hospital bed is painful in a way that's hard to articulate. Your feelings are valid. At the same time, your sister might be dealing with her own complicated feelings — worry, guilt, or helplessness. Illness affects the whole family differently. If this resentment is building up, talking to a psychologist or social worker can help you work through it without it damaging your relationship. You're allowed to feel what you feel.
How do I get an interpreter?

Ask your care team. LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients, including spoken languages and sign language. If you're more comfortable communicating in a language other than English, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, they'll arrange the right support. A downloadable list of available spoken languages is on the LHSC website.
I'm having surgery tomorrow and I can't stop thinking about it.

Pre-surgery anxiety is one of the most common things hospital staff see, and there's no shame in it. Here's what might help: Children's Hospital has a Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program, which means a parent might be able to be with you in the operating room until you're asleep. Before surgery, the anaesthesia team will explain exactly what's going to happen. You'll be asleep the whole time, you won't feel anything, and a team of specialists monitors you every second. If the anxiety is really intense, talk to your care team — there are things they can offer to help you feel calmer. Write down your questions so you don't forget them. Knowledge is usually the best antidote to fear.
What arts and therapeutic programs are available?

Quite a few. Art Therapy lets you express thoughts and feelings through creative activities. Music Therapy is provided by an accredited music therapist — no musical skill needed. The Heroes' Circle is a weekly program involving breathing techniques, relaxation, and martial arts. Ollie the therapeutic clown visits to bring play and laughter. And the Bravery Beads program lets you document your journey with beads representing each element of your care.
What's the B6 inpatient unit like and who works there?

The B6 inpatient unit houses paediatric patients on the sixth floor of Zone B. It's a locked unit — your family gets a confidential code upon admission. The team includes nurses (RNs and RPNs), physicians, residents, Child Life Specialists, social workers, and other allied health professionals. There are two sections — B6-100 and B6-200 — each with their own contact number. The unit has pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks, a family fridge, the Culliton Family Lounge in B6-110, Ashley's Backyard playroom in B6-259, quiet rooms, the SMILE Room in B6-261, and the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065. One overnight sleep space is provided for a family member.
What do I need to know about going home?

Before discharge, your care team will review everything — medications, care instructions, diet, follow-up appointments. Make sure you understand dosages, side effects, and who to call if something goes wrong. Have your ride arranged in advance and bring a car seat if required by law. If you need home care equipment, it has to be assessed by an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator before you leave. Ask for written instructions so you have everything in hand.
What happens in the Emergency Department if I need to stay overnight?

There aren't dedicated sleeping accommodations in the Paediatric Emergency Department. One caregiver should stay with you at all times. Staff will do their best to provide a reclining or fold-out chair, plus pillows and blankets, so you can rest as comfortably as possible. If you end up being admitted, you'll be moved to an inpatient unit with better overnight facilities.
Who's the attending physician and what's the hierarchy on my care team?

The attending physician is the senior doctor who oversees your care. They're ultimately responsible for all clinical decisions. Below them in the training hierarchy are residents — fully graduated medical school doctors doing specialty training — and then medical students, who are still in medical school and participate in care under supervision. Nurse practitioners also partner with the medical team and function similarly to residents in terms of care planning. Your attending leads this team, communicates the care plan to your family, and supervises everyone else's work.
Where are the information desks?

Information Desks are staffed from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Monday through Friday, and noon to 4:00 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday. Guide volunteers are at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. You can also call the hospital operator at 519-685-8500 and press 0.
Why is there a Paediatric Emergency Department separate from the adult one?

Children aren't just small adults — paediatric medicine involves different physiology, different common conditions, different medication dosing, and different communication approaches. A separate paediatric ED means the staff are specifically trained in treating children and teens, the equipment is sized appropriately, and the environment is designed to be less intimidating for younger patients. It also means the care protocols are paediatric-specific, which leads to better outcomes.
Who has access to my medical information?

Your personal health information (PHI) can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). At LHSC, you have the right to consent to or refuse the collection, use, and disclosure of your health information, to access your records, to request corrections, to know who's seen your records, and to be notified if your information is accessed inappropriately. If you have concerns about your privacy, the hospital's privacy office can be reached at 519-685-8500 extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.
What does an X-ray involve?

An X-ray is a quick imaging test that uses a small amount of radiation to produce images of internal structures, most commonly bones. You'll be positioned by a radiologic technologist — standing, sitting, or lying down depending on what's being imaged. A lead apron may be placed over parts of your body that don't need to be scanned to minimize radiation exposure. The machine makes a brief click or buzzing sound when the image is captured. The entire process is usually done in minutes. It's painless, though holding a specific position can be mildly uncomfortable if you're injured. X-ray results typically get reviewed by your care team quickly.
What does the hospital smell like and why?

Hospitals have a distinctive smell that mostly comes from cleaning agents and alcohol-based hand sanitizer used to maintain sterile environments. You might also pick up the scent of medical supplies and adhesives. LHSC is a fragrance-free facility, which means staff, patients, and visitors are asked not to wear perfume, cologne, or scented products — this is to prevent allergic reactions and respiratory issues for sensitive patients. So the overall scent profile is clinical rather than pleasant, but it's a sign that infection control is being taken seriously.
I have exams coming up and I'm stuck here. I'm going to fail everything.

Academic pressure on top of a hospital stay is incredibly stressful, and I hear you. But your school is required to work with you when you're dealing with a medical situation — that means accommodations, extensions, and alternative testing arrangements. Your parents can contact your school to explain the situation, and the hospital has people who can help coordinate that transition. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital actually supports students moving between school and hospital. Your health has to come first right now, and no exam is more important than that. You won't fail because of a medical situation — there are systems in place to protect you.
I don't see the point anymore. Everything just keeps getting worse.

I hear you, and I want you to know that feeling this way is a signal that you need more support, not that things are truly hopeless. When you're dealing with a lot of pain, frustration, or a long hospital stay, it can narrow your view until it feels like nothing will get better. That feeling is real, but it's not the whole picture. Please talk to someone you trust — your parent, your nurse, or a social worker. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychologists who are trained to help with exactly these kinds of feelings. You don't have to carry this alone, and reaching out isn't weakness. It's the strongest thing you can do right now.
Why would my nurse ask me questions when my parents aren't in the room?

It's standard practice for health-care providers to have some one-on-one time with adolescent patients.
