This gives you a safe space to ask questions, share concerns, or discuss things you might not feel comfortable bringing up in front of your parents. It could be about your health, your emotional state, or anything else. It's not about excluding your parents — it's about respecting your developing autonomy and giving you room to be honest. Whatever you discuss is treated with appropriate confidentiality.
How can I participate in research?

During your stay, your physician or a research team member may discuss studies with you. All clinical research at LHSC is reviewed and approved by the Research Ethics Board. Participation is always voluntary — declining won't affect your care. If you're interested, ask your care team about clinical trials or studies that might be a fit. Take your time to read the Letter of Information and ask questions before committing.
I just got my license and now I can't even walk to the bathroom on my own.

That contrast between the freedom you just gained and the restrictions you're now facing is genuinely jarring. Going from driving a car to needing help getting to the bathroom is a huge shift, and your frustration is completely warranted. But this is temporary. Your body is in a healing phase, and the limitations you're experiencing now aren't permanent. Physical therapists and occupational therapists here are specifically focused on getting you back to independence as quickly and safely as possible. Think of this as your body's pit stop — necessary maintenance before you're back on the road. Your license will be there when you're ready.
Where is the Ronald McDonald House?

The Ronald McDonald House is available for families who live outside London. Ask your care team about eligibility and availability. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room within the hospital — you can reach them at 519-685-8500, extension 56896. If you need an escort to the Ronald McDonald House, Security can help — call extension 52281.
How does the hospital protect my privacy?

At LHSC, your health information can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have specific rights regarding your personal health information, including the right to consent to or refuse how it's collected, used, and disclosed, the right to access it, and the right to be notified if it's accessed inappropriately. During your stay, your family might consider designating one contact person who can relay updates to extended family, so the care team isn't sharing information repeatedly. If you want to call the unit to check on something, provide the patient's full name and ask for their nurse. Just be aware that calls during nursing shift changes (6:45–7:30 a.m. and 6:45–7:30 p.m.) may be harder to get through.
What should I expect the operating room to look like?

The OR is a brightly lit, temperature-controlled room designed for sterile procedures. You'll see an operating table in the centre, large overhead surgical lights, and various monitors and screens. Equipment and instruments are arranged on trays nearby. The team will be wearing full surgical attire — scrubs, caps, masks, and sterile gloves. The anaesthesiologist and their equipment will be near the head of the table. It can look intimidating because of all the technology, but every piece of equipment has a specific function in keeping you safe during the procedure. If you're anxious about what you'll see, ask for a pre-op tour through the PPI program or talk to a Child Life Specialist beforehand.
Is the person taking X-rays the same as my doctor?

No — that's typically a medical imaging technologist or radiologic technologist. They're specifically trained to operate diagnostic imaging equipment like X-ray machines, CT scanners, and other imaging technology. They capture the images, which are then reviewed and interpreted by a radiologist (a physician who specializes in reading medical images). Your attending physician receives the results and incorporates them into your care plan. The technologist is focused on getting clear, accurate images while keeping your radiation exposure as low as possible.
Why do some medications come through an IV instead of as a pill?

Several reasons. Some medications are broken down by stomach acid and would lose their effectiveness if swallowed. IV delivery also gets medication into your bloodstream immediately, which matters when timing is critical. Dosing can be more precisely controlled through an IV infusion. Some patients can't take anything by mouth — they might be nil by mouth before a procedure, nauseous, or unconscious. And certain medications are too irritating to the GI tract. Your care team chooses the delivery method based on what's most effective and safe for your specific situation.
Why did a nurse ask my parent to leave the room briefly?

There are a few reasons this might happen. Sometimes it's to provide care that requires clinical focus and space. Other times, it could be during mandatory safety checks or a procedure. In some cases, your care team may want to talk to you privately — this is standard practice with adolescent patients to give you the opportunity to share concerns or ask questions you might not feel comfortable raising in front of a parent. It's not unusual and it's not a sign of anything being wrong. Your parent is always welcome to come back right after.
I hate walking through the hospital with my IV pole. Everyone looks at me.

Feeling exposed while moving through public areas with medical equipment is understandable. But here's the truth: in a hospital, IV poles are as common as backpacks in a school hallway. You're not the only one walking around with one, and most people who notice aren't thinking anything negative. If it makes you feel better, you can ask your nurse about the best times to move around when hallways are quieter. You can also personalize your IV pole a bit — some patients name theirs or decorate them. But fundamentally, there's nothing to be ashamed of. You're getting treatment. That's strength, not weakness.
Why is this hospital a teaching hospital?

Children's Hospital is part of London Health Sciences Centre, which is one of Canada's largest teaching hospitals affiliated with Western University's medical school. That means medical students, residents, and fellows train here alongside experienced physicians. Research also happens here — the Children's Health Research Institute is dedicated to advancing paediatric health science. For you as a patient, this means you'll likely encounter learners during your care. They're always supervised, and the teaching environment often means access to the latest evidence-based practices.
Can I have a say in my own care?

Absolutely. Children's Hospital sees families — and that includes you — as partners in care. You're encouraged to ask questions, request explanations of any tests or treatments, understand the risks and benefits, and express your preferences. There's even a formal process called Shared Decision Making where patients work with care teams and a Decision Coach to make informed choices. You're also invited to participate in bedside shift change reports where nurses review your care plan. Don't hesitate to speak up — your voice matters.
Can my friends visit me?

Yes. The general visitor policy allows up to two care partners at the bedside at one time for inpatients. Visiting is flexible and varies by unit and patient condition, so check with your unit's staff about optimal times. Visitors need to practice hand hygiene before and after visiting, and shouldn't come if they've been sick in the last week. Overnight visitors (between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m.) are asked to stay in the patient's room and notify unit staff when arriving and leaving.
Who is the social worker and why do they want to talk to me?

Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical help to both patients and families. They might want to talk to you for a number of reasons — to see how you're coping emotionally, to help with family communication, to assist with discharge planning, or to connect you with community resources. They can also help with things like financial support, navigating insurance, and school transitions. It's not because something is wrong — it's a standard part of holistic care. Whatever you share with them is treated with confidentiality and respect.
What's the Culliton Family Lounge?

The Culliton Family Lounge is at B6-110 on the inpatient unit. It's a shared space where patients can hang out, relax, and socialize with family or friends outside of their room. It's also used for group events and family coffee hours.
What if there's an emergency on the unit?

For any emergency in the hospital, the extension to call is 55555. Security can be reached at extension 52281 for non-emergency safety concerns. If something feels wrong or unsafe during your stay, speak up to your nurse or any staff member immediately.
Can I talk to someone about the cost of my care?

The Business Office at Victoria Hospital, located in Zone D, third floor, room D3-400, handles billing questions. While most care is covered by OHIP, there may be charges for certain supplies or devices — crutches, surgical supplies, breast pumps, and similar items. You'll receive an invoice by mail, and payment can be made at the bank, by cheque, or online by credit card with a small convenience fee. A social worker can also help if your family is facing financial strain — they're trained to connect families with financial resources and community support programs.
Is there WiFi?

Yes, the hospital has WiFi available for patients. You can connect your phone, tablet, or laptop. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming services. If you need help with WiFi, you can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958.
I'm bored out of my mind. What is there to do?

I get it — hospital stays can drag. Here's what's available: the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) has board games, puzzles, crafts, and LEGO. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with bubble columns and fibre optics. There's art therapy, music therapy, and the Heroes' Circle martial arts program. Upopolis is a secure social network for patients aged 8–18. You've got free TV and can use your own streaming services over Wi-Fi. The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a space to hang out with visitors. And ask Child Life about any special events — they run activities regularly.
What does the Transitions in Care team do for someone my age?

The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital supports patients and families through key transition points. For teens, two of the biggest ones are transitioning from paediatric to adult care as you age out of the children's system, and navigating the shift between school and hospital and back again. They help coordinate communication between your care team, your school, and your family so nothing gets lost in the gaps. If you're approaching 18 or have a chronic condition that will require ongoing adult care, this team is especially relevant — they help make sure the transition is planned rather than abrupt.
Who can see my health information?

Your personal health information can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent to or refuse the collection and sharing of your health information, request access to your records, ask for corrections, and be notified if it's accessed inappropriately. For questions, contact the Privacy Office at extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.
How does pain assessment work for teens?

Your care team will regularly assess your pain using standardized scales. For teens, the most common is the Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) — you rate your pain from 0 to 10, where 0 is no pain and 10 is the worst pain you can imagine. They may also ask about the location, type (sharp, dull, throbbing), and duration of your pain. Being accurate and honest matters — underreporting pain because you think you should 'tough it out' can actually lead to worse outcomes, including increased anxiety for future procedures and delayed recovery. Children's Hospital takes pain management seriously through the Comfort Promise, so speak up if something hurts.
What's the deal with the Paediatric Medical Day Unit?

The Paediatric Medical Day Unit (PMDU) is where children and teens receive treatments that don't require an overnight stay — things like infusions, transfusions, or other medical procedures that can be completed in a single day. The team there includes nurses and other health-care professionals who specialize in outpatient paediatric care. They provide light snacks for patients receiving treatment. The PMDU can be reached at extension 58434 if your family has questions.
What is Upopolis?

Upopolis is a free, secure social networking platform specifically for paediatric patients ages 8 to 18. It lets you connect with other young patients across Canada who are going through similar experiences. You can access it through laptops available from Child Life Services. It's a way to find peer support and feel less isolated during your hospital stay. If you're interested, speak with a Child Life Specialist on your unit and they can help you get set up.
I'm worried the hospital won't respect my pronouns.

That's a valid concern, and I want you to know that Children's Hospital has a Gender Pathways Service specifically for gender-diverse and transgender patients. You can let your care team know your correct name and pronouns, and they should use them. If someone on staff makes a mistake or doesn't respect your identity, you can speak to your nurse, a social worker, or contact the Gender Pathways Service directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca. You shouldn't have to fight for basic respect during a hospital stay. The hospital's job is to care for the whole you, and that includes your identity.
What's PSMSC? Someone mentioned it.

PSMSC stands for Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care Services. It's a specialized service at Children's Hospital for infants, children, and teens with serious illnesses, regardless of the underlying condition. Their goal is to alleviate all kinds of pain and suffering and support the best possible quality of life — including for children approaching end of life. PSMSC provides an additional layer of care on top of what your primary team is doing. If you or your family has been introduced to this team, it means the hospital is making sure all aspects of your comfort and well-being are being addressed.
I'm going to lose my spot on the team. I've worked so hard for this.

I can only imagine how frustrating that is. You've put in real work, and the idea of losing your position because of something you can't control is gut-wrenching. Talk to your coach if you haven't already — most coaches understand medical situations, and many will hold a spot or find a way to keep you involved. Your physiotherapist at the hospital can also help you understand your timeline for returning to activity. This isn't the end of your athletic journey. Athletes deal with setbacks, and coming back from something like this can make you mentally tougher. But right now, your body needs to heal first.
Can I store my own food here?

Yes — there's a family fridge with a freezer available for personal food storage. Just label everything with your name and the date. The hospital can't be responsible for food that gets removed from the fridge by mistake. If you're on the B6 inpatient unit, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. The PCCU also has a small fridge in the waiting room. Always check with your care team about any dietary restrictions before eating food from home.
Is there a social worker I can talk to?

Yes. Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical help — like information about community resources and financial supports. They can also help with communication between your family and the care team, and with planning for discharge. Ask your nurse or a member of your care team to connect you. The social work line is 519-685-8500, extension 33131.
What if my family can't afford parking?

Parking can add up, especially during a longer stay. Multi-day passes bring the daily cost down significantly — a 30-day pass is $75, working out to $2.50/day. 5- and 10-day passes are also available on request from the parking office in P8, ground floor, Room 105. Your social worker may also be able to help connect your family with financial resources.
Is there a place for Indigenous families?

The Indigenous Healing Space at E1-204 is open to all, with priority given to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous Peoples accessing care at LHSC and their families. There's also a Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant who supports mental health and cultural wellness. For more information, speak with your care team or email IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
What is the parking situation?

The closest lot to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, a parking garage off Baseline Road near the northwest corner of the campus. When entering, take a ticket from the gate machine. Rates are $4 for the first hour, $2 for each additional half hour, up to a daily max of $12 (no in-and-out privileges at the standard rate). You can pay at automated stations near the second-floor elevators in the P8 garage. For longer stays, passes with in-and-out privileges are available from the parking office (P8, ground floor, room 105, open Monday–Friday 8 a.m.–8 p.m.): 7-day for $45, 14-day for $65, or 30-day for $75. All passes are valid across LHSC sites for one year from purchase.
What should I expect when I arrive at Children's Hospital for the first time?

When you arrive at Children's Hospital, you'll enter through the B Tower main entrance at 800 Commissioners Road East in London. The entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily — after that, Security controls access. Head up to the second floor of Zone B for Patient Registration, where you'll check in with your health card and appointment details. You'll be given an identification armband with your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode. Staff will scan this band before any procedure, test, or medication, so expect to be asked to confirm your name and date of birth frequently. It's a standard safety protocol, not a sign that anything's wrong.
Is there support for Indigenous patients?

Yes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Program has a consultant who supports mental health and cultural wellness for Indigenous children accessing care at Children's Hospital. They bridge traditional ways of knowing with western approaches to healing. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space (E1-204) that's available with priority given to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous patients and families. You can ask your care team or contact the hospital's Indigenous Health team by email at IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
Can my parents both stay with me?

If you're an inpatient, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at the same time. For outpatient visits, it's one care partner per patient. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., whoever is staying with you overnight should remain in your room and let the unit staff know they're there.
What should I expect about sleep during my stay?

Hospital sleep is different from home sleep. Expect interruptions from overnight vitals checks, IV pump alarms, and ambient hallway noise. The nurses try to minimize disturbance, but patient safety checks are non-negotiable. To help, bring comfortable sleep wear, earplugs, or noise-cancelling headphones, and an eye mask if light bothers you. Your bed is adjustable, so find a comfortable position. Keep in mind that medications, anxiety, and an unfamiliar environment all affect sleep quality. If poor sleep becomes a persistent issue, let your care team know — they can look at scheduling adjustments or other interventions.
What should I know about getting a urinary catheter?

A urinary catheter is a thin, flexible tube inserted into the bladder through the urethra to drain urine. It's used when you can't get out of bed, during surgery, or when your medical team needs to monitor urine output precisely. Insertion involves cleaning the area, applying lubricant, and gently threading the tube in. You'll feel pressure and possibly some discomfort during insertion. Once in place, it shouldn't be painful, but you might feel a persistent urge to urinate — that's the catheter, and it's normal. If you experience sharp pain, burning, or see blood, tell your nurse immediately. Removal is quick and typically painless.
What's the SMILE Room?

It's a multi-sensory room on the sixth floor (B6-261) designed to help with relaxation or sensory stimulation. It has bubble columns, fibre optic lights, mirrors, and music. It can be used for calming down, managing sensory overload, or just experiencing something different from the standard hospital environment. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about access and availability.
What time is breakfast here?

Breakfast is served between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m. You'll get a form on your breakfast tray to choose what you want to eat the next day. If you have any food allergies or dietary needs — like halal, kosher, vegan, or allergen-free — make sure your care team knows so they can set up the right menu for you.
What's a physiotherapist going to do for me?

A physiotherapist, or PT, focuses on your body's movement and physical function. At Children's Hospital, they might work with you on rehab exercises, mobility training, strengthening, pain management, or helping you safely use mobility aids like crutches or walkers. They assess where you are physically and create a plan to help you recover function or manage a condition. If you're post-surgical or dealing with an injury, your PT is key to your recovery. They'll explain the rationale behind what they're asking you to do, and you should feel free to ask questions.
I'm going to miss prom because of this. I've been looking forward to it all year.

That's a real loss, and I'm sorry. Missing a milestone event like prom because of something completely out of your control is heartbreaking. You're allowed to be upset about it — don't let anyone tell you it's 'just a dance.' If there's any chance the timing works out, talk to your care team about your discharge timeline. If it doesn't work out, maybe your friends can video you in, or you can plan something special of your own when you're better. The disappointment is real, but this moment doesn't define your high school experience. You have a lot of life ahead, and this is one chapter of it.
My little brother is probably confused about why I'm here. I'm worried about him.

That shows how much you care about your family. Siblings often struggle when a brother or sister is hospitalized — they might feel scared, confused, or even a little jealous of the attention. Your parents can help by explaining the situation in age-appropriate terms and reassuring him that you're being taken care of. When you're up to it, a phone or video call could really help him feel connected to you. Some of the family support services here, including social work, can offer guidance to your parents on how to support siblings. You worrying about him shows what a great older sibling you are.
I've been Googling my condition and now I'm freaking out.

Dr. Google is notorious for worst-case scenarios. Medical information online is often incomplete, out of context, or written for general populations that don't match your specific situation. The best source of information about YOUR health is your actual medical team who has YOUR test results, YOUR medical history, and can answer YOUR questions. Make a list of everything you've read that worried you and bring it to your doctor. Let them address each concern with facts specific to you. Curiosity about your own health is great — just make sure you're getting your information from the people who actually know your case.
What's the Heroes' Circle program?

The Heroes' Circle is a year-round program that offers weekly visits for inpatients and clinic patients, including siblings. You learn breathing and relaxation techniques along with martial arts. It's designed to help you feel more in control and cope better during your hospital experience. You can contact them at info@kidskickingcancer.ca.
The food here is honestly awful. I can't eat another day of this.

I won't argue with you — hospital food has a well-earned reputation. But there are options. The Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B is open on weekdays until 8 p.m. There are vending machines near the Zone B elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors. Your family can bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit — just check with your nurse first to make sure it fits your diet. The inpatient pantry in B6 has drinks and light snacks too. And if you have dietary preferences like halal, kosher, or vegetarian, let your care team know. It won't be gourmet, but there may be more variety than you've been offered so far.
What should I know about the hospital's research programs?

London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI) and the Children's Health Research Institute (CHRI) conduct research connected to the care delivered at the hospital. During your child's stay, a physician or research team member may ask about participating in a study or clinical trial. All studies must be approved by LHSCRI and a Research Ethics Board. Participation is always voluntary and won't affect your care if you decline. You'll receive a Letter of Information to review, and you should take your time to ask questions. If you're interested in being part of a study, you can proactively ask your care team about current opportunities.
Someone said there's a SMILE Room. What's that about?

The SMILE Room is in room B6-261 on the sixth floor. It's a sensory room filled with equipment designed for relaxation or stimulation — bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, music, and more. It can be used by patients who need a sensory break, whether that's calming down or being gently stimulated. A Child Life Specialist or your nurse can help you access it. It's one of those resources that might sound unusual but is actually well-grounded in therapeutic approaches to sensory regulation.
Is there Indigenous cultural support available?

Yes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant supports mental health and cultural wellness for Indigenous kids at Children's Hospital, bridging traditional ways of knowing with western approaches to healing. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space at E1-204, open to all with priority to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous Peoples. Ask your care team about access or visit the LHSC website for details.
What is the art therapy program like?

Art therapy at Children's Hospital gives you a space to express thoughts and feelings through creative activities — drawing, painting, and other media. It's run by a trained art therapist, so it's more than just making crafts. The process is designed to be empowering and to offer a sense of personal control when your medical situation feels unpredictable. It's individualized to your interests and what you're going through. You don't need to be 'good at art' — it's about expression, not skill.
Do I have to wear the hospital bracelet?

Yes, the ID bracelet is a requirement for your safety. It has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode. Staff will check it before administering any medication, performing tests, or taking you for a procedure. If you have allergies, you'll also get a red allergy bracelet. If your bracelet falls off or is damaged, let your nurse know immediately.
Can my family ask for a different room?

Your family can request a specific room type, but the hospital makes assignments based on availability and infection-control requirements. Insurance-related requests may also not always be possible to accommodate. If you have a specific concern — like needing more space for medical equipment, privacy issues, or infection control — communicate that to your nurse or care team and they'll do what they can. Room assignments aren't arbitrary, but the hospital does try to meet family preferences where feasible.
I've been asked about research. What should I know about the people running these studies?

Clinical research at LHSC is conducted by researchers and physicians, and every study must be reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (LHSCRI) and a qualified Research Ethics Board. Children's Hospital is also home to the Children's Health Research Institute (CHRI), which focuses specifically on child health. If you're approached about a study, you should receive a Letter of Information that explains everything — the purpose, risks, what's expected of you, and your rights. Participation is always voluntary, and declining won't affect your care in any way. Take your time reading the materials and ask as many questions as you need.
My phone is dead and I feel completely cut off from everything.

A dead phone in the hospital can feel like losing your lifeline — it's your connection to friends, entertainment, and normalcy. Ask your parent to bring a charger and maybe a portable power bank for your next visit. If you're stuck waiting, the patient phone by your bed can be used for free local and toll-free calls. The hospital also has a data valet/Wi-Fi support line if you're having connection issues. For now, see if a nurse can help you find a charger — staff sometimes have extras at the station. Staying connected is genuinely important for your mental health, and it's okay to prioritize that.
I don't want my parents reading my chart or knowing everything. I need some things to be private.

As a teenager, the desire for medical privacy is understandable and the hospital takes it seriously. You can talk to your nurse or doctor about which conversations you'd like to have privately. While your parents or guardians are generally included in your care because you're under 18, there are sensitive topics where your care team can respect your need for confidentiality within appropriate limits. If you're unsure about what's shared and what isn't, ask your nurse to explain. You can also speak with a social worker about navigating boundaries with your family during your stay. Your comfort with the process matters.
Who manages the locked unit on B6?

The B6 inpatient unit is managed by the nursing and clinical team assigned to that floor. It's a locked unit, meaning the doors require a confidential code to enter and exit. When you're admitted, your nurse provides the code to your family. The locked setup is a safety measure to protect the patients on the unit. If you have questions about the unit's policies or need to contact staff directly, B6-100 can be reached at extension 52060 and B6-200 at extension 58196.
I feel like the hospital is my whole world now. I've forgotten what outside even looks like.

When you're in the hospital for an extended period, the walls can start to feel like the edges of your universe. That shrinking feeling is real and it's disorienting. Try to stay connected to the outside world however you can — video calls with friends, watching content that reminds you of your normal life, looking at photos on your phone. If you're mobile enough, ask your nurse about visiting Alex's Butterfly Garden in Zone D, Level 2. It's a peaceful outdoor space with benches and a water fountain. Fresh air and a change of scenery can break the mental loop. Your world hasn't actually shrunk — your view of it just has, temporarily.
What is the Paediatric Medical Day Unit?

The PMDU (Paediatric Medical Day Unit) is where children receive treatments or procedures that don't require an overnight stay — things like infusions, transfusions, or other day treatments. Light snacks are provided for children receiving treatment there. You can reach the PMDU at 519-685-8500, extension 58434. If your care involves regular day visits, the PMDU team will become quite familiar to you.
What does the monitor next to my bed track?

The bedside monitor typically tracks several vital parameters in real time. The most common readings are your heart rate (displayed as a waveform and a number), oxygen saturation via a pulse oximeter, blood pressure (taken at intervals through an automated cuff), and respiratory rate. Some monitors also display temperature and cardiac rhythm. Each parameter has a set alarm range — if a reading falls outside that range, the monitor will beep. Most alarms are triggered by benign causes like movement or a loose sensor, but a nurse will always check. You can ask your nurse to explain what each line and number on the screen means.
How do I contact Patient Relations?

You can reach Patient Relations by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca (preferred), by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, through the contact form on the LHSC website, or by mail to 800 Commissioners Road East, PO Box 5010, Stn. B, London ON, N6A 5W9. They check messages Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Try speaking with your care team first, as they may be able to resolve your concern directly.
What are the SMILE Room and other special spaces?

The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room equipped with bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music, designed to help with relaxation or stimulation depending on what you need. Beyond that, there's Ashley's Backyard (B6-259), a nature-themed playroom primarily for younger patients; the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) with crafts, board games, and LEGO; the Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) for socializing; quiet rooms in B6-119 and B6-257 for private conversations or a break; and the Sanctuary (C3-402), a 24/7 sacred space open to everyone for prayer, meditation, or quiet reflection. There's also Alex's Butterfly Garden in Zone D on Level 2 — an outdoor space with benches and a water fountain.
Who's responsible for the after-hours entrance?

Security controls the after-hours entrance. The B Tower main entrance is open from 6 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily. After 8:30 p.m., access is controlled by security — caregivers need to check in with the guard for permission to enter. The parking garage entrance is technically open 24 hours, but after hours you'll still need to check in with security. Zone D entrances on Levels 2 and 3 are locked from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., and Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked 24/7. If you need to contact security, dispatch is at extension 52281.
Can I keep using my phone in the hospital?

Absolutely. The hospital encourages patients to use their own phones to stay connected with friends and family. There's free Wi-Fi, and the patient telephones are available for free local and toll-free calls too. Just be mindful in shared spaces — keep the volume reasonable, use headphones when you can, and be aware that some areas might ask you to silence your phone for medical reasons.
What's the B6 unit like?

B6 is the paediatric inpatient unit. It's a locked unit — once you're admitted, you get a confidential code to enter. There's one overnight sleep space per patient for a family member, with clean bedding provided. The unit has pantries in B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks, a family fridge, the Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110), quiet rooms (B6-119 and B6-257), the SMILE Room (B6-261), Ashley's Backyard playroom (B6-259), and the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065).
Nighttime is the worst. I just lie here overthinking everything.

Nighttime in the hospital can amplify every worry you have. Without distractions, your brain runs wild. You're not alone in that — a lot of patients struggle with nighttime anxiety. Some things that might help: listen to a podcast or calming music with headphones, try guided breathing exercises (inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 4), write your thoughts in a journal or your phone's notes app to get them out of your head. If the anxiety is severe or persistent, tell your nurse and ask about a referral to a psychologist. You shouldn't have to white-knuckle through every night.
I should be handling this better. Other people my age would.

I want to challenge that assumption. You have no idea how other people your age would handle this — most haven't had to. And the ones who have would tell you it's hard. You're not falling short of some invisible standard. There's no 'right' way to handle being in the hospital. Some days you're okay, some days you're not, and both are fine. The pressure to perform strength or resilience all the time is exhausting. Let yourself be wherever you are. If that means crying, being angry, or just being tired — that's all valid. This is hard. Full stop.
How does the hospital handle medication errors?

Hospitals have multiple safety layers to prevent medication errors. At Children's Hospital, your armband is scanned before every medication is given, pharmacists review prescriptions, and nurses follow a 'five rights' protocol — right patient, right drug, right dose, right route, right time. If an error does happen, the hospital has a reporting and review system to understand what went wrong and prevent it from happening again. Patient safety is taken extremely seriously. If you ever notice something that doesn't seem right about a medication you're given, speak up — you're part of that safety system.
What does the Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant do?

The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant at Children's Hospital supports the mental health and cultural wellness of Indigenous children and youth accessing care at the hospital. Their approach bridges traditional Indigenous ways of knowing with Western medical approaches to healing. This service is available to all Indigenous kids — First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous. There's also an Indigenous Healing Space in the hospital that's open to Indigenous families with priority access. If you'd like to connect with the consultant, your care team can facilitate that, or you can reach Indigenous Health via email at IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
Where can I do something fun during my stay?

There are several spaces: the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) has crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO — open daily Monday through Saturday. Ashley's Backyard (B6-259) is a nature-themed playroom. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with bubble columns, fibre optics, and music. The Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) is a social space. There's also art therapy, music therapy, the Heroes' Circle, and Ollie the Clown visiting sometimes.
What are the rules about bringing toys and stuff?

You can bring personal items to make your stay more comfortable, but keep it reasonable — clutter can interfere with cleaning and safe care, and excess items may be sent home with visitors. Toys should be clean and wipeable/washable. Don't share personal items with other patients to prevent infection spread. Staff may clean or restrict certain items if there are infection control concerns. Leave latex balloons, fragranced items, and small choking-hazard items at home.
What should I expect from psychology services?

Paediatric Psychology Services at Children's Hospital provide assessment and treatment for patients and families who are struggling with the emotional and behavioural impact of illness or hospitalization. Psychologists can help you develop coping strategies to manage physical symptoms, anxiety, fear, frustration, or changes in your mood. If your medical condition has affected your thinking or learning, they can assess cognition and provide recommendations for supports at home, school, and in the community. Access is typically through your care team — if you're struggling emotionally, ask your nurse or doctor to refer you.
What do I need to know about the people in the Emergency Department?

The Paediatric Emergency Department team includes emergency physicians, nurses, triage nurses (who assess how urgently you need care), and potentially specialists called in for specific issues. You'll pass through a weapons detection system at the entrance staffed by security. A triage nurse will evaluate your symptoms and assign a priority level. One caregiver is expected to stay with you at all times. There are no sleeping accommodations in the ED, but staff will try to provide a reclining chair, pillows, and blankets. The ED can be reached at extension 58141. Wait times vary based on severity — patients with the most urgent needs are seen first, not necessarily in arrival order.
Can I bring my pet?

Family pet visits are generally not permitted to protect the health and safety of patients, visitors, and staff. Service animals are the exception. In very rare compassionate cases, a pet visit might be approved by the unit manager, but it requires proof of vaccination and a signed waiver. The hospital also has a therapy dog program through St. John Ambulance — ask your care team about scheduled visits.
Is there anyone who can help with school work while I'm here?

The Transitions in Care team and social workers can help coordinate with your school about missed work and re-entry plans. Child Life Specialists may also help facilitate educational activities. If you're on the B6 unit, the School-Age Activity Room in B6-065 has structured activities available. For formal school support — like having assignments sent to the hospital or arranging accommodations for your return — your social worker can communicate directly with your school administration. Bring this up with your care team early in your stay so arrangements can be made before you're discharged.
What is a spiritual care specialist?

Spiritual care at LHSC is a professional service that supports all patients and families regardless of religious beliefs — or lack thereof. Spiritual care practitioners can help with things like grief, existential questions, finding meaning during a difficult time, or simply having someone listen without judgment. The hospital also has a Sanctuary (room C3-402) open 24/7 for quiet reflection, prayer, or meditation. You can request a spiritual care visit through your nurse using pager 14693.
I keep crying in front of the nurses and I feel so stupid.

Crying in the hospital doesn't make you stupid — it makes you a person dealing with a genuinely hard situation. Nurses see patients cry every day, and they don't think less of anyone for it. Holding everything in doesn't make you tougher; it just means the pressure builds up with nowhere to go. If you want privacy when you're emotional, that's okay — you can close the curtain or ask for a moment. But please don't apologize for having feelings. The staff here understand, and most of them chose this career because they care about people during their most vulnerable moments.
Where do I register when I arrive?

Patient Registration is on the second floor of Zone B, above the main entrance. Your admitting time is scheduled in relation to your procedure. If you need to find out a patient's room or phone number, you can call the Patient Information Desk at 519-663-3163.
Why does the IV pump keep beeping?

IV pumps are designed to be cautious — they'll alarm for a range of reasons. The most common ones are: the bag is nearly empty, there's a kink in the line, a bubble of air has been detected, or the flow is being blocked (sometimes just from bending your arm). It doesn't usually mean something is wrong. Your nurse will silence the alarm and fix whatever triggered it. If a pump is beeping and nobody comes quickly, press your call button.
How do I manage boredom during a long hospital stay?

Long stays require some intentional planning around entertainment and mental health. On the infrastructure side, you have WiFi, free Rogers TV, and access to your own streaming services. The hospital offers art therapy, music therapy, the Heroes' Circle program, and the SMILE Room for sensory relaxation. Upopolis lets you connect with other teen patients across Canada. The School-Age Activity Room and Culliton Family Lounge provide spaces to socialize. Bring your own entertainment — tablet, headphones, books, sketch pad, whatever keeps you engaged. If you're falling into a pattern of boredom and low mood, mention it to your care team; they can connect you with a Child Life Specialist or psychology services.
How do cast removals work?

When it's time to remove your cast, a technician will use a specialized oscillating saw. Despite looking and sounding intense, the saw vibrates rather than spins — it cuts through the hard cast material but is designed not to cut skin. You'll feel vibration and warmth, and the noise can be loud, but it shouldn't be painful. If you're anxious, let the team know — headphones or distraction can help. Once the cast is cut, it's pried open and peeled off. Your skin underneath might look pale, dry, or flaky, and the area may feel stiff — all normal. Your care team will advise on exercises and follow-up.
What does the unit clerk do and can I ask them questions?

The unit clerk works at the nurses' station and handles a lot of the administrative coordination on your unit — answering phones, processing orders, managing paperwork, and helping keep operations running smoothly. You can ask them general questions about the unit, like where something is located or when a visitor might be able to come, but clinical questions about your care should go to your nurse or doctor. They're approachable and can usually point you to the right person if they can't answer something directly.
What do I do if my health gets worse after I go home?

Before discharge, make sure you know exactly who to call if your health worsens or you have questions — your care team will go over this with you. You should have written instructions for your care at home. If it's an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest Emergency Department. Don't hesitate to reach out to your care team with concerns, even if they seem small.
Can I bring my own food? Who do I check with?

You should always check with your care team before eating anything that wasn't provided by the hospital. There may be medical reasons — like upcoming tests, procedures, or a prescribed diet — that restrict what you can eat. If your care team approves outside food, the B6 inpatient unit has a family refrigerator with a freezer for personal food storage in the pantries at B6-149 and B6-231. Label and date your items. The PCCU has a small fridge in the waiting room. The closest retail food option is On the Go featuring Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays 6:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vending machines are on the first and third floors of Zone B near the elevators.
What should I know about the therapy dog visits?

Children's Hospital partners with St. John Ambulance to run a therapy dog program in several units. Therapy dogs are specially trained and screened for temperament and vaccination status. Visits have been shown to improve patients' sense of wellbeing and can aid in treatment and rehabilitation. To find out if a visit is scheduled for your unit, ask your care team. Personal pet visits are generally not permitted for infection control reasons, though compassionate exceptions may be considered with manager approval — this involves several steps including proof of vaccination and a pet waiver form.
Where can I do laundry or get toiletries?

If you need personal care items like a toothbrush, deodorant, or shampoo, check the Paediatric Family Resource Centre (B1-006), the Ronald McDonald Room, or the hospital gift shops. As for laundry, the guide doesn't mention on-site laundry facilities for families, so you'd want to ask your care team about local options or have someone bring fresh clothes.
Who handles the food I get while I'm here?

Patient Food Services is responsible for your meals during your hospital stay. Your physician prescribes a diet based on your medical needs, and the food services team prepares meals accordingly. Breakfast is typically served between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch between 11:45 a.m. and 12:45 p.m., and dinner between 4:45 and 5:45 p.m. You'll get a form on your breakfast tray to select food for the next day. The hospital accommodates a range of dietary needs — vegan, vegetarian, Halal, Kosher, and allergen-specific diets. If you have concerns about your diet, talk to your care team or ask to speak with a dietitian.
Someone at the hospital mentioned the Heroes' Circle. What is that?

The Heroes' Circle is a year-round program that provides weekly visits to both inpatients and clinic patients at Children's Hospital. It teaches breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and martial arts. It's designed to help paediatric patients and their siblings manage stress, build confidence, and develop coping skills. It's not just for younger kids — the techniques are relevant for anyone dealing with medical challenges. If it sounds like something you'd want to try, ask your care team about the next session.
I'm worried my boyfriend/girlfriend will break up with me because of all this.

That's a real worry, and I understand why your mind goes there. Being in the hospital can make you feel vulnerable in all your relationships, including romantic ones. The best thing you can do is be honest with your partner about what you're going through and what you need from them. A good partner will step up. If they don't, as painful as that would be, it tells you something important about the relationship. Right now, your energy needs to go toward healing. The people who matter will still be there. And if this is weighing on you, talking to a social worker or psychologist here could help you process it.
Is there somewhere quiet I can go?

There are a few options. The Sanctuary (C3-402) is a sacred space open 24/7 for quiet reflection, meditation, or prayer. On the sixth floor, there are Quiet Rooms at B6-119 and B6-257 — these can be used for private phone calls, short breaks, or family meetings. Just check with your nurse or unit clerk before using the quiet rooms. They're not meant for sleeping.
Who's the person who scanned my armband barcode before drawing blood?

That was either a nurse, a phlebotomist (a technician trained specifically in blood draws), or a lab technician. The barcode scan is a safety check — it verifies your identity against the lab order to ensure the right blood work is being done on the right patient. Your armband contains your name, date of birth, and hospital ID number encoded in that barcode. It's a quick step, but it's a critical layer of error prevention in the hospital's patient safety protocol.
I've gained weight from the medication and I don't feel like myself.

Medication-related weight changes can be really hard to deal with, especially when they change how you see yourself. Your feelings about this are valid. Talk to your doctor about the side effects you're experiencing — in some cases, there may be alternatives or adjustments. A dietitian can also help you with nutrition that supports your health without adding to the problem. Most importantly, be patient with your body. It's adapting to medication while also healing, which is a lot to ask of it. If body image is weighing on you emotionally, the psychologists here are a safe space to talk about it without judgement.
How does the hospital handle food allergies?

LHSC's Patient Food Services can accommodate a wide range of dietary needs, including priority allergens like eggs, milk, mustard, nuts, and more. When you're admitted, inform your care team of all food allergies — they'll be flagged in your chart, and you'll receive a red allergy bracelet. Your prescribed diet will reflect your restrictions, and the menu card delivered to your tray will only offer safe options. Don't introduce new foods during your stay without checking with your care team first, especially if your condition or medications might affect how you respond to certain foods.
Why do I have to wear this wristband?

Your armband is your hospital ID — it has your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a scannable barcode. Staff check or scan it before every medication, test, or procedure as a safety measure to prevent any mix-ups. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red allergy bracelet. Babies under one year get a security alarm band as well. It's not optional — it's one of the most important safety measures in the hospital.
I'm being discharged soon. Who all is involved in that process?

Discharge planning at Children's Hospital is a team effort that starts early in your stay. Your physician determines when you're medically ready. Your nurse reviews medications, care instructions, and follow-up appointments with your family. A pharmacist may prepare a medication calendar. If you need home care services or equipment, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator assesses your needs. A social worker may help with financial resources, school re-entry, or community services. A physiotherapist or occupational therapist may advise on mobility and safe transportation. Your family is responsible for arranging your ride home — your nurse can provide a brochure about transport options if needed. The goal is for you to leave with a clear plan and no unanswered questions.
Everyone's moving forward with university applications and I'm falling behind.

The pressure of life milestones continuing while you're dealing with a health situation is incredibly stressful. But universities understand medical circumstances, and gap years or delayed applications are far more common than you think. Your school guidance counsellor can help with accommodations and documentation. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital also supports young people navigating these kinds of life transitions. Your timeline doesn't have to match everyone else's, and a few weeks or months won't derail your future. Take care of your health now — the rest will follow.
Where can I get food at the hospital?

If you're admitted, patient meals are served at set times: breakfast from 7:45 to 8:45 a.m., lunch from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m., and dinner from 4:45 to 5:45 p.m. You'll get a menu card on your breakfast tray to select your next day's meals. The hospital accommodates a range of dietary needs including vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, and specific allergen restrictions — just let your care team know. For snacks between meals, the inpatient unit on B6 has pantries in rooms B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks. There's also a Tim Hortons ('On the Go') on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., and vending machines near the Zone B elevators on the first and third floors. Always check with your care team before eating, as some tests or procedures require fasting.
What is the pharmacy at Children's Hospital?

The Children's Hospital Pharmacy and Compounding Centre is on the first floor (B1-001), right near the B1 entrance. It's open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. excluding holidays. You can fill prescriptions there before you leave, which is convenient for discharge day. They also sell breast pump kits. If you have questions about any of your medications, your nurse can arrange for a pharmacist to come talk to you directly. The pharmacy's extension is 58082.
What exactly happens during a shift change? I always notice a lot of activity around 7.

You're picking up on the nursing shift change, which happens at approximately 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. daily. During the transition period — roughly 6:45 to 7:30 — the outgoing and incoming nurses exchange information about each patient. At Children's Hospital, this includes a bedside shift change report where both nurses come to your room, review your care plan, complete safety checks, and invite you and your family to ask questions or share anything relevant. It's about a three to five minute process. Phone calls to the unit may be harder to get through during these windows, so it's best to avoid calling between 6:45 and 7:30 if possible.
Why are there so many people on my care team? It's overwhelming.

That's a really valid feeling. The number of people involved in your care reflects the complexity of paediatric medicine and the hospital's commitment to treating you holistically — not just the medical issue, but your nutrition, mobility, mental health, family dynamics, and comfort. At Children's Hospital, your team might include a physician, residents, nurses, nurse practitioners, a pharmacist, dietitian, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist, social worker, Child Life Specialist, and others depending on your needs. Not all of them will be actively involved at all times. If it feels overwhelming, ask your primary nurse to help you understand who's doing what — they're your best point of contact for navigating the team.
Who are the people involved in the Comfort Promise?

The Comfort Promise is a hospital-wide commitment at Children's Hospital to minimize pain and anxiety during needle procedures. It involves multiple members of your care team. Your nurse will typically apply topical anesthetic to numb the skin before a needle stick. A Child Life Specialist might offer distraction techniques. Your care team will use comfort positioning — supportive body positions rather than restraint — to help you feel more in control. For infants, sucrose and breastfeeding are used. The philosophy is evidence-based: untreated procedural pain can lead to increased pain sensitivity, health-care avoidance, and even vaccine hesitancy. You're encouraged to advocate for yourself and ask about these options before any needle procedure.
Can I bring my own food?

You can, but you need to clear it with your care team first. Depending on your treatment, you might be on a prescribed diet. If approved, you can store personal food in the family fridge in your unit's pantry area — label it with your name and date. On B6, pantries are at B6-149 and B6-231. The hospital isn't responsible for food that gets taken from the fridge.
What does the dietitian actually do and why do they need to talk to me?

A dietitian at Children's Hospital is a nutrition expert who works with your medical team to ensure your diet supports your recovery and overall health. They might talk to you for several reasons — your medical condition may require a specific diet, you may have allergies or dietary restrictions that need to be managed, or they may need to adjust your nutrition plan post-surgery. LHSC offers a range of diets including vegan, vegetarian, Halal, Kosher, and allergen-specific options. If you have specific preferences or needs, the dietitian is the person to coordinate that. They're not there to lecture you — they're there to work with you.
Why aren't latex balloons allowed?

Latex allergies can range from mild skin irritation to severe anaphylaxis, which is a life-threatening reaction. Since hospitals treat immunocompromised and allergy-prone patients, even airborne latex particles could put someone at risk. That's why LHSC bans latex balloons completely. If you want to brighten someone's room, mylar (foil) balloons are a safe alternative. Interestingly, poinsettia plants are also banned because they contain a compound similar to what's found in rubber latex.
Can I get help with schoolwork while I'm here?

If your hospital stay affects school, there are support systems in place. The Transitions in Care team helps coordinate the shift between school and hospital and back again. Before discharge, your family can discuss with your teacher and school administration about homework assignments, return-to-school timelines, and any accommodations you might need. The hospital's discharge checklist specifically includes talking to your school about your condition and healthcare needs. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre where you can access the internet for schoolwork. While the hospital doesn't run a formal school program, your care team can help your family navigate the educational disruption.
They keep asking me what I think about my treatment. I just want someone to decide for me.

Decision fatigue is real, especially when you're dealing with a health situation. It's okay to feel overwhelmed by the responsibility of participating in your care. You can tell your team that you'd like your parent or your doctor to take the lead on decisions for now. That's a valid choice. Shared decision-making is offered because your input matters, but it should never feel like pressure. When you're ready, you can re-engage in those conversations. For now, focus on healing and let the adults around you carry the decision-making load. There's no wrong way to navigate this.
Someone mentioned the Paediatric Family Resource Centre. What's there?

The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is in room B1-006 on the first floor of Zone B. It offers patients and families peer support, help with forms and applications, health information from a lived-experience perspective, and internet access. Hours are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday and Thursday; and 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday by appointment only. It's also a quiet place to go when you need a break from your room. The people there have real-world experience navigating the system and can point you toward useful resources.
What if I need legal help related to my hospital stay?

There's actually a program for that. Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) has a partnership with Children's Hospital that helps families identify and resolve legal issues that could impact a child's health or the family's ability to provide care. It provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. Your social worker can refer your case to the on-site triage lawyer.
Is there spiritual care available?

Yes. LHSC has Spiritual Care Specialists who provide support that's respectful of all spiritual and religious needs, beliefs, and practices. You can reach one through your nurse at pager number 14693 or by calling extension 58418. There's also the Sanctuary in Zone C, Level 3, room C3-402 — it's a sacred space open 24/7 for prayer, reflection, or quiet time.
Someone mentioned they're a resident. What exactly is a resident?

A resident is a doctor who has completed medical school and is now doing additional training in a specific specialty — like paediatrics, surgery, or critical care. Residency is a hands-on phase where they work directly with patients under the supervision of an attending physician. At Children's Hospital, residents help develop and carry out your care plan. They've earned their medical degree, so they do have real medical knowledge — they're just in the process of getting deeper expertise. Your attending physician oversees everything they do.
If I talk to the psychologist, does that mean something's wrong with me?

Absolutely not. Talking to a psychologist while you're in the hospital is like stretching when your muscles are sore — it's basic care for something that's under strain. Hospitalization is stressful. Having someone to talk to about that isn't a sign of weakness or mental illness. The paediatric psychologists here work with kids and teens every day on things like coping with being in the hospital, dealing with anxiety, adjusting to a diagnosis, and managing stress. It's confidential, it's normal, and it's there because emotional health matters. You wouldn't skip physiotherapy for a broken leg — same logic applies here.
Why is the hospital fragrance-free?

LHSC has a fragrance-free policy because scented products — cologne, perfume, scented lotions, even hair products — can trigger allergic reactions and respiratory distress in patients and staff. In a hospital where many people have compromised immune systems or sensitive airways, even common fragrances can cause real problems. The policy covers the entire facility, including all buildings, grounds, and parking lots.
What should I bring for my hospital stay?

For your stay, bring your own clothes (including slippers with non-slip soles and an outfit for going home), toiletries like toothbrush, shampoo, and deodorant, and any medical aids you use — glasses, hearing aids, braces, etc. A few favourite items from home like books or photos can help. You'll also need your Ontario health card and a list of any medications you take. Leave latex balloons, perfume/fragrances, baby walkers, and electrical equipment at home.
What should I know about privacy here?

LHSC takes your privacy seriously. Information about you is only shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent or refuse the collection and use of your personal health information, access your records, request corrections, be notified if your information is accessed inappropriately, and know who it's been shared with. If you have concerns, contact the Privacy Office at 519-685-8500 extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca.
What are meal times at Children's Hospital?

Meals at Children's Hospital are served at set times each day. Breakfast is between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m., lunch runs from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m., and dinner is served from 4:45 to 5:45 p.m. You'll receive a menu form with your breakfast tray to select your meals for the following day. If you have dietary restrictions or allergies, let your care team know — they accommodate vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, and allergen-specific diets.
I was in an accident and I keep replaying it in my head.

What you're describing — replaying a traumatic event over and over — is a very normal response to what you went through. Your brain is trying to process something that was shocking and overwhelming. It doesn't mean you're broken or that this will last forever. But it's really important that you talk to someone about it. The psychologists at Children's Hospital are experienced in helping young people who've been through traumatic events. You don't have to wait until you're 'worse' to ask for help. The sooner you talk about it, the better equipped you'll be to process it. Please tell your nurse or parent you'd like to speak with a psychologist.
Can I request to talk to a pharmacist about my meds directly?

Yes, absolutely. At Children's Hospital, a pharmacist is available to come to your room and answer your questions or address concerns about your medications. Just ask your nurse to arrange it. Pharmacists can explain what each medication does, how to take it, potential side effects, and drug interactions. If you're on several medications, they can also prepare a medication calendar for you and your family before discharge. Being informed about what you're taking is a reasonable and important expectation.
Can I have some control over when people come into my room?

To some extent, yes. Certain visits — vital sign checks, medication administration, physician rounds — are scheduled and necessary. But for non-urgent things, you can talk to your nurse about coordinating visits to give you blocks of uninterrupted time, especially for sleeping, studying, or just having privacy. The quiet rooms on B6 (B6-119 and B6-257) are also available for private time. You're a partner in your care, and reasonable requests about your schedule and space are respected.
What is Upopolis?

Upopolis is a free, secure social networking platform specifically for paediatric patients aged 8–18 across Canadian hospitals. It lets you connect with other patients who get what you're going through. You can chat, share stories, and find community. Laptops are available through Child Life Services if you need one. If you're interested, ask a Child Life Specialist to help you get set up.
What if I don't speak English well?

LHSC provides free interpretation services for patients. If you're more comfortable communicating in a language other than English, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, ask your care team to arrange an interpreter. You deserve to fully understand your care, and the hospital takes that seriously. They support spoken languages and sign language.
Someone mentioned a Black Health Navigator. What do they do?

Black Health Navigators are trained, registered health-care workers at LHSC who support Black patients and families in navigating the health-care system. Their role includes providing information about health-care options, ensuring your voice is heard in conversations with your care team, and advocating for equitable care. You can access this service through Black Health at the hospital — ask your care team or email BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca. It's a resource designed to address specific systemic barriers that Black patients may face in health care.
Who are the people at the nurses' station?

The nurses' station is the operational hub of your unit. You'll typically see your assigned nurses, the charge nurse (the nurse overseeing the unit for that shift), the unit clerk (who handles administrative tasks like phones and paperwork), and sometimes residents, nurse practitioners, or physicians reviewing charts or making calls. Other team members — dietitians, pharmacists, therapists — may stop by to discuss patient care. It's a busy area, but the people there are your front line for questions, requests, and updates.
Who manages infection control on my unit and what are the precautions about?

Infection prevention and control is managed hospital-wide by LHSC's Infection Prevention and Control team, with protocols carried out by every member of your care team. If extra precautions are needed — for example, if you have an infectious condition — a sign will be posted at your room entry. Visitors should stop at the nurses' station for instructions before entering. Precautions might include wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection. You may be asked to stay in your room and keep personal items minimal to facilitate cleaning. Alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method for hand hygiene and is available throughout the unit. These measures protect you, other patients, and staff.
Is there anyone who can help me deal with going back to school after this?

The Transitions in Care team and social workers at Children's Hospital can help with the school transition. They can coordinate communication with your school — speaking with your teacher, principal, or other staff about what you've been through, homework you've missed, accommodations you might need, and a return plan. Psychologists can also help if you're anxious about going back. It's worth bringing this up with your care team before discharge so everything is in place by the time you're ready to return.
What does a nurse practitioner do compared to a regular nurse or doctor?

Nurse practitioners (NPs) sit somewhere between registered nurses and physicians in terms of scope. They've completed advanced education — typically a master's degree — and can assess patients, order tests, diagnose conditions, and plan treatment, much like a doctor. At Children's Hospital, NPs work closely with attending physicians and function similarly to residents. Registered nurses focus more on day-to-day patient care: administering medications, monitoring vitals, coordinating appointments, and being the consistent face you see during your stay.
What shared decision making means here?

Shared Decision Making at LHSC is a structured process where you and your caregivers work with health-care providers and a Decision Coach to make important care choices together. It combines the best medical evidence with your personal values. It's about making sure you have a real say in decisions about your own care. Ask your care team or visit the LHSC website to learn more.
Who works in the NICU and what do they do for the babies?

The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) has a team of neonatologists (doctors specializing in newborn care), specially trained nurses, respiratory therapists, dietitians, and other specialists focused on critically ill or premature infants. They manage everything from breathing support and feeding to monitoring for complications. The NICU is a high-tech environment with a lot of equipment, but the team also prioritizes family-centred care — parents are encouraged to participate through skin-to-skin kangaroo care and bedside presence. There's a separate family guide for the NICU with more details if you have a sibling there.
What's the Comfort Promise?

The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to managing pain and anxiety during needle procedures using evidence-based strategies. These include topical anaesthetic cream to numb the skin, comfort positioning (sitting upright in supportive positions rather than being held down), distraction techniques like watching a video, and for infants, sucrose or breastfeeding. Research shows that untreated needle pain can lead to long-term health care avoidance and increased pain sensitivity in future procedures. You can always ask for these strategies before any needle procedure — it's your right.
What is the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program?

The PPI program prepares one caregiver to accompany and support you in the operating room during the start of anaesthesia. It includes an education session and/or a tour of Day Surgery and the OR to help you both get ready. Not everyone is eligible, so check with your care team or a Child Life Specialist to see if this is an option for your procedure.
Can I get therapy dog visits?

Children's Hospital has partnered with St. John Ambulance to offer a therapy dog program on several units. These are certified therapy dogs that are trained to be calm and gentle. Research supports that interacting with therapy dogs can improve a patient's sense of wellbeing and support rehabilitation. Ask your care team if there's a scheduled visit on your unit. Regular pet visits from home aren't typically allowed, but compassionate exceptions can be considered with manager approval, proof of vaccination, and a signed waiver.
What happens if I need care at night?

Nursing care doesn't stop overnight. A nurse will check on you at regular intervals throughout the night to monitor your vitals, check your IV, and ensure you're comfortable. If you need anything between checks, press the call button by your bed. Be aware that nursing shift changes happen around 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and p.m., so responsiveness may be slightly delayed during those windows. Overnight, the B Tower entrance is controlled by security — if a family member needs to leave and return, they'll check in with the guard. The hospital environment quiets down at night but doesn't go dark or silent; corridor lights stay dimmed and staff continue to move around.
I'm going to have a scar and I hate it.

Concerns about scarring are completely normal, especially when your body image matters to you. Your surgeon or doctor can talk to you about what to expect in terms of healing and what the scar will likely look like over time — many scars fade significantly. There may also be treatments that can minimize scarring, so it's worth asking. Beyond the physical, if you're struggling with how a scar makes you feel about your body, that's something a psychologist here can help with. A scar tells a story about something you survived. That's not nothing. But your feelings about it are yours to have.
What kind of support is there for transitioning between youth and adult care?

The Transitions in Care team specifically supports paediatric patients and families through key milestones — like transitioning from youth to adult care, and moving between school and hospital. If you're approaching 18 or nearing a transition point, ask your care team about connecting with them.
When I go back to school, everyone's going to ask questions and I don't want to explain.

You get to decide how much or how little you share. You're under no obligation to explain your health to anyone. It can help to have a simple go-to response ready, like 'I had a health thing but I'm doing better now' and leave it at that. You could also ask a close friend to help deflect questions. If you're worried about the transition back to school, the Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital specifically helps with that. Some schools can also brief teachers without going into detail. You control your story. Practice your response beforehand so it feels natural.
What's a nurse practitioner? Are they as qualified as a doctor?

A nurse practitioner, or NP, is a highly qualified health-care provider — they're registered nurses who went on to complete advanced graduate-level education and training. At Children's Hospital, NPs partner with the medical team and work closely with attending physicians to plan patient care. They can assess patients, order tests, and make treatment decisions. While NPs and physicians have different training pathways, both bring serious expertise to your care. If you're being seen by an NP, you're in very capable hands.
Why do I need to wear slip-proof socks?

Your nurse provided those as part of falls prevention. Hospital floors can be slippery, and when you're recovering from illness, injury, or a procedure, your balance and strength might not be what they usually are. Slip-proof socks, slippers, or shoes reduce your risk of a fall. Your nurse does a formal falls assessment and will discuss other prevention steps with you, like keeping bed rails up and asking for help before getting out of bed. It might seem minor, but falls in hospitals can cause real setbacks in your recovery.
What monitoring equipment might I be connected to?

Depending on your condition and what you're being treated for, you might be connected to several pieces of monitoring equipment. Common ones include a cardiac monitor that tracks your heart rate and rhythm via adhesive electrodes on your chest, a pulse oximeter clipped to your finger for oxygen saturation, an automatic blood pressure cuff on your arm, and a temperature probe. If you have an IV, the infusion pump regulates flow rate and will alarm if there's an air bubble or occlusion. In more acute settings like the PCCU, you might also have additional lines and sensors. Each device will generate some sounds — steady beeps, periodic inflation of the BP cuff, and occasional alarms. Ask your nurse to walk you through what each device does if you want to understand your setup.
How do they manage dietary restrictions during a stay?

When you're admitted, your care team prescribes a diet based on your medical condition. This could range from regular meals to specialized diets — vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, no pork, or allergen-specific restrictions. Patient Food Services will deliver a menu based on your prescribed diet. You fill out a form on your breakfast tray to choose the next day's meals. If your dietary needs change or you have concerns, talk to a member of your care team — a dietitian is available. Don't introduce new foods or snacks without clearing it with staff first, especially if you're on a modified diet or awaiting procedures.
I'm worried my friends will forget about me while I'm here.

That worry is understandable, especially when your friends are together and you're not. But real friendships don't dissolve because of a hospital stay. Your friends are probably thinking about you more than you realize. Stay connected however you can — text, video calls, social media. If you're comfortable with it, let them visit.
