Up to two people can be at your bedside during visiting hours. You might be surprised how much your friends want to be there for you. And if anyone does pull away, that says more about them than about you. Focus on the people who show up.
What if my family lives far from London?

If your family lives outside London, the Ronald McDonald House is a nearby accommodation option specifically for families with a child in the hospital. Your care team can help determine eligibility and connect your family. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room right in the hospital (extension 56896). LHSC maintains a list of local hotels and motels on their website, and some offer discounted 'hospital rates' upon request. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre can also help your family navigate logistics.
What happens after general anaesthesia?

After a procedure under general anaesthesia, you'll wake up in a recovery area often called the PACU (Post-Anaesthesia Care Unit). The process of waking up can feel disorienting — you might feel groggy, confused, cold, or nauseated. Some people feel emotional or tearful, which is a normal response to the anaesthetic, not a sign of anything wrong. Nurses will monitor your vital signs closely as you wake up. You'll gradually become more alert, and once the anaesthesia team is satisfied with your recovery, you'll be moved back to your room. The timeline varies, but full alertness usually returns within a few hours. Nausea can often be managed with medication — let your nurse know if you feel sick.
Can I ask to see a psychologist?

Yes. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychology services available. Psychologists can help with things like adjusting to illness, managing anxiety or stress related to your condition, and developing coping strategies for physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. They can also assess cognitive and learning impacts if your medical condition affects those. Talk to your nurse or your care team and they can arrange a referral.
What role does the pharmacist play?

Pharmacists at Children's Hospital do more than fill prescriptions. They review your medication list for potential interactions, verify dosages, and ensure compatibility with any allergies. If you're on multiple medications, a pharmacist can prepare a medication calendar and review it with you before discharge. You or your family can request to speak with a pharmacist at any time — just ask your nurse to arrange it. The Children's Hospital Pharmacy is located at B1-001, next to the B1 entrance, open Monday to Friday from 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. Prescriptions can be filled there before you leave.
I don't fully trust the doctors here. How do I know they're making the right decisions?

Questioning your care team isn't disrespectful — it's your right. This is your body and your health. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital affiliated with Western University, and the physicians here are specialists in paediatric care. That said, trust is earned, not assumed. You can ask your doctor to explain their reasoning, request information about alternative options, or ask for a second opinion. The Shared Decision Making program here encourages exactly this kind of collaboration between patients and providers. You should feel informed and involved. If you don't, raise it with your nurse, your parent, or the Patient Relations office.
Where is the pharmacy?

The Children's Hospital Pharmacy and Compounding Centre is at B1-001, on the first floor of Children's Hospital next to the B1 Entrance. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. (closed on holidays). You can fill prescriptions there before discharge.
What if I need legal help?

Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) has a partnership with Children's Hospital. They provide free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. The program helps identify and resolve legal problems that could impact a child's health or a family's ability to provide care. Your social worker can refer your case to their on-site triage lawyer.
How much does parking cost?

It's $4 for the first hour and $2 for each additional half hour, up to a $12 daily maximum without in-and-out privileges. If your family needs to come and go, a daily pass with in-and-out privileges is $14 (valid 24 hours). For longer stays, passes are available: $45 for 7 days, $65 for 14 days, and $75 for 30 days. These are valid at all LHSC sites.
What happens during an MRI?

An MRI uses powerful magnets and radio waves to create detailed images of your body's internal structures — no radiation involved. You'll lie on a narrow table that slides into a large tube-shaped scanner. The machine produces loud rhythmic knocking and humming sounds, so you'll be given ear protection. The key requirement is staying completely still for the duration of the scan, which can range from 20 minutes to over an hour depending on what's being imaged. The space inside the scanner is fairly tight, which can feel claustrophobic for some people — let your care team know beforehand if that's a concern. You won't feel any pain during the scan itself.
What is the Transitions in Care team?

The Transitions in Care team supports paediatric patients and families through major transition points. Two of the biggest are the transition from youth to adult care — which happens when you age out of paediatric services — and moving between school and hospital environments. They help coordinate the logistics and emotional aspects of these shifts so that gaps in care or support don't happen. If you're approaching a transition point and have concerns about continuity of care, ask your care team to involve the Transitions in Care team.
What's the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?

It's located on the 1st floor of Zone B (room B1-006) and it offers patients and family members peer support, help with forms and applications, and access to information on children's health topics from a lived-experience lens. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Tuesday and Thursday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.; and Saturday and Sunday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. by appointment. It's also a quieter space to step away from the unit for a bit.
Why do they need to check my identity so many times?

It might feel repetitive, but it's one of the most critical patient safety protocols in any hospital. Every time someone checks your armband — which has your name, date of birth, hospital ID, and a barcode — they're verifying they have the right patient before giving medication, running a test, or starting a procedure. Mix-ups in hospitals can have serious consequences, so this is a hard rule that applies to everyone. If you have allergies, you'll also have a red bracelet so every member of your team is aware.
What is the bedside shift change?

At Children's Hospital, nursing shift changes happen at your bedside rather than behind closed doors. Shifts change around 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. During this handover, the incoming nurse will introduce themselves, both nurses will review your care plan and complete mandatory safety checks, and you'll have a chance to ask questions or share anything you think is important. The whole process takes about three to five minutes. You and your family are encouraged to participate — it's a direct way to stay informed about your care and ensure nothing gets lost in translation between shifts.
What is the Sanctuary space?

The Sanctuary is a sacred space in Zone C, Level 3, room C3-402, open 24/7 to all patients and families regardless of faith or belief. It's intended for prayer, meditation, quiet reflection, or simply a moment of silence away from the clinical environment. If you need spiritual support from a professional, Spiritual Care Specialists are available through your nurse (pager 14693). Spiritual Care is a people-centred service that is respectful of all spiritual and religious backgrounds, beliefs, values, and practices.
What does the Paediatric Family Resource Centre offer?

The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is in room B1-006 on the first floor of Zone B. It's run by people with lived experience and offers peer support, help with forms and applications, and information about children's health topics. It's also a quiet spot to access the internet or just take a moment. Hours are Monday, Wednesday, and Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; Tuesday and Thursday from 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.; and Saturday and Sunday by appointment only from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Both patients and family members can use it.
What does the pre-op fasting process involve?

Before certain procedures and surgeries, you'll be required to fast — meaning no food or drink for a specified period. Your care team will give you specific instructions about when to stop eating and drinking. The purpose is to ensure your stomach is empty, which reduces the risk of aspiration (food or liquid entering your lungs) during anaesthesia. The fasting window varies depending on the procedure and the type of anaesthesia being used. It can be uncomfortable, especially if you're already anxious, but it's an essential safety precaution. Once your procedure is complete and your care team clears you, you'll be able to eat and drink again.
Can I get a security escort?

Yes. If you need an escort to or from your car, or to the Ronald McDonald House, security patrols are available. You can request one by calling the security dispatch line at extension 52281 (full number: 519-685-8500, ext. 52281). This service is available at any time. If you're leaving late at night and feel unsafe walking through the parking lot alone, don't hesitate to call. The emergency response extension is 55555.
I don't want my family to see me like this, so I pretend I'm fine.

Protecting your family is a loving instinct, but it comes at a cost to you. Pretending to be fine when you're not is exhausting and isolating. Your family is here because they can handle seeing you through this — that's what family does. Being honest about how you're feeling actually helps them support you better. It also models something important: that vulnerability isn't weakness. If a full emotional download feels like too much, start small. You can say something like 'I'm having a rough day' without going into every detail. You don't have to carry everything alone just to spare others. That's too much to ask of yourself.
What if I have ethical concerns about my care?

LHSC has a clinical ethics consultation service. If you or your family are struggling with a difficult ethical decision around your care, the ethicist can help identify and work through those concerns. Ethics consultations are available to patients, families, and health-care providers. More info is on the LHSC website, or ask your care team.
What do I do if I see a sign on someone's door?

Signs posted at a patient's room or bed space indicate that extra infection control precautions are in effect. Stop at the nurses' station before entering and they'll tell you what's needed — it might mean wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection. A staff member can help you put these on. These measures protect both you and the patient.
Everyone keeps telling me to stay positive and I can't do it anymore.

Toxic positivity in a medical setting can be exhausting. You don't owe anyone a good attitude when you're going through something this difficult. Being realistic, being frustrated, or being sad doesn't mean you're not fighting. Forced optimism can actually be counterproductive because it makes you stuff down legitimate feelings. You're allowed to have bad days. You're allowed to say 'this sucks.' The people who truly support you will accept that. If you need space from the positivity pressure, set that boundary. And if you need to talk to someone who'll just listen without trying to fix your attitude, ask for a psychologist or social worker.
What if I wake up during surgery? I've heard that can happen.

That's a common fear, and it's been dramatized in movies far more than it reflects reality. Anaesthesia awareness is extremely rare, especially with modern monitoring equipment and the dedicated team of anaesthesiologists watching over you the entire time. They're tracking your brain activity, heart rate, oxygen levels, and more — every second. If you're concerned, bring this up directly with your anaesthesiologist before the procedure. They can walk you through the safeguards in detail. Being informed is the best way to reduce fear, and no question is too small or silly to ask your care team.
What happens if I'm on a locked unit?

The B6 inpatient unit is locked for patient safety. When you're admitted, you'll receive a confidential code to enter the unit. This isn't meant to feel restrictive — it's a security measure to protect everyone on the floor. Your visitors and family will need to follow the unit's entry procedures too.
What's a speech therapist actually for? I can talk fine.

That's a common misconception — speech therapists (also called speech-language pathologists) do way more than help with talking. At Children's Hospital, they also work on swallowing difficulties, voice disorders, language processing, and communication challenges that might result from a medical condition, surgery, or neurological issue. If you're seeing a speech therapist, it could be for any of those reasons. They're trained specialists who assess and treat a range of communication and swallowing needs.
Can I ask for a specific diet?

Yes. LHSC offers a range of diets including vegan, vegetarian (with various levels — dairy and eggs, or dairy/eggs/fish), halal, kosher, no pork, and meals free of priority allergens like eggs, milk, nuts, and mustard. Your physician prescribes a diet based on your medical needs, and Patient Food Services creates a menu from there. Talk to your care team to get the right diet set up.
My condition is embarrassing. I don't want to talk about it with anyone.

First, nothing about a medical condition is something to be ashamed of. But I understand that certain conditions can feel deeply personal, especially at your age. You get to set the boundaries on who knows what. With your care team, though, I'd encourage you to be as open as possible — they've seen everything, and they're bound by strict confidentiality rules. Nothing you tell a nurse or doctor leaves the room without your consent. If you're uncomfortable discussing things in front of a parent, you can ask for a private conversation with your provider. Your health depends on honest communication, and the medical staff here will never judge you.
Why does my nurse do a report at my bedside when the shifts change?

That's called a bedside shift change report, and it happens twice a day — typically around 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. The outgoing nurse and incoming nurse meet at your bedside to review your plan of care, complete safety checks, and make sure nothing falls through the cracks. You and your family are invited to participate — you can ask questions, share observations, or add information you think is important. It takes about three to five minutes. It's designed to keep communication transparent and to make sure your new nurse is fully up to speed on your situation.
What can I expect from physiotherapy or occupational therapy?

Physiotherapists and occupational therapists are part of the care team at Children's Hospital. Physiotherapy focuses on physical recovery — strengthening, mobility, balance, and getting you back to full function. Occupational therapy helps with daily activities and adapting to any temporary or permanent changes in your physical abilities. If you need either service during your stay, they'll be incorporated into your care plan. Before discharge, a PT or OT will also help assess your safe transportation home, especially if you have mobility or transfer needs. They'll work with your family to ensure a smooth transition.
What does an ECG measure?

An ECG — electrocardiogram — records the electrical activity of your heart. Those sticky pads (electrodes) placed on your chest, arms, and legs detect the tiny electrical signals generated each time your heart beats. The ECG produces a tracing that shows the rhythm, rate, and electrical pattern. Cardiologists can read these tracings to identify irregular rhythms, structural issues, or other heart-related conditions. It's non-invasive, painless, and takes just a few minutes.
The medication makes me feel weird and foggy. I don't like it.

Feeling foggy or not like yourself from medication is really unsettling, and it's valid to dislike it. You should absolutely tell your doctor or nurse about these side effects — there may be alternative medications, different dosages, or timing adjustments that can help. You don't have to just accept it. Your care team needs to know how medications affect you in order to find the right balance between managing your condition and your quality of life. Never stop taking a prescribed medication on your own, but always speak up about how it's making you feel. Your experience matters in these decisions.
What is a CT scan?

A CT (computed tomography) scan is essentially a series of X-ray images taken from different angles, which a computer combines into cross-sectional slices of your body. It gives much more detail than a regular X-ray and can show soft tissue, blood vessels, and bones. The machine looks like a large donut — you lie on a table that slides through the centre. The scan itself is painless and usually quick, though you might need contrast dye injected through an IV to make certain structures more visible.
Do I need a car seat when I leave?

By law, children must travel in an approved car seat. Your family should bring your car seat when they come to pick you up. If your condition has changed or you have new mobility needs, a physiotherapist or occupational therapist will help figure out safe transportation options. LHSC's Trauma Program also offers consultations with certified Car Seat Technicians to make sure the seat is properly installed.
How do I prepare for an outpatient appointment?

Bring your Ontario health card, your appointment card or letter, a list of any medications you're currently taking (including dosage and frequency), and your family doctor's name and contact information. If you have referral letters, imaging results (X-rays, CT scans), or your vaccination record, bring those too. Wear comfortable clothes, and leave fragrant products, electrical equipment, and latex balloons at home. Arrive with enough time to find parking (P8 garage off Baseline Road is closest) and navigate to your appointment location. If it's your first visit, allow extra time for registration on the second floor of Zone B.
How do I navigate the hospital?

Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital campus. Zones are labeled with letters (B, C, D, E), and room numbers encode the zone, floor, and room — like B6-261 means Zone B, sixth floor, room 261. For wayfinding, you have several options: download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map, use wayfinding kiosks located throughout the building, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays. Information Desks are staffed 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers are at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on weekdays.
I'm back again. I'm so tired of this being my life.

Coming back to the hospital again when you've already been through it is exhausting — physically and emotionally. It's okay to be fed up. Living with a condition that brings you back here takes a kind of resilience that most people your age don't have to develop. That doesn't make it easier, but it does make you stronger than you probably give yourself credit for. If you're feeling burned out, that's worth talking about with your care team, a psychologist, or a social worker. The Bravery Beads program can also help you visualize your journey and acknowledge everything you've been through. You're not just 'back again' — you're still fighting, and that matters.
Where can I park?

The closest lot to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, the garage off Baseline Road. Other options include P1 and P2 off Commissioners Road, P3 south of Zone E, and P7 off Baseline Road north of Zone E. All lots are paid, open 24/7. Rates start at $4 for the first hour. The parking office in P8 (ground floor, Room 105) is open Monday to Friday 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
Why do I keep getting woken up at night?

Night checks are part of standard nursing care. Your nurse needs to periodically assess your vital signs, check your IV, and make sure you're safe and comfortable. The frequency depends on your condition — some patients are checked every few hours, others more frequently. They try to be as unobtrusive as possible. If the disruptions are seriously affecting your sleep, talk to your care team about whether the frequency can be adjusted or if any checks can be consolidated.
What does it feel like to get an IV?

Having an IV placed involves a needle puncture into a vein, typically in your hand or forearm. You'll feel a pinch or prick when the needle goes in, but the Comfort Promise means your care team will offer topical anesthetic to numb the area first, and you can use distraction techniques like listening to music or watching something on your phone. Once the IV catheter is in place, the needle is actually removed — what stays in your vein is a thin, flexible plastic tube. The tube is secured with tape or a clear dressing. After placement, you might feel mild pressure at the site, but it shouldn't be painful. If it starts hurting, feels swollen, or looks red, tell your nurse immediately.
I'm nervous about being in the hospital. I've never stayed overnight before.

A first overnight stay in the hospital is a big deal, and feeling nervous about it is completely understandable. The unfamiliarity is usually the hardest part. Here's what to expect: your room will have a bed, and many rooms have space for a parent or caregiver to stay overnight too. Nurses check on you regularly, even through the night, so you're never really on your own. You can bring your own clothes, chargers, headphones, and comfort items from home. There's free Wi-Fi and a patient entertainment site for streaming. Once you settle in, it usually feels less intimidating than you imagined. If anything worries you, just talk to your nurse — they do this every day and they're genuinely here to help.
Is there financial help available for families?

Social workers can help your family access financial resources and community services. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre offers help with forms and applications. Pro Bono Law Ontario provides free legal assistance for low-income families. Some hotels nearby may offer hospital rates. Ask your care team or social worker — they're there to help navigate these things.
What if my family needs accommodations in London?

The Ronald McDonald House may be an option for families from outside London — speak with your care team about eligibility. LHSC also maintains a list of local hotels and motels on their website. Some offer preferred hospital rates, so it's worth asking when booking. The hospital doesn't endorse specific accommodations but provides the list as a community service.
I have a follow-up appointment in two weeks and I'm already anxious about it.

Anticipatory anxiety about medical appointments is very real, and it can start way before the actual event. Your brain is trying to prepare you, but sometimes it overdoes it. It might help to write down specifically what you're anxious about — is it the waiting? The potential news? A procedure? Once you name it, you can address it. If it's about information, prepare questions in advance so you feel in control. If it's about anxiety itself, ask your care team now about coping strategies you can use before and during the appointment. Two weeks is a long time to carry that weight. Don't wait until the appointment to address it.
How can I give positive feedback about someone who helped me?

LHSC has a Great Moments Recognition Program. You can fill out a short form on the LHSC website to recognize a staff member, physician, volunteer, or learner who made a difference. The person you recognize will receive a letter of appreciation from LHSC leadership and a small token. If you don't remember the person's exact name, include as many details as possible about when and where you interacted and the program will try to identify them.
What is security like at the hospital?

Security at Children's Hospital operates 24/7. The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m.; after hours, you'll need to check in with the security guard. The parking garage entrance is open 24 hours, but after-hours access also requires a security check-in. Some zone entrances have specific lock times — Zone D Level 2 and 3 doors lock from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m., and Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked around the clock. If you need an escort to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House, security patrols are available by calling extension 52281. The emergency response extension is 55555.
What does the Car Seat Technician do?

The Car Seat Technicians at LHSC's Trauma Program offer one-on-one consultations — both virtually and in person — to make sure car seats are installed correctly. By law, all children must travel in an approved car seat, so this is especially important when you're being discharged. If your child has specific mobility or medical needs post-discharge, a physiotherapist or occupational therapist may also help explore safe transportation options. Your nurse can help schedule a car seat consultation before you leave.
How is the hospital different at night versus during the day?

The hospital has a noticeably different atmosphere at night. Corridor lights are dimmed, hallway traffic decreases, and the general noise level drops — though it never reaches true silence because monitoring equipment runs continuously. Nursing staff are still fully active but work more quietly. Overnight visiting is restricted to those staying in the patient's room. Certain services are unavailable — the pharmacy, Tim Hortons, information desks, and parking offices all close in the evening. Entrances become security-controlled after 8:30 p.m. The shift change at 6:45 p.m. marks the transition, and the morning shift change at 6:45 a.m. signals the start of a new day of activity.
What is the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction (PPI) program?

The PPI program at Children's Hospital prepares one caregiver to accompany you into the operating room during the initial stage of anaesthesia — when you're being put to sleep. Before the procedure, the program offers an education session and/or a tour of Day Surgery and the OR so both you and your caregiver know what to expect. Having a familiar person present during induction can significantly reduce anxiety. Not every patient is eligible for PPI, so discuss it with your care team or a Child Life Specialist to find out if it's an option for your procedure.
What's the bedside shift change report?

It's a handoff process that happens when one nursing shift ends and another begins. The outgoing and incoming nurses review your care plan together, and you and your family are invited to listen and participate. The incoming nurse introduces themselves, they go over your care plan, complete safety checks, and ask if you have questions or anything to add. It typically takes three to five minutes. It's a good opportunity to stay informed about your care and flag anything the team might not know.
I'm worried about how I'll look when I get out. I've lost weight and I look sick.

It's natural to be concerned about your appearance, especially when your body has been through a lot. Physical changes from illness or a hospital stay are usually temporary — once you're eating normally, moving around, and recovering, your body will start to bounce back. Your care team, including a dietitian if needed, can help with a recovery plan. If these concerns feel overwhelming or start to really affect how you feel about yourself, the paediatric psychologists here are experienced with body image and self-esteem. What your body is doing right now is surviving and healing. Give it credit for that, even when the mirror feels unkind.
Can I use Upopolis?

If you're between 8 and 18, yes. Upopolis is a free, secure social networking site where paediatric patients can connect with each other across Canada. Laptops are available through Child Life Services for you to use it. Talk to a Child Life Specialist to get set up.
I hate that two nurses are in my room talking about me during shift change. It feels invasive.

The bedside shift change is actually designed to include you — it's your chance to hear what's happening with your care, ask questions, and correct anything that doesn't sound right. But if it feels invasive or you'd rather not be present for it, you can tell your nurse. The handover can happen outside your room. You can also use it to your advantage: listen for information about your care plan, and speak up if something is inaccurate or if you have concerns. If the conversation feels too clinical or ignores your presence, say so. You're a participant in your care, not just the subject of a report.
What is the Gender Pathways Service?

The Gender Pathways Service (GPS) provides gender-affirming care for gender diverse and transgender children and adolescents 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service that follows North American and international guidelines, including those from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health. You can learn more by contacting gps@lhsc.on.ca.
Who handles my personal health information and privacy?

Privacy at LHSC is taken seriously. Your personal health information (PHI) can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have the right to consent to or refuse collection, use, and disclosure of your PHI; to access your records; to be notified of inappropriate access; and to challenge the hospital's compliance with privacy laws. The Privacy Office can be reached at extension 32996 or privacy@lhsc.on.ca. If you have concerns about who's seeing your information, that's a conversation worth having with your care team. Your rights around your health information are protected by law.
I have a serious needle phobia. I literally cannot do this.

Needle phobia is really common and it's a real thing — you're not being dramatic. The staff at Children's Hospital take it seriously, and they have specific strategies to help. They can apply a topical anesthetic cream to numb the area beforehand so you feel less, and they can help you find a comfortable position. Distraction techniques like watching something on your phone or doing breathing exercises genuinely work for a lot of people. Let your nurse know how intense your fear is — they won't judge you, and they may be able to adjust the approach. You're allowed to feel scared AND get through it.
Is there Wi-Fi here and who do I contact if it's not working?

Yes — the hospital has Wi-Fi for patients. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free and access your own streaming accounts. If you're having trouble connecting, the Data Valet/Wi-Fi support line is 1-800-642-3958. You can also use your own cell phone to make calls and stay connected with friends and family. Patient telephones are available too for local and toll-free calls at no cost.
People keep offering to help and it makes me uncomfortable. I don't want pity.

Distinguishing between pity and genuine care is important, and I get that it can feel blurry. Most people offering help aren't pitying you — they're just responding to a situation where someone they care about is having a hard time. Accepting help isn't admitting defeat. You can accept help while still maintaining your dignity and independence in other ways. If certain offers feel patronizing, it's okay to decline them specifically. And if you'd rather channel support in a particular way — like asking friends to send memes instead of sympathy — tell them. You get to define how people show up for you.
Where does my parent sleep if they stay?

Most inpatient rooms provide a sleep space for one family member with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. In the PCCU, there are two sleep spaces at the bedside plus a nearby quiet room and sleep room. On B6, there's one overnight spot per patient. The NICU has kangaroo and sleeper chairs, though space can be limited. Each child must sleep in their own hospital bed — parents can't share it.
Is there a lawyer I can talk to? My family is going through a lot.

Children's Hospital has a partnership with Pro Bono Law Ontario (PBLO) that provides free legal assistance to low-income families whose child is an inpatient or outpatient. It's a medical-legal partnership that recognizes legal problems — housing, benefits, custody, immigration — can directly affect a child's health and a family's ability to provide care. A social worker on your care team can refer you to the on-site triage lawyer. It's a legitimate resource that's there specifically for families in your situation.
Who handles my medications when I'm admitted and is it different from home?

When you're admitted, your care team does a medication reconciliation — they review everything you're currently taking, including prescriptions, over-the-counter products, herbal supplements, vitamins, creams, inhalers, and eye drops. Medications from home shouldn't be taken unless approved by your care team, because the hospital will supply what's been prescribed and approved for use at LHSC. Your nurse administers your medications during your stay, scanning your armband each time. Before discharge, you'll receive an updated medication list to share with your family doctor and pharmacy. A pharmacist can come to your room to answer any questions about changes to your medications.
Are there any support resources specifically for my siblings?

Yes — Children's Hospital recognizes that a sibling's hospitalization affects the whole family. Child Life Specialists work with siblings as well as patients, and the Heroes' Circle program is available to siblings too, teaching breathing, relaxation, and coping techniques. Social workers can support your family as a unit, and spaces like the School-Age Activity Room and Ashley's Backyard are available to visiting siblings. If your brother or sister is struggling, your care team can help connect them with age-appropriate support.
How does the Bravery Beads program work?

Bravery Beads is a voluntary program open to patients of all ages who are dealing with a long-term or chronic illness or injury. Each bead represents a specific element of your care or treatment — procedures, tests, milestones in your journey. You string them together to create a tangible record of what you've been through. It's a way to acknowledge and document your experience, and many patients find it empowering to see their resilience represented physically. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to participate.
I keep seeing different students on my care team. How much of my care are they actually involved in?

Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital connected to Western University, so you'll likely interact with medical students as part of your care. They participate in things like physical exams, history-taking, and care discussions, but always under the supervision of residents and attending physicians. No medical student makes independent decisions about your treatment. They're there to learn, and your care quality isn't compromised — if anything, teaching hospitals tend to have strong protocols and oversight. If you're ever uncomfortable with a student being involved, you have the right to say so.
Who is involved in the PPI program?

PPI stands for Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction. The program involves your care team, a Child Life Specialist, and an anaesthesiologist. It offers an education session and potentially a tour of Day Surgery and the Operating Room to help you and one caregiver prepare for surgery. The program allows one caregiver to accompany you into the OR during the induction phase of anaesthesia — the part where you're falling asleep. Not every patient or caregiver is eligible, so discuss it with your care team or a Child Life Specialist if you're interested.
I have to use a wheelchair to get around and I feel like everyone is staring.

Self-consciousness about a wheelchair is really common, but in a hospital, you'll see wheelchairs everywhere — they're just a way to get around safely. Nobody is judging you for using one. If anything, people are probably wrapped up in their own concerns and barely noticing. The wheelchair is a tool that helps you move around while your body heals — it's not a statement about who you are. If it's bothering you emotionally, that's worth mentioning to a counsellor or social worker. But know that using a wheelchair right now is a practical, temporary measure, and it says nothing about your strength or your future mobility.
I feel like I have zero privacy here. People keep walking in.

Having your privacy disrupted is frustrating, especially as a teenager when privacy matters a lot. In a hospital, staff do need to check on you, but you have every right to ask them to knock, to close the curtain, or to give you a minute to get ready. If you're sharing a room, the curtain partition is there for you — use it. During nursing shift changes (around 6:45–7:30 a.m. and p.m.), things can be a bit busier. For more sensitive conversations, there are quiet rooms on the unit that can be used for privacy. Don't hesitate to tell your nurse what you need. Your comfort and dignity matter here.
What if I need to go to school while I'm here?

The Transitions in Care team helps with the school-to-hospital-to-school transition. Before discharge, it may be useful to speak with your teacher about missed work and your return. On the discharge checklist, the hospital reminds families to discuss conditions and health-care needs with principals or relevant school staff. Your social worker can also help with this.
What food options are there if I'm vegetarian?

The hospital offers vegetarian options as part of its patient food menu, including vegan meals and vegetarian options with dairy and eggs, or dairy, eggs, and fish. They also accommodate halal, kosher, and allergy-specific diets. You'll get a form with your breakfast tray where you can choose your meals for the next day. If you have specific preferences or concerns, ask your nurse to connect you with a dietitian — they can help customize your meals.
Are there charges for anything during my stay?

Most of your care is covered, but there may be charges for certain supplies and devices not covered by OHIP — things like crutches, breast pumps, or surgical supplies. The Business Office is in Zone D, 3rd floor, Room D3-400. You'll receive an invoice by mail and can pay online, at the bank, or by cheque. Parking is also a paid service.
What if I have a complaint about my care?

Start by talking with your care team directly — they may be able to resolve it right away. If that doesn't work, you can contact Patient Relations by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, or through the online contact form on the LHSC website. They check messages Monday to Friday between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.
What does a Child Life Specialist actually do for teenagers? I'm not a little kid.

Totally fair question. Child Life Specialists aren't just for young kids — they work with patients up to age 18. For teens, their role shifts from play-based support to things like procedural preparation, pain management strategies, coping techniques, and emotional support. They can help you understand what's going to happen during a procedure in a straightforward way, connect you with resources like Upopolis (a secure social network for hospitalized patients ages 8–18), and advocate for your preferences to the care team. They're also available if you just need someone to talk to who isn't your parent or your doctor.
Why is my nurse always documenting everything?

Nurses are required to chart every aspect of your care — vitals, medications given, assessments, your responses, communications with your team, and more. This documentation serves several purposes: it ensures continuity when shifts change, provides a legal record of your care, allows your whole team to track your progress, and supports quality assurance. It might seem like they're always on the computer, but that charting is directly tied to the quality and safety of your care.
What exactly does a dietitian do at the hospital?

A hospital dietitian assesses your nutritional needs based on your medical condition and treatment. They might modify your diet to support healing, manage a condition, account for food allergies, or ensure you're getting adequate nutrition if you have reduced appetite. They can accommodate religious and ethical dietary preferences too. If you're on a specific diet and have questions or concerns, ask your nurse to arrange a consultation with a dietitian.
I keep asking myself 'why me?' and I can't find an answer.

That's one of the most human questions there is, and the hard truth is that there isn't usually a satisfying answer. Illness doesn't target people who deserve it. It's random, and that randomness can feel maddening. You didn't do anything to cause this. Some people find that instead of answering 'why me,' it helps to shift toward 'what now' — not because the question isn't valid, but because it's a question that has actionable answers. If this question is consuming you, talking to a spiritual care practitioner, psychologist, or someone you trust could help you process it. You don't have to figure this out alone.
How do room numbers work?

Room numbers at Children's Hospital follow a consistent format that's actually pretty straightforward once you know the code. A room number like B2-503 breaks down as: B = Zone B (the zone of the hospital), 2 = second floor, and 503 = the specific room number. Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital campus. Knowing this system helps you navigate independently. You can also download the MazeMap app for an interactive indoor map, use wayfinding kiosks on-site, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays.
Someone asked me about research participation. Is that safe?

Clinical research at LHSC must be reviewed and approved by the London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute and a qualified Research Ethics Board before any patient is ever approached. These boards exist to protect participants. You should receive a detailed Letter of Information explaining the study's purpose, procedures, risks, and your rights. Participation is always completely voluntary — declining has zero effect on your care. Take your time, read everything, and ask as many questions as you need. If you have concerns about a study, you can contact LHSCRI's Quality Assurance and Education Team or the Patient Relations Office. Being cautious about research participation is not just okay — it's expected.
My family uses traditional tobacco for cultural purposes. Does anyone here accommodate that?

Yes. Under the Smoke-Free Ontario Act, there's an exemption for traditional use of tobacco by Indigenous peoples. LHSC provides a designated space for Indigenous peoples to use tobacco for traditional, cultural, or spiritual purposes. The Youth Indigenous Wellness Consultant can also support cultural practices during your stay. If you'd like to access this space or connect with Indigenous Health services, ask your care team or email IndigenousHealth@lhsc.on.ca. The hospital is committed to respecting cultural and spiritual practices.
My parents were told about a 'Decision Coach.' What is that?

A Decision Coach is part of LHSC's Shared Decision Making program. When you and your family face an important medical choice — like deciding between treatment options — a Decision Coach helps structure the process. They work with you, your caregivers, and your health-care providers to make sure you understand the evidence, weigh the risks and benefits, and factor in your personal values. It's about making informed decisions collaboratively rather than having something just decided for you. Your care team can refer you, or you can ask about it directly.
Family members keep calling for updates and I just want to be left alone.

Caring can sometimes feel overwhelming when you're dealing with your own health. It's okay to set boundaries. You can ask your parent to be the single point of contact — one person who shares updates with the wider family so you're not fielding calls constantly. The hospital's privacy policies actually support this approach; information is only shared with parents or guardians, and they can coordinate from there. It's okay to say 'I appreciate the care, but I need quiet time right now.' Anyone who truly cares about you will respect that. Protecting your energy is part of your recovery.
I don't want to need help for everything. It makes me feel weak.

Needing help isn't weakness — it's being human in a situation that demands more than one person can handle alone. You'd never think a friend was weak for needing help in the hospital, right? Give yourself the same compassion. This dependency is temporary. As you heal, you'll gradually regain your independence. In the meantime, accepting help is actually a strength — it means you're focused on recovery, not on proving something. The doctors, nurses, physios, and other staff here are specifically trained to help you get back to independence. That's the goal for everyone involved.
Why do they keep talking to me like I'm five? I'm sixteen.

That's frustrating, and you shouldn't have to deal with that. You're a young adult and you deserve to be spoken to accordingly. Some staff may default to a younger communication style because they work with a wide age range, but that doesn't make it okay. You can say something like, 'I appreciate you explaining that, but I'd like the full details — you can talk to me like an adult.' Most professionals will adjust immediately once they realize. You're entitled to understand your own health in real terms. Advocating for how you want to be treated is an important skill, and this is a good time to use it.
I'm going to lose my job because I can't tell them when I'll be back.

That's a real concern, and the financial independence that a job provides matters. If you haven't already, have your parent help you communicate with your employer about your situation. Many employers are more understanding than you'd expect, and depending on the circumstances, there may be legal protections. A social worker at the hospital can also help you understand your options. Try not to add job stress on top of health stress — right now, your primary job is recovering. You can find another position if needed, but you only get one body. Take care of it first.
What's the security situation here?

LHSC has security patrols and several access control measures. The B Tower entrance is open 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. and controlled by security after hours. Certain zones lock at 8:00 p.m. or are locked 24/7. The Emergency Department has a weapons detection system. If you need a security escort to your car or the Ronald McDonald House, call dispatch at extension 52281. For emergencies, the extension is 55555.
What is the PCCU like for overnight stays?

In the Paediatric Critical Care Unit, there are two sleep spaces right at your bedside for family members, with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets provided. There's also a nearby quiet room that sleeps one and a sleep room that sleeps two — they share a bathroom with a shower. Space is set up to keep family close while giving the care team room to do their work.
I feel like all anyone sees is a patient. Not me.

That's a profound observation, and it's something a lot of hospitalized teens feel. When your identity gets reduced to a diagnosis or a room number, it can feel dehumanizing. You are so much more than a patient — you're a person with interests, goals, opinions, and a life outside these walls. Remind people of that. Talk about your interests, put up photos, wear your own clothes when you can. The staff here do their best to see the whole person, but you can help by bringing your personality to the forefront. And if you want to talk through this with someone, the psychologists here understand this particular kind of struggle well.
What is the Ronald McDonald House?

The Ronald McDonald House is an accommodation option for families of patients who live outside of London. It's located near the hospital, and your care team can provide more details about eligibility and how to access it. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room within the hospital itself. If you need personal care items during your stay — things like a toothbrush, deodorant, or shampoo — you can find them at the Paediatric Family Resource Centre, the Ronald McDonald Room, or the hospital gift shops.
I noticed my care partner can only bring one other person. Who decides that?

The Care Partner Presence Policy at LHSC sets those limits. For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at the bedside at one time. For outpatients, it's one care partner per patient. The policy is monitored to align with provincial standards and infection prevention recommendations. During outbreaks or for patients with COVID precautions, only essential care partners are allowed. These aren't arbitrary rules — they're designed to balance family presence with patient safety and infection control. Your care team can provide more details about specific permissions and any exceptions.
What are the visitor rules?

Visiting is based on your condition, care needs, and your wishes, so times may vary between patients and units. Check with the unit staff about optimal visiting times. A few key rules: visitors should not come if they've been sick in the last week, everyone must wash their hands or use hand sanitizer before and after visiting, and visiting may be paused temporarily for care needs or privacy reasons. Overnight visitors (8:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.) should stay in the patient's room.
Where's the ATM?

ATMs are located near the elevators in Zone B on the 1st and 3rd floors, right next to the vending machines. If you need to pay a bill at the Business Office, that's in Zone D, 3rd floor, Room D3-400.
What time do the doors lock?

The B Tower main entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily. After 8:30 p.m., entry is controlled by Security and caregivers need to check in with the guard. The parking garage entrance is open 24 hours, but after hours you still need to check in with Security. Zone D entrances on Levels 2 and 3 lock at 8:00 p.m. and reopen at 6:00 a.m., while Zone D Level 4 and Zone B Level 8 are locked 24/7.
What if I need home care after discharge?

If you need equipment or services at home after discharge, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator will assess your needs before you leave. If you're already receiving community services, contact the coordinator at extension 52249 before going home. For stays longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required — nursing staff can help facilitate the doctor's referral.
Can I ask the doctors to explain what's happening to me?

Yes, and you should. You have every right to understand your care plan, your diagnosis, what tests are being ordered and why, what medications you're taking, and what the expected outcomes are. If something isn't clear, ask them to explain it differently. If you feel like you're being talked around rather than talked to, let your care team know — you can also ask your nurse to help facilitate better communication.
What accessibility supports are available?

LHSC provides drop-off points at main doors for people with mobility challenges, wheelchairs at entrances, amplified phones, relay services, and sign language and deaf-blind translation upon request. All required documents can be provided in accessible formats. If you need accommodations, let your care team know. Accessible parking spaces are available throughout visitor lots and garages.
Is there anyone who can help me figure out my feelings about a chronic diagnosis?

There are several people on your team who can help. Paediatric psychologists specialize in helping children and teens adjust to illness and develop coping strategies for managing physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. Social workers provide emotional support and can connect you with community resources. Child Life Specialists can help you process your feelings through conversation, activities, or creative expression. Spiritual Care Specialists are also available regardless of your religious background. You're not expected to handle a chronic diagnosis on your own — ask your nurse for a referral to whichever service feels like the right fit.
Is there anywhere private I can go in this hospital?

There are a few options. The Quiet Rooms on B6 (rooms B6-119 and B6-257) are available for private conversations, phone calls, or just needing a moment to yourself — check with your nurse or unit clerk before using them. The Sanctuary (C3-402) is open 24/7 for quiet reflection. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre (B1-006) offers a quieter space as well. If you just need space from the constant activity in your room, let your nurse know and they can help you find somewhere.
What's the role of the respiratory therapist?

A respiratory therapist, or RT, specializes in your lungs and breathing. At Children's Hospital, RTs manage ventilators and breathing equipment, perform breathing tests like spirometry, administer inhaled medications, and help with airway management. In critical care settings like the PCCU, they work closely with the medical team to support patients who need mechanical ventilation. If you're having breathing difficulties or have a respiratory condition, an RT is a key member of your care team. They can explain what the equipment does and answer questions about your respiratory treatment plan.
Can I request a specific nurse or doctor?

You can express a preference, and your care team will do their best to accommodate it where possible. However, staffing assignments depend on factors like nurse-to-patient ratios, shift schedules, and unit needs, so there's no guarantee. If you have a specific reason for the request — like a strong rapport with a particular nurse or a communication issue with a team member — it's worth mentioning to the charge nurse or your care team. At the very least, they'll take your feedback seriously.
I had a scholarship offer for next year. I don't know if I can still take it.

That must feel devastating — working toward something and then having it threatened by something completely beyond your control. Before you spiral, here's what I'd suggest: most scholarship programs have processes for medical deferrals or accommodations. Have your parent contact the institution to explain the situation. A letter from your doctor can go a long way. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital may also be able to support you with documentation and planning. Don't give up on that scholarship before you've explored every option. And even if adjustments need to be made, this setback doesn't erase the achievement that earned you the offer in the first place.
How do I prepare to leave the hospital?

Your care team starts planning for discharge early in your stay. Before you leave, you'll go over your medications (purpose, dosage, side effects, next dose timing), any equipment needs, follow-up appointment schedules, and any activity or dietary changes at home. Make sure you know who to contact in an emergency. Pack up all your belongings, confirm your ride, and bring a car seat if needed. If you've been here more than 14 days with existing community services, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required.
What does an overnight stay look like?

If you're admitted as an inpatient, you'll be assigned a room on the ward. Your bed has adjustable positioning and side rails. One family member can stay overnight — a sleep space with clean linens is provided in most rooms. Nurses will check on you regularly throughout the night to monitor your safety and comfort. Meals are served at set times, and you can use the family pantry for snacks. You can wear your own clothes, use your phone, watch TV, and access streaming services. During nighttime hours (8 p.m. to 8 a.m.), visitors should remain in the room. You'll sleep in your own hospital bed — no doubling up — so nurses can access you easily.
When's lunch?

Lunch is from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. You pick your meals ahead of time on a form that comes with breakfast. Before you eat anything — including food people bring you from outside — always check with your care team. There could be dietary restrictions tied to your treatment.
Is there a therapist I can talk to?

There are several options. Paediatric Psychology Services offers assessment and treatment for adjustment challenges, coping strategies, and emotional and behavioural support. Social workers provide emotional support and advocacy. Child Life Specialists help with coping and self-expression. There's also Spiritual Care if that's helpful for you. Ask your care team to connect you with whoever fits best.
Why can't I bring latex balloons?

Latex balloons are banned throughout LHSC due to latex allergy risk. Latex allergies can cause severe reactions including anaphylaxis in sensitized individuals, and in a hospital where immunocompromised and allergic patients are nearby, this is a serious concern. Foil (mylar) balloons are a safe alternative. Similarly, poinsettia plants are prohibited because they contain a compound chemically similar to rubber latex that can trigger reactions through touch or inhalation.
What is the Black Health Navigator service?

Black Health Navigators are trained, registered healthcare workers available to help Black patients and families navigate the healthcare system at LHSC. They can provide information about healthcare options and ensure your voice is heard in conversations with your care team. This service is accessed through Black Health at LHSC. You can ask your care team to connect you or reach out directly by email at BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
How do I talk to my care team about my concerns?

Open communication is actively encouraged at Children's Hospital. You can raise questions or concerns with any member of your care team at any time. During bedside shift changes and daily rounds, you're invited to participate and share input. If something isn't being addressed, ask to speak with the charge nurse or the attending physician directly. Writing down your questions beforehand helps you cover everything. If you're uncomfortable speaking up in front of a group, ask for a private conversation. Your care team also includes social workers who can help facilitate communication if needed. You have the right to understand your care, ask for things to be re-explained, and express disagreement.
What does it feel like when they remove stitches?

Removing stitches is usually much less uncomfortable than people expect. The nurse or doctor uses small scissors to cut the thread and then gently pulls each stitch out with tweezers. You'll feel a slight tugging sensation, but it typically isn't painful — more like a mild pulling. If the wound has healed well around the stitches, removal is quick. Some patients describe a brief stinging sensation. The area might feel slightly tender afterward. Dissolving stitches don't need removal — they break down on their own over time. If you're nervous, let your care team know and they can talk you through it step by step.
Can I get a security escort to my car?
Yes. Security patrols are available to escort you to your car or to the Ronald McDonald House. Just call Security dispatch at extension 52281. It's a smart move if you're leaving late at night.
What's the difference between a resident and a medical student?

Medical students are still in medical school — they've graduated university and are completing their MD degree. Residents have already finished medical school and earned their degree, and they're now doing hands-on specialty training. Both may be involved in your care, but they're always supervised by attending physicians. It's a layered system: the attending physician oversees residents, who in turn oversee medical students. You have every right to ask who's who on your care team.
I don't really feel anything anymore. I'm just... numb.

Emotional numbness can be your mind's way of protecting you when there's too much to process. It's not weakness or being broken — it's a coping mechanism. But if it persists, it's worth paying attention to. You might be experiencing emotional exhaustion from everything you've been through. Please mention this to your care team. Children's Hospital has psychologists who work with teens specifically, and they can help you work through what you're feeling — or not feeling. There's no wrong way to react to a difficult situation, but you deserve support through all of it.
Why do hospitals use so much hand sanitizer instead of just soap?

Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) is actually the preferred hand hygiene method in hospitals when hands aren't visibly dirty. It's faster, more effective against most pathogens, and can be placed at point-of-care — meaning right outside every room and at every bedside. The alcohol denatures the proteins of bacteria and viruses almost instantly. Soap and water is reserved for visibly soiled hands or specific situations like C. difficile, since alcohol doesn't kill those spores. It's all about efficiency and accessibility in a setting where hand hygiene compliance literally saves lives.
How many visitors can I have?

For inpatients, up to two care partners can be at your bedside at one time. The hospital encourages keeping visits manageable — too many visitors at once can be tough when you're trying to rest and recover. If your unit is on outbreak precautions, only essential care partners may be permitted. Check with your care team for specifics.
Can I go outside the hospital during my stay?

That's up to your care team and depends on your condition. Some patients may be able to visit outdoor spaces like Alex's Butterfly Garden (D Zone, Level 2), which is a peaceful landscaped area with benches and a water fountain. Others may have restrictions due to their care plan, IV lines, or infection control precautions. Always get permission from your nurse first. If you're feeling cooped up, let your team know — sometimes even a brief change of scenery helps.
What's the Great Moments Recognition Program?

It's LHSC's way of recognizing staff, physicians, volunteers, learners, and patient partners who go above and beyond. If someone on your care team made a real difference in your experience, you or your family can fill out a short form on the LHSC website. The person you recognize receives a letter of appreciation from an LHSC supervisor and a small item of recognition, supported by London Health Sciences Foundation and Children's Health Foundation. You don't even need to remember their exact name — if you describe the details of the interaction, the program can help identify who it was.
What do all those numbers on the monitor mean?

The bedside monitor typically displays several vital signs. Heart rate (HR) is how many times your heart beats per minute. Blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) shows the percentage of oxygen-carrying haemoglobin in your blood. Blood pressure might show as two numbers (systolic/diastolic). Respiratory rate (RR) tracks your breaths per minute. Each parameter has an acceptable range, and the monitor alarms if a reading falls outside that range. If you want to know what your specific numbers mean, ask your nurse — they can walk you through what's normal for you.
I feel like I have no control over anything in my life right now.

That loss of control is one of the hardest parts of being hospitalized, and it's even harder when you're at an age where you're supposed to be gaining more independence. While you can't control your medical situation, there are things within your control: you can ask questions and participate in care decisions, choose what you eat within your diet options, decide when to have visitors, keep up with your own routines. Reclaiming even small choices can help. If this feeling of helplessness is becoming overwhelming, please talk to someone — a psychologist or social worker here can help you find strategies for coping.
What are Bravery Beads?

Bravery Beads is a voluntary program where each bead represents a different element of your care or treatment — an IV insertion, a blood draw, a surgery, an MRI, etc. Over time, you build a personal record of what you've been through. It's available for patients of all ages dealing with long-term or chronic conditions. Some people find it a meaningful way to track and acknowledge their experience. Ask your care team or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to participate.
What are the accommodation options for my family?

Most inpatient rooms at Children's Hospital have space for one family member to stay overnight, with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets provided. In the PCCU, there are two bedside sleep spaces plus a nearby quiet room and a sleep room with a shared bathroom. For families coming from outside London, the Ronald McDonald House is an option — ask your care team for details. There's also a Ronald McDonald Family Room within the hospital. For extended stays, some London-area hotels and motels offer 'hospital rate' discounts — a list of local accommodations is on the LHSC website, though it's not comprehensive or endorsed.
What does the hospital operator do?

The hospital operator is the person who answers the main LHSC phone line at 519-685-8500 when you press 0. They route incoming calls to the correct department, unit, or staff member. If someone outside the hospital wants to reach you, they'll likely go through the operator first. The operator can connect callers to pretty much any department — from your inpatient unit to Patient Relations to the parking office. It's the central switchboard for the entire hospital.
Can I get music therapy?

Yes. An accredited music therapist at Children's Hospital uses music-based activities to support patients in areas like pain control and rehabilitation. It's available for patients of any age, illness, or disability, and you don't need any musical skill to participate. Ask your care team to arrange a session.
What interpretation services are available?

LHSC offers free interpretation services for patients and families. If you or your family are more comfortable communicating in a language other than English, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, ask your care team to arrange an interpreter. The hospital emphasizes that clear communication between you and your care team is essential for safe care, so don't hesitate to request this service. A downloadable list of available spoken languages is on the LHSC website. For hearing support specifically, amplified phones, relay services, and sign language translation are all available.
Is there someone I can talk to about end-of-life stuff?

Yes — and it takes courage to ask that question. The Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care Services (PSMSC) team specializes in caring for children and teens with serious illnesses, including those approaching end of life. Their focus is on quality of life and easing pain and suffering. Spiritual Care Specialists are also available for emotional and existential support regardless of your faith background. Social workers can help with family communication and planning. Psychologists offer therapeutic support for processing what you're going through. You can ask your care team to connect you with any or all of these services. You don't have to navigate this alone.
Why do I have to fast before surgery?

When you're under general anaesthesia, the reflexes that normally prevent stomach contents from entering your lungs are suppressed. If there's food or liquid in your stomach, it could come back up and be aspirated into your lungs, which can cause a serious condition called aspiration pneumonia. Fasting guidelines are based on evidence about how long different types of food and liquid take to leave the stomach. It's not fun, but it's one of the most important pre-surgical safety measures.
I overheard someone mention ethics consultation. When would that happen?

LHSC has a clinical ethics consultation service available when patients, families, or health-care providers are facing a difficult ethical decision in a care situation. This could involve choices about treatment options, end-of-life care, consent, or other complex situations where there isn't one clear right answer. The ethicist is trained to help all parties identify, clarify, and work through ethical concerns. Any patient, family member, or care provider can request an ethics consultation. It's not adversarial — it's a structured way to navigate genuinely hard decisions together.
Can I ask for numbing cream before a needle?

Yes — it's actually part of the hospital's Comfort Promise. They offer topical anesthetic (usually a cream or gel) that numbs the skin before needle procedures. It works quickly. You can also ask about comfort positioning and distraction techniques. Don't hesitate to advocate for yourself — the whole point of the Comfort Promise is that you shouldn't have to just tough it out.
I heard there's a therapeutic clown. Isn't that kind of childish?

I get why that might seem that way. Ollie is a therapeutic clown at Children's Hospital, and while the approach is definitely geared more toward younger patients, the role is actually more nuanced than you'd think. Therapeutic clowns are trained professionals who use humour and play to help normalize the hospital environment. For teens, Ollie might not be your thing — and that's completely fine. Children's Hospital has plenty of other support options for older patients, like music therapy, art therapy, the Heroes' Circle program, and Upopolis. You get to choose what works for you.
What does my nurse actually do all day?

Your nurse is the backbone of your daily care. They administer medications, monitor your vital signs, assess your condition, manage IVs and other equipment, coordinate tests and appointments, communicate with your physicians and the rest of your care team, document everything in your chart, provide patient education, and respond to your needs and concerns throughout their shift. They also participate in bedside shift change reports twice a day and perform regular safety checks — including overnight. Nurses at Children's Hospital work closely with families, organize discharge follow-ups, and serve as your primary point of contact for navigating the hospital system.
My nurse said I should talk to someone about how I'm adjusting. Who did she mean?

She was likely referring to a paediatric psychologist or possibly a social worker. Psychologists at Children's Hospital provide assessment and treatment for patients experiencing challenges adjusting to illness, hospitalization, or disability. They teach coping strategies for managing physical, emotional, and behavioural symptoms. They can also assess cognitive and learning skills if your medical condition affects those areas. Social workers provide emotional support too, along with practical advocacy. Both are solid options depending on what you're dealing with — your nurse can help facilitate a referral.
What if my nurse isn't available when someone calls for me?

It can be harder to get through to the unit by phone during nursing shift changes, which happen from 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. The hospital suggests having one family member act as the main contact person who can relay updates to everyone else. When calling the unit, provide your full name and ask to speak with your nurse.
I can't do my daily prayers properly in here. It feels wrong.

Maintaining your spiritual practices is important, and the hospital recognizes that. There's a sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C — room C3-402 — that's available 24/7 for prayer, meditation, and quiet reflection, and it's open to people of all faiths. If you need specific accommodations — a particular direction to face, specific times, dietary requirements — let your care team know. There's also a Spiritual Care service that can help. If you're Indigenous, the Youth Indigenous Wellness Program and the Indigenous Healing Space in E1-204 may be resources for you. Your spiritual wellbeing is part of your care, and the hospital should support it.
Who's the music therapist and what can they actually do for me?

Children's Hospital has an accredited music therapist who uses music-based activities to support patients' health and well-being. It's not just background music — music therapy is a clinical intervention that can help with pain management, rehabilitation, emotional processing, and stress reduction. You don't need any musical skill to participate. Sessions are individualized and can range from listening to making music depending on what you're dealing with. It's available to patients of any age, illness, or disability. If you're interested, ask your nurse to set up a session.
What does it mean to be on a locked unit?

The B6 inpatient unit is a locked unit, which means doors are secured and access is controlled. Once you're admitted, you'll be given a confidential code to get in and out. This isn't about restricting you — it's a security measure to protect all patients on the floor, especially younger children. One family member can stay overnight with you. Clean sheets, pillows, and blankets are provided for the sleep space. If you feel uncomfortable with the locked setup, talk to your care team about any concerns.
I'm bored out of my mind. There's literally nothing to do.

Hospital boredom is real, and it can make everything feel worse. Here are some options you might not know about: there's free Wi-Fi, a patient entertainment site for streaming, and your own phone works here. But beyond screens — the hospital has art therapy, music therapy, and a School-Age Activity Room with games and crafts on the sixth floor. There's also the SMILE Room in B6-261 with sensory equipment. Child Life Specialists can connect you with activities, and if you're into martial arts or mindfulness, the Heroes' Circle program visits patients weekly. Ask your nurse what's happening this week. There's more going on than it seems from your room.
What are vital signs and how are they measured?

Vital signs are routine measurements that give your care team a snapshot of your basic body functions. They include: temperature (measured with an oral, ear, or forehead thermometer), heart rate (pulse, often measured via a monitor or manually), blood pressure (using an inflatable cuff that temporarily squeezes your arm), respiratory rate (counting your breaths per minute), and oxygen saturation (measured with a pulse oximeter clipped to your finger, which uses a light sensor to measure blood oxygen levels). These checks are done frequently — sometimes every few hours — and are completely painless. Changes in vital signs help your care team detect issues early.
What should I expect from a blood pressure check?

A blood pressure cuff is wrapped around your upper arm and inflated either manually with a pump or automatically by a machine. As it inflates, it squeezes your arm progressively tighter — it's not painful but can feel uncomfortable for the few seconds it's at maximum pressure. Then it slowly deflates while the device reads your blood pressure. The result is two numbers (systolic over diastolic) that tell your care team how hard your heart is working to pump blood. If you've had blood pressure taken before, it's the same process. If the cuff is too tight or uncomfortable, let your nurse know — a different size cuff can make a difference.
What happens if I feel unsafe or uncomfortable with someone on my care team?

You have every right to speak up. Start by telling your parent or caregiver, and then communicate your concern to your nurse or another trusted member of your care team. If the situation isn't resolved, the Patient Relations Office is your next escalation point — extension 52036 or patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca. You can also ask to speak with a social worker. LHSC is committed to safe, respectful care. Advocating for yourself when something doesn't feel right is not only okay — it's exactly what the hospital encourages.
What if I need an interpreter?

LHSC offers free interpretation services for patients who are most comfortable speaking in a language other than English, or for those who are deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing. Just ask your care team to arrange one. They can also set up sign language or deaf-blind translation. You're entitled to communicate with your care team in a language you're comfortable with — never hesitate to ask for this.
What is the Paediatric Medical Day Unit (PMDU)?

The PMDU is where paediatric patients go for day treatments — procedures or therapies that don't require an overnight stay. You come in, receive your treatment, are monitored for the appropriate period, and go home the same day. Light snacks are provided for patients receiving treatment there. The environment is generally less intense than the inpatient ward, and you won't be assigned a permanent room. The types of treatments vary widely depending on your condition. Your care team will let you know in advance what to expect for your specific appointment at the PMDU.
What's the Wi-Fi situation here?

The hospital has free Wi-Fi available. You can connect your phone, laptop, or tablet to it. There's also a patient entertainment site where you can stream live Rogers TV for free or log into your own accounts on services like Netflix. If you run into connection issues, you or your family can call the Data Valet service at 1-800-642-3958 for help.
Can I get my prescriptions filled at the hospital before I leave?

Yes. The Children's Hospital Pharmacy (B1-001, near the B1 entrance) can fill prescriptions for you before discharge. They're open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5:30 p.m., excluding holidays. Getting your prescriptions filled before you leave is convenient and means you don't have to make a stop on the way home. Make sure your care team sends the prescription down in time, especially if your discharge is in the afternoon.
What happens if I press the emergency call button by accident?

Nothing bad — it happens all the time. A nurse will respond to check on you, and you just tell them it was accidental. They'd much rather respond to a false alarm than have you hesitate to use it when you actually need something. The call button is your direct line to your nursing team, and there's no limit on how often you can use it. Use it for pain, questions, needing to get up, feeling unwell — anything.
The Wi-Fi here is so slow. It's the one thing keeping me sane.

I hear you — reliable internet is basically a lifeline when you're stuck in a hospital, and slow Wi-Fi makes everything more frustrating.
