If you're having connection issues, you can call the data valet and Wi-Fi support line for help. Sometimes switching between the available networks or moving closer to a different access point helps. You can also download content at home before a hospital visit when possible, so you have shows, music, and podcasts available offline. It's not a perfect solution, but it's a workaround. And for what it's worth, the hospital does recognize that connectivity matters for patient wellbeing.
Is there a place to pray or meditate in the hospital?

The Sanctuary (room C3-402, Zone C, level 3) is a dedicated sacred space open 24/7 for prayer, quiet reflection, and meditation. It's open to everyone regardless of faith or belief. There's also the Indigenous Healing Space (E1-204), which is available with priority to First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous people. If you'd like spiritual support from a practitioner, you can request one through your nurse (pager 14693). LHSC's spiritual care service supports all spiritual and religious needs.
What happens before surgery?

Before surgery, your care team will explain the procedure, risks, benefits, and what to expect for recovery. You'll likely need to fast for a specific period beforehand — your nurse will give you exact instructions on when to stop eating and drinking. On the day of surgery, you'll change into a hospital gown, and staff will confirm your identity using your armband multiple times. Your vitals will be checked, and you'll meet the anaesthesia team. If you're eligible for the PPI program, one caregiver can accompany you into the OR during anaesthesia induction. A Child Life Specialist can also help with preparation if you're anxious. After surgery, you'll be monitored in a recovery area before returning to your room.
Can I take my own meds while I'm admitted?

Bring your medications or a complete list of them (including over-the-counter, herbal products, vitamins, creams, inhalers, and eye drops), but don't take anything from home unless your care team explicitly approves it. While admitted, the hospital will supply any medications prescribed for use at LHSC. Let your nurse and physician know about any recently stopped medications and any allergies.
The nurses keep checking on me at night and waking me up. Who told them to do that?

Night-time checks are a standard part of nursing care ordered by your physician and carried out by the nursing team. They're there to ensure your safety, comfort, and to catch any changes in your condition early. The frequency of checks depends on your medical situation — some patients require more frequent monitoring than others. I know interrupted sleep is frustrating, especially when you're trying to recover. If it's really affecting your rest, it's worth mentioning to your nurse or doctor to see if there's any flexibility, but safety always comes first.
My parents are stressed. Is there someone who can help them too?

Absolutely — and it's good that you're thinking about them. Social workers at Children's Hospital provide emotional support, advocacy, and practical information for families coping with a child's hospitalization. They can connect your parents with community resources, financial support, and counselling. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre in B1-006 that offers peer support and help with forms and applications. A Spiritual Care Specialist is available via pager 14693 for emotional and spiritual support. Your parents can also access a quiet Sanctuary space on the third floor of Zone C anytime. Encourage them to talk to your care team about what they need.
They keep doing tests. How many more do I need?

Test fatigue is real. Every time you think it might be the last one, there's another. It can feel like your body is just a specimen. You have every right to ask your doctor why each test is being done and what they're looking for. Understanding the purpose can make it feel less arbitrary. Ask if there's a testing plan and how many more are anticipated. Informed patients feel more in control. And if a test feels unnecessary or you have concerns, speak up — you're part of the decision-making process. Your care team should be transparent with you about what's happening and why.
I noticed some staff wearing different coloured scrubs. Does the colour mean something?

In many hospitals, scrub colours can indicate different departments or roles — for example, surgical staff might wear one colour while nurses wear another. The specifics vary between hospitals, and LHSC doesn't have a universally standardized colour-coding system that's been published for patients. If you're curious about what a particular person's role is, the most reliable approach is to check their name badge, which should display their name and title. You can also just ask — staff expect that question and are happy to introduce themselves.
There are interpreters here? How does that work?

LHSC offers free interpretation services for patients. If English isn't the language you're most comfortable with, or if you're deaf, deafened, or hard of hearing, you can request an interpreter through your care team. The hospital provides sign language and deaf-blind translation, relay services via the telephone company, and spoken language interpreters. There's a downloadable list of available spoken languages on the LHSC website. The goal is to make sure you can fully understand and participate in conversations about your care — and that your care team understands you. Don't hesitate to ask for this service.
What support is there for trans or gender-diverse patients?

Children's Hospital has a dedicated Gender Pathways Service (GPS) that provides gender-affirming care for children and teens 17 and under. It's a multidisciplinary service that follows guidelines from the World Professional Association for Transgender Health and other North American and international standards. If you'd like to learn more or access the service, you can contact them directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca or ask your care team for a referral.
How is a breathing treatment delivered?

Breathing treatments are typically administered through a nebulizer or a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. A nebulizer converts liquid medication into a fine mist that you breathe in through a mask or mouthpiece — the session usually lasts 10 to 15 minutes. You'll hear a gentle hissing or humming from the machine. With an inhaler and spacer, you take coordinated breaths to draw the medication deep into your lungs. Both methods are painless. Your respiratory therapist or nurse will guide you through proper technique. If you have questions about why a specific method was chosen for you, ask your care team.
How does a pulse oximeter actually work?

A pulse oximeter clips onto your finger and uses two wavelengths of light — one red, one infrared — that pass through your fingertip. Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb these wavelengths differently, so a sensor on the other side of the clip reads the ratio and calculates your blood oxygen saturation (SpO2). It also picks up your pulse rate from the fluctuation in blood volume with each heartbeat. It's completely non-invasive, painless, and gives results in seconds.
What can I expect from the discharge process?

Discharge planning starts early in your admission. Before you leave, your care team will go over your care instructions, including medications (purpose, dosage, timing, side effects), dietary needs, activity restrictions, and follow-up appointments. You'll receive written instructions to take home. Make sure you understand everything — ask for clarification if anything's unclear. Your family should bring a car seat if required by law (all children legally need one). If your stay was longer than 14 days or you need home care services, a referral to Ontario Health atHome may be needed. Try to be ready to leave at your scheduled discharge time, though it may shift. If transportation is an issue, ask your nurse about options.
I can't sleep here. It's too noisy and people keep coming in.

Hospital sleep is notoriously terrible, and you're not imagining it. Between the beeping monitors, hallway noise, and regular check-ins, getting proper rest is a real challenge. There are some things that can help: bring headphones and use a white noise or sleep sounds app, ask your nurse if the lights can be dimmed, wear an eye mask, and request that non-urgent checks be consolidated when possible. The nursing staff does need to check on you during the night for safety, but they'll try to be quick and quiet. Let your nurse know that sleep is a real issue — they deal with this a lot and may have additional suggestions.
My parents are hovering and it's driving me crazy. I need space.

That tension between needing your parents and needing your independence is already real at your age — and a hospital stay dials it up to eleven. Your parents are probably in overdrive because they're scared and don't know how else to help. Try having an honest conversation: acknowledge that you know they're worried, and then explain what you actually need — maybe it's some alone time during the day, or having them step out during certain check-ups. Most parents respond well when they know what helps. You can also talk to your nurse about facilitating that conversation if it feels too hard to do directly.
What does it feel like to wake up from sedation?

Waking up from sedation or anaesthesia is a gradual process. You might feel groggy, disoriented, or like time has skipped — one moment you were counting backwards and the next you're in a different room. Common experiences include drowsiness, mild confusion, dry mouth, slight nausea, and feeling cold. Some people feel emotional — crying or feeling upset without a clear reason is a normal pharmacological effect, not a psychological issue. Your alertness will return in stages over the next few hours. Nurses in recovery monitor you closely throughout this process. If you feel nauseous or in pain, tell them right away so they can manage it with medication.
I saw them code someone down the hall. I'm really shaken.

Witnessing a medical emergency — even from a distance — is frightening and can leave you feeling shaken for a while. That's a completely normal reaction. The staff responding to that situation are highly trained, and the fact that there was an immediate response shows the level of care this hospital provides to every patient. What you witnessed doesn't reflect your own situation. If you're feeling anxious, scared, or just need to process what happened, please tell your nurse you'd like to talk to someone. A psychologist or social worker can help you work through that experience. You don't have to sit with it alone.
Where can I charge my phone?

Your room should have outlets you can use — just bring your own charger. The hospital's WiFi is available for connecting to the internet. If you're having any trouble with WiFi, you can call the Data Valet at 1-800-642-3958 for help.
What is shared decision making?

Shared Decision Making is a formal process at LHSC where you, your family, and your healthcare providers collaborate on important care decisions. It goes beyond just being told what will happen — it incorporates the best clinical evidence alongside your personal values, preferences, and circumstances. There's even a Decision Coach you can work with. If you're facing a significant care decision and want to be more actively involved, ask your care team about accessing this process.
What is the Paediatric Critical Care Unit (PCCU) like?

The PCCU is the intensive care unit for paediatric patients. It has higher nurse-to-patient ratios and more advanced monitoring equipment than a general ward. At the bedside, there are two sleep spaces available for family members, with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets provided. There's also a nearby quiet room that sleeps one and a sleep room that sleeps two — both share a bathroom with a shower. Expect to see more machines and monitors than in a regular room, and more frequent check-ins from the care team. The environment can feel intense, but the staff are specialists in critical care for children and teens.
What should I expect with blood draws?

A blood draw (venipuncture) involves a phlebotomist or nurse inserting a needle into a vein, usually at the inside of your elbow or on the back of your hand, to collect blood samples for lab testing. Under the Comfort Promise, you can request topical anesthetic to numb the site beforehand. The needle insertion feels like a quick pinch — most of the discomfort is over in a couple of seconds. Distraction techniques like music, conversation, or looking at your phone can help. After the draw, they'll apply a small bandage. Mild bruising at the site is normal and resolves within a few days. If you're someone who's had bad experiences with needles in the past, tell your care team — they can plan extra comfort measures.
Someone brought up spiritual care. I'm not religious — is that still relevant to me?

It can be. Spiritual Care at Children's Hospital is available to everyone regardless of religious background. Spiritual Care Specialists provide what the hospital calls 'people-centred care' — they work with patients and families on emotional support, coping, grief, meaning-making, and reflection. They're respectful of all beliefs, values, and practices, including having none. There's also a Sanctuary space in Zone C on the third floor that's open 24/7 for anyone who wants quiet time, reflection, or meditation. If you're dealing with heavy emotions during your stay, Spiritual Care can be a resource even if religion isn't part of the picture.
Are there resources for Black patients and families navigating care?

LHSC has a Black Health Navigator program. Black Health Navigators are trained and registered healthcare workers who help Black patients and families navigate the health system — they provide information on healthcare options and help ensure your voice is heard during conversations with your care team. You can access this through your care team or by emailing BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
Can a pharmacist explain my medications to me?

Yes. If you have questions about your medications, ask your nurse to contact a pharmacist on your behalf. The pharmacist can come talk to you directly. If you're on several medications, they can also prepare a medication calendar and review it with you before you go home.
They just told me I have a chronic condition. I don't even know how to process this.

A new diagnosis — especially a chronic one — can feel like the ground just shifted under you. It's okay to not know how to feel right now. Shock, denial, anger, sadness — all of those are normal responses. You don't have to process everything at once. Give yourself time. When you're ready, your care team can help you understand what this means for your daily life, and Children's Hospital has psychologists who specifically help young people adjust to diagnosis. The Transitions in Care team is also there for long-term support. This isn't the end of your story — it's a new variable in it. But right now, it's okay to just sit with the news.
What's the NICU?

NICU stands for Neonatal Intensive Care Unit. It's the specialized unit that cares for newborns — particularly premature babies or those born with medical conditions that require close monitoring and intervention. The environment is carefully controlled, and the nurse-to-patient ratio is high. Parents can be present and are encouraged to participate in care. The NICU at Children's Hospital can be reached at 519-685-8500, extension 64427.
I met a younger kid here who seems really scared. I want to help them.

That empathy says a lot about who you are as a person. Sometimes a kind word from someone who's been through a similar experience means more than anything an adult can say. If you see the younger kid in a shared space, a friendly smile or a simple 'hey, I know it's scary, but it gets easier' could really help. Just being visible as a teen who's handling their own hospital stay can be reassuring. You could also talk to a Child Life Specialist about volunteer or peer support opportunities. Just remember to take care of yourself first — you can't pour from an empty cup. But your instinct to help is genuinely admirable.
Can I go out to smoke or vape during my stay?

No. LHSC is entirely smoke-free — all buildings, grounds, and parking lots. That includes cigarettes, e-cigarettes, vapes, cigars, and cannabis. There's no designated smoking area. If you're dealing with cravings, talk to your care team — they may be able to help.
What is the Comfort Promise?

The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety during needle procedures. They use evidence-based strategies: topical anesthetic to numb the skin, comfort positioning (sitting upright with secure, supportive holds instead of restraint), and distraction techniques like watching videos or playing with something. For infants under 12 months, sucrose and breastfeeding are also used. You're encouraged to ask about these strategies before any needle procedure.
What happens with my personal belongings during surgery?

Before surgery, you'll change into a hospital gown and need to remove all personal items — jewellery, piercings, glasses, hearing aids, and personal clothing. Your family or caregiver should hold onto these, or they'll be stored securely until after your procedure. It's best to leave valuables at home. The hospital recommends bringing minimal personal belongings to reduce clutter and the risk of items getting lost. After your procedure and once you're back in your room, your belongings will be returned. Make sure to account for everything on your discharge checklist before leaving.
What if this changes my life forever?

That's a heavy question, and it makes sense that you'd be thinking about it. The honest answer is that your doctor is the person who can talk to you about long-term outcomes for your specific situation. Some health events are temporary, others require ongoing management, and both are livable. What I can tell you is that whatever happens, you will adapt. People — especially young people — are remarkably resilient. And you won't have to figure it out alone. There are medical teams, counsellors, and support systems built for exactly this. Please have this conversation with your doctor. You deserve honest answers, not spinning scenarios in your head.
Someone from security scanned me at the ER entrance. Why?

Children's Hospital has a weapons detection system at the Emergency Department entrance. Everyone entering the ED is required to pass through it — including patients, visitors, and even kids with a parent or guardian. The system uses non-invasive technology that lets you walk through without stopping or removing personal items. If something flags, a trained security guard may check your belongings. It's about maintaining a safe environment for patients and staff. There are accommodations available if someone can't go through the system in the standard way — you can speak with the security guard at the entrance about that.
What if I have a complaint about my care?

Start by talking directly to your care team — they may be able to resolve it quickly. If that doesn't work, LHSC has a Patient Relations office you can contact. They're reachable by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca, by phone at 519-685-8500 extension 52036, or via a contact form on the LHSC website. They handle questions, concerns, and formal feedback about care experiences. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.
What should I bring for a hospital stay?

For your stay, you'll want to bring your Ontario health card, any appointment letters, a list of your current medications (including over-the-counter and herbal supplements), and your family doctor's contact info. For personal comfort, pack your own clothes including sleepwear and slippers, toiletries, and any medical aids like glasses or braces. You can bring a few comfort items — books, a tablet, headphones, family photos — but keep it manageable since clutter can interfere with care delivery and cleaning. Toys and items should be clean and ideally wipeable. Don't bring latex balloons, perfume or fragranced products, electrical equipment, or baby walkers. Keep valuables to a minimum and bring a small amount of cash for vending machines or snacks.
What's the PPI program?

PPI stands for Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction. It's a program that prepares one caregiver to accompany and support you in the operating room while you're being put under anaesthesia. It includes an education session and possibly a tour of the Day Surgery area and OR beforehand. It's not available for every case, so you'd need to discuss eligibility with your care team or a Child Life Specialist. If going into the OR is something that causes you anxiety, this is worth asking about.
What's Upopolis and who runs it?

Upopolis is a free, secure social networking site for hospitalized paediatric patients ages 8 to 18. It lets you connect with other patients across Canadian hospitals who are going through similar experiences. It's managed through Child Life Services at Children's Hospital, and laptops are available to access it. If you're interested, talk to a Child Life Specialist — they can set you up. It's a way to feel less isolated during a hospital stay, especially if your friends at home can't fully relate to what you're dealing with.
How does the hospital decide what diet I'm on?

Your physician prescribes your diet based on your medical condition and treatment plan. It could range from a regular diet to specialized options — clear fluids, soft foods, or nil by mouth before a procedure. Food Services then provides a menu that matches your prescribed diet. If you have religious, cultural, or ethical dietary preferences (like halal, kosher, or vegan), let your care team know and they'll accommodate it. A dietitian is also available to work with you if you have specific needs or concerns.
I don't even recognize myself anymore. This whole thing has changed me.

Going through a significant health event can absolutely change how you see yourself and the world. That shift can be disorienting and even scary. Some of those changes might be temporary — fatigue, mood shifts, physical changes. Others might be deeper. What I want you to know is that change isn't the same as losing yourself. You're still you at your core. If you feel like you're losing touch with who you are, talking to a psychologist can help you make sense of the experience and integrate it into your identity without it taking over. Growth through adversity is real, but you don't have to navigate it alone.
Why does the hospital ask about my mental health?

Being hospitalized affects your mental health, not just your physical health. Anxiety, frustration, sadness, and fear are all common and valid responses. Your care team asks because they want to identify if you need additional support — whether that's a conversation with a social worker, a referral to paediatric psychology, or just acknowledging that what you're going through is hard. It's not about judging you; it's about treating you as a whole person, not just a diagnosis.
Who can walk me through what's going to happen during my procedure?

A Child Life Specialist is specifically trained to prepare patients for procedures — they'll explain what will happen step by step, describe what you might see, hear, and feel, and help you develop a coping plan. Your nurse and physician can also walk you through the clinical details. For surgical procedures, the PPI program may offer a tour of Day Surgery and the Operating Room. You're entitled to understand what's happening to your body before it happens. Don't hesitate to ask for as much information as you need.
Can my friend visit me? Who decides?

Visiting at Children's Hospital is based on the patient's condition, care needs, and wishes, as well as unit-specific guidelines. It's best to check with your unit staff about optimal visiting times. Visiting may be restricted for infection control, patient safety, or privacy reasons. After 8 p.m., visitors are asked to remain in the patient's room and let unit staff know when they arrive or leave. Everyone visiting should wash their hands and shouldn't come if they're sick or have been unwell in the past week. Talk to your nurse about the visiting guidelines for your specific unit — they can help you figure out the best time for your friend to come.
What does 'Zone' mean in the hospital's layout?

The Victoria Hospital site is divided into lettered zones — A, B, C, D, E — each representing a different section of the building. Children's Hospital is in Zone B. Room numbers encode location: the first letter is the zone, the next digit is the floor, and the remaining numbers are the room. So B6-261 = Zone B, floor 6, room 261. Understanding the zone system makes navigating the building a lot easier. There's also an app called MazeMap and on-site QR codes that pull up interactive maps.
What is the discharge checklist?

Before leaving the hospital, you and your family should work through a comprehensive checklist. Key items include: understanding your medication schedule (purpose, dosage, side effects, next dose timing, cost), knowing your follow-up appointment dates and locations, confirming any home care equipment delivery, assessing whether your home needs modifications, clarifying any activity or diet changes, communicating your diagnosis and care needs to your school, and ensuring you have written care instructions. You should also know who to call if your condition changes or you have an emergency. Make sure all personal belongings are packed and your transportation home is arranged with an appropriate car seat if required.
What is a Child Life Specialist, and would they even work with teens?

Child Life Specialists work with patients of all ages, including teens. They're professionals trained to help you cope with the stress of hospitalization. For teens, that might look like preparing you for a scary procedure, teaching pain management or coping techniques, or just being someone outside your medical team you can talk to honestly. They're not therapists and they're not there to babysit you — they're there to help you process what you're going through and advocate for your comfort.
What if I go home and something goes wrong and there are no nurses to help?

That anxiety about transitioning home is incredibly common and shows that you're thinking ahead, which is smart. Before you leave, your care team will go through detailed discharge instructions — medications, warning signs to watch for, activity levels, and who to call if something happens. If you need equipment or special care at home, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator will assess that before discharge. You won't be sent home unprepared. Write down every question you have now so you can go through them before you leave. And remember, you can always call the hospital or go to the emergency department if something feels wrong. You're not being abandoned — you're being promoted.
Someone mentioned an Ontario Health atHome referral. Does that mean I'm going home soon?

Not necessarily in the immediate sense, but it does mean your care team is starting to think about your discharge plan — which actually begins early in your hospital stay. An Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator assesses what equipment or services you might need at home. If your stay is longer than 14 days, a new referral is required. The coordinator at extension 52249 helps arrange things like home nursing, therapy services, or medical equipment. It's a standard part of discharge planning, and it's a good sign that your care team is proactively preparing for your transition home.
What happens during a code or emergency in the hospital?

Hospitals have very structured emergency response systems — sometimes called 'code' systems — for different types of emergencies (cardiac arrest, fire, security, etc.). Each code triggers a specific response from designated teams. If a code is called near you, the most important thing is to stay calm and follow any instructions from staff. They're highly trained for these situations. If you ever feel unsafe or see something concerning, tell your nurse immediately or call the emergency response extension at 55555.
Is there someone who can help me advocate for my own care?

Several people can support you in that. Your primary nurse is your daily advocate and point of contact. Social workers specialize in advocacy and can help you communicate with your care team, navigate decisions, and prepare for discharge. The Shared Decision Making program provides Decision Coaches who ensure your values are part of the decision-making process. Patient Relations is available if you feel your voice isn't being heard. And honestly, you're already advocating for yourself by asking this question. Children's Hospital explicitly encourages patients and families to be active partners in care.
What should I expect from art therapy?

Art therapy at Children's Hospital is facilitated by a trained art therapist and uses creative activities — drawing, painting, sculpting, mixed media — as a form of expression and emotional processing. You don't need any artistic talent or experience. The focus isn't on producing good art; it's on the process of creating as a way to explore thoughts and feelings that might be hard to verbalize. It can be empowering and provide a sense of control during a time when a lot of decisions are being made for you medically. Sessions are individualized to your needs and interests. Ask your care team or a Child Life Specialist to set up a session.
Last time I had this procedure it was awful. I don't want to go through that again.

A bad experience with a procedure leaves a mark, and it's completely reasonable to dread repeating it. But this time doesn't have to be a repeat of last time. Tell your care team exactly what happened before and what made it bad — was it pain, anxiety, communication, something unexpected? When they know specifically what went wrong, they can plan around it. Maybe they can use a different approach, offer more numbing, provide anxiety support, or simply keep you better informed. You've been through this before, which means you know what questions to ask and what to advocate for. Use that experience to make this time better.
What does the art therapist do? Is it just drawing?

It's more than that. The art therapy program at Children's Hospital provides kids and teens with a way to express thoughts and feelings through creative activities — and that can include drawing, but also painting, sculpting, collage, and other media. The point isn't to make great art; it's that the creative process itself can be empowering, relaxing, and therapeutic. Art therapy can give you a sense of personal control during a time when a lot feels unpredictable. For teens especially, it can be a way to process complex emotions that are hard to put into words.
What does a typical day look like as an inpatient?

A typical day on the ward generally follows this rhythm: early morning begins with the nursing shift change around 6:45–7:30 a.m., followed by morning rounds where the medical team reviews your case. Breakfast arrives between 7:45 and 8:45 a.m. Throughout the morning, you might have scheduled tests, procedures, or visits from therapists (physio, OT, child life). Lunch is served 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. Afternoons may include more appointments, rest time, or activities. Dinner comes at 4:45–5:45 p.m. The evening shift change is around 6:45–7:30 p.m. The pace varies — some days are busier than others depending on your care plan.
I feel so isolated. Everyone's living their life and I'm stuck here.

That feeling of watching life continue without you from a hospital bed is genuinely painful. It's a loss, even if it's temporary, and it's okay to grieve that. But you're not as cut off as it might feel. The hospital has free Wi-Fi, you can use your phone, and the patient phones allow free local calling. You could FaceTime your friends, stay active on group chats, or even have visitors — up to two people can be at your bedside at a time. If you're here for a while, there's also Upopolis, a secure social platform for patients aged 8–18 to connect with other kids across Canada. You haven't been erased from your life. This is a pause, not an ending.
Who's the Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator and why did they talk to my family?

The Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator helps patients and families plan for services and equipment that may be needed at home after discharge. If your hospital stay is longer than 14 days, a new referral to Ontario Health atHome is required. They assess your needs — things like home nursing support, medical equipment, or therapy services — and coordinate access to those community-based resources. If you're already receiving community services, you need to connect with the coordinator at extension 52249 before going home. They're essentially the bridge between hospital care and home care.
Who should I reach out to if I want to give feedback about my care — good or bad?

There are a couple of options. For concerns or complaints, the first step is to talk directly to your care team. If that doesn't resolve things, you can contact the Patient Relations Office — they're reachable by phone at extension 52036 or by email at patientrelations@lhsc.on.ca. They check messages between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. on weekdays. If you want to recognize someone who made a difference, Children's Hospital has the Great Moments Recognition Program — you can fill out a short form on the LHSC website, and that person will receive a letter of appreciation. Your voice matters, whatever the feedback.
What do white blood cells actually do?

White blood cells (WBCs) are a key part of your immune system. There are several types, each with a different job. Neutrophils are first responders that engulf and destroy bacteria. Lymphocytes include T-cells (which coordinate the immune response and kill infected cells) and B-cells (which produce antibodies). Monocytes clean up dead cells and debris. Eosinophils fight parasites and are involved in allergic responses. When your doctors check your blood count, WBC levels help them understand how your immune system is functioning. If you have questions about your specific results, your care team can explain what they mean for you.
What does the identification armband do?

Your ID armband is a critical safety tool. It contains your full name, date of birth, a unique hospital ID number, and a scannable barcode. Before any medication, test, procedure, or transport, a member of your care team will scan or visually check your armband to confirm your identity. You'll also be verbally asked to confirm your name and birthday — sometimes multiple times a day. It might feel repetitive, but it's a core patient safety practice designed to prevent errors. If you have known allergies, you'll also receive a separate red allergy bracelet so every staff member is immediately aware.
What happens during the bedside shift change?

At shift change, the outgoing and incoming nurses meet at your bedside for about three to five minutes. The new nurse introduces themselves, they review your care plan, complete mandatory safety checks, and ask if you or your family have questions or anything to add. You're encouraged to participate — it's your care, and your input matters. Nursing shift changes happen daily around 6:45–7:30 a.m. and 6:45–7:30 p.m.
Who are the people at the information desk?

They're typically volunteers and staff whose job is to help you navigate the building. Information desks at Children's Hospital are open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and from noon to 4 p.m. on weekends. You can also find guide volunteers at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby weekdays from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. They can help with directions, answer general questions, and point you to the right department.
What's the deal with the fragrance-free rule?

LHSC is entirely fragrance-free. That means no perfume, cologne, scented lotion, body spray, or any scented products. Some patients and staff have respiratory conditions or allergies that can be triggered by fragrances, and in a hospital setting where people are already vulnerable, it's an important precaution. Ask anyone visiting you to skip fragrances too.
I don't want a student examining me. Do I have the right to refuse?

Yes, you have the right to decline having a medical student involved in your care or examination. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, and medical students participate in care under supervision as part of their training, but your consent matters. If you're uncomfortable, communicate this to your nurse or attending physician. Your care will not be affected by your decision. It's your body and your care experience — having the confidence to set that boundary is completely reasonable.
What's different about the NICU?

The Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) is a specialized unit for critically ill or premature newborns. It's distinct from the paediatric ward in several ways: the environment is kept quieter and dimmer to support infant development, equipment is scaled for very small patients, and parents interact with their baby through specific protocols. Kangaroo chairs and sleeper chairs are available, but due to the large equipment and limited space, there's not always room to stay directly at the bedside. The NICU has its own family guide with detailed information. If you're visiting a sibling or have questions about the NICU environment, ask the unit staff.
What is a pulse oximeter?

A pulse oximeter is a small, clip-like device placed on your fingertip. It shines infrared and red light through your skin to measure the oxygen saturation of your blood — essentially, how well your body is transporting oxygen. It also reads your pulse rate. The clip feels like a gentle clothespin and doesn't cause any pain. You'll see a number displayed on a monitor, usually between 95 and 100 percent for healthy levels. If the reading drops or fluctuates, it might trigger an alarm on the monitor — often it's just because the clip shifted. Your nurse will check and reposition it if needed.
What happens if I need to be transferred between units?

Transfers between units happen when your care needs change — for example, moving from the PCCU to the general inpatient ward as your condition stabilizes, or moving from the ED to an inpatient bed. During a transfer, your care team will communicate your full medical history and care plan to the receiving team. Your belongings will come with you. You'll be reoriented to the new unit's layout, routines, and staff. You'll likely need to confirm your identity again via your armband. If you have questions about why you're being transferred or what the new unit will be like, ask before the move happens.
What's with the hospital smell?

That distinctive smell is mostly industrial-strength disinfectants used to keep every surface as sterile as possible. Hospitals have very strict cleaning protocols because patients with compromised immune systems are particularly vulnerable to infections. You might also be noticing hand sanitizer — the alcohol-based kind is used constantly throughout the building. The fact that it's a fragrance-free facility also means you're not getting the mix of perfumes and products you'd encounter elsewhere, which can make the antiseptic smell more noticeable.
Where can I find information about my condition?

The Paediatric Family Resource Centre at B1-006 has health information resources and internet access. Online, the hospital recommends AboutKidsHealth (from SickKids), Caring for Kids (from Canada's paediatricians), and MedlinePlus. For questions specific to your care, always ask your care team — they're the best source for your situation.
I hate having to ask permission for everything. I'm not a little kid.

That frustration is completely valid. Being a teenager is about gaining independence, and the hospital environment can feel like it strips that away — someone else controls when you eat, when you sleep, who comes in your room. It can feel infantilizing. Here's the thing, though: you still have agency here. You can advocate for yourself, ask questions, participate in decisions about your care, and set boundaries around your space and privacy. The staff here should treat you as a partner in your care, not just a patient. If you feel like you're not being heard, say so. Your voice matters, and good care teams will respect that.
Can I use my phone and access WiFi at the hospital?

Yes. The hospital supports and encourages patients to use their own cell phones. There's WiFi available, and the hospital provides a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming services. Patient telephones in your room can also be used for local and toll-free calls at no charge. If you run into any issues with WiFi connectivity, you can call the Data Valet/WiFi support line at 1-800-642-3958.
What's the Black Health Navigator?

Black Health Navigators are registered health-care workers who help Black patients and families navigate the health-care system. They provide information about health-care options and make sure your voice is heard in conversations with care teams. You can access this service through Black Health — ask your care team or email BlackHealth@lhsc.on.ca.
How does an MRI work?

An MRI — magnetic resonance imaging — uses powerful magnets and radio waves to create detailed images of the inside of your body, without radiation. You lie in a tube-shaped machine that generates a strong magnetic field, which causes hydrogen atoms in your body to align. Radio wave pulses knock them out of alignment, and as they realign, they emit signals that a computer processes into images. It's loud (you'll hear knocking and humming), it takes a while, and you need to stay still, but it's not painful. If you're anxious about it, let your team know — there are ways they can help.
What does a social worker at the hospital actually do?

Hospital social workers provide emotional support and practical help. They can assist your family with things like navigating the hospital system, accessing community services, handling insurance or financial challenges, and communicating with your care team when things get complicated. They can also help with discharge planning, school transitions, and connecting you with mental health resources. If you or your family are feeling overwhelmed by anything beyond your medical care, a social worker is the person to ask about.
I really hate being examined. It's so awkward.

Physical examinations can feel uncomfortable and invasive, especially during adolescence. Your feelings are completely normal. Here are your rights: a medical professional should always explain what they're going to do before they do it, you can request a same-gender provider if that makes you more comfortable, you can have a parent or nurse present (or ask them to leave), and you can ask questions at any point. No one should examine you without your understanding and cooperation. If anything during an exam makes you uncomfortable, say something. Your boundaries matter, and a good care team will respect them.
I was already dealing with anxiety before this. Being here is making it so much worse.

That sounds really tough. A hospital stay can amplify existing anxiety significantly — the loss of control, the unfamiliar environment, the medical uncertainty. It makes sense that you're struggling. The important thing is to not ignore it. Let your care team know about your pre-existing anxiety, because it's relevant to your care and there are things they can do to help. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychologists on staff who specifically help young people cope with the emotional side of hospitalization. You can also ask for a social worker. Managing your mental health alongside your physical health isn't optional — it's essential. Please speak up about this.
I don't want anyone posting about me being in the hospital.

You have every right to control that narrative. Your health information and your image are your own, and you get to decide who knows what. If you're worried about a family member or friend posting, tell them directly. Most people will respect that once they know it matters to you. The hospital also takes your privacy seriously — staff aren't allowed to share your information without consent. If someone does post something you didn't authorize, you can ask them to take it down. You're not being controlling — you're protecting your boundaries, and that's a mature and healthy thing to do.
Can I vape at the hospital?
No. Under the Smoke-Free Ontario Act, LHSC is entirely smoke-free — that includes e-cigarettes and vapes. The policy covers all buildings, grounds, and parking lots without exception.
How does the hospital's Comfort Promise work for teens?

The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety during needle procedures, and it applies to patients of all ages, including teens. Evidence-based strategies include topical anesthetic (a numbing cream or gel applied to the skin before a needle), comfort positioning (sitting upright in a supportive position rather than being restrained), and distraction (watching something on your phone, listening to music, or any activity that redirects your focus). Research shows that untreated needle pain can lead to long-term effects like healthcare avoidance, increased pain sensitivity, and even vaccine hesitancy. You have every right to ask for these comfort measures — it's not just for younger kids.
I want to leave. Can I just sign myself out?

I understand you want out — hospital stays can feel suffocating. As a minor, discharge decisions involve your parents and your medical team, so you can't sign yourself out unilaterally. But your frustration deserves to be heard. Talk to your nurse or doctor about how you're feeling and ask them to explain the specific reasons you need to stay and what milestones would need to be met for you to go home. Having a clear timeline and understanding the 'why' can make the wait more manageable. If you're feeling trapped or overwhelmed, a social worker or psychologist can also help. Your feelings aren't being dismissed — but your safety comes first.
Where's the breast pump room?

The breast pump room is in Zone B, 6th floor, room B6-235. Nurses can provide containers and computer-generated labels for breast milk. Labeled containers should be given to the nurse for refrigeration or freezing. Breast pump kits can be purchased at the pharmacy (B1-001).
Can anyone explain the Comfort Promise to me in a way that's not patronizing?

Sure. The Comfort Promise is an evidence-based commitment to reduce pain and anxiety during needle procedures. Here's what it involves: topical anesthetic to numb the site, comfort positioning (supportive positions rather than being held down, which research shows has significant negative effects), and distraction techniques. The clinical rationale is solid — untreated procedural pain is linked to increased pain sensitivity in future procedures, health-care avoidance, slower recovery, and vaccine hesitancy. You're encouraged to actively participate in choosing which strategies work for you. You can ask for any or all of them before any needle procedure. It's not about coddling — it's about evidence-based pain management.
Someone mentioned a 'charge nurse.' What's that?

The charge nurse is the nurse who oversees the entire unit for a given shift. They manage patient assignments, coordinate admissions and discharges, handle staffing issues, and serve as a resource for other nurses. If you have a concern that your assigned nurse can't resolve, or if you want to discuss something at a unit-management level — like a room issue or care concern — the charge nurse is a good person to ask for. They're typically based at or near the nurses' station and have a broader view of what's happening across the whole unit.
What can I expect during daily rounds?

Rounds are when your care team — which may include the attending physician, residents, medical students, nurse practitioners, and your nurse — gathers to discuss your case and care plan. This often happens in the morning and sometimes at your bedside. They'll review your progress, test results, medications, and next steps. You and your family are encouraged to participate — ask questions, raise concerns, or share how you're feeling. It's a good idea to write down any questions beforehand so you don't forget them in the moment. Rounds are a key part of how decisions about your care get made.
Some kids here seem way sicker than me. I feel guilty for complaining.

Pain and difficulty aren't a competition. Someone else having a harder time doesn't invalidate what you're going through. Your feelings, your fear, your frustration — they're all legitimate, regardless of what the person in the next room is dealing with. This is called 'comparative suffering' and it actually prevents people from getting the support they need. You're allowed to struggle. You're allowed to complain. And you're allowed to ask for help. Every patient here deserves the same quality of care and emotional support, including you. Don't minimize your own experience.
What is a blood gas test?

A blood gas test (arterial blood gas or ABG) measures the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in your blood, along with your blood's pH. It's taken from an artery, usually in your wrist, rather than a vein. The skin over the artery will be cleaned, and you may feel a sharper poke than a standard blood draw since arteries are deeper and more sensitive. Tell your care team if you're anxious — comfort strategies can still be applied. The test gives your care team critical information about how well your lungs are functioning and whether your body's acid-base balance is normal. Results are typically available quickly.
I keep telling them something feels wrong but they say my tests look fine. Am I imagining it?

You are not imagining it. You know your body better than anyone, and if something feels wrong, that's information worth taking seriously. 'Tests look fine' doesn't mean 'nothing is wrong' — it means the tests they've run haven't found the issue yet. Be persistent and specific about your symptoms: when they happen, how severe, what triggers them. Ask if there are other tests or specialists that could be consulted. You can also request a patient advocate through the Patient Relations office. Your voice is your most important medical tool. Don't let anyone dismiss what you're experiencing.
Why do so many different people come into my room?

Hospital care is team-based. Your team might include an attending physician, residents, nurse practitioners, registered nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers, and more — each responsible for a different aspect of your health. It can feel like a revolving door, but each person has a specific role. You're absolutely entitled to ask anyone who enters your room to identify themselves and explain why they're there. If the traffic is overwhelming, let your nurse know.
What can I actually do for entertainment here?

More than you might expect. The hospital has a patient entertainment site with free live TV and the ability to use your own streaming accounts. There's a School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) with games, crafts, puzzles, and LEGO. The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room with fibre optics, bubble columns, and music. Upopolis is a free, secure social network for patients aged 8–18. There's also music therapy, art therapy, and the Heroes' Circle martial arts program. Ask a Child Life Specialist what's available during your stay.
Why are hospitals so concerned about infection control?

Hospitals bring together a concentration of vulnerable patients — people with weakened immune systems, open wounds, surgical sites, and invasive devices like IVs. Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are a real and significant risk. The infection prevention protocols you see — hand hygiene, isolation precautions, gowns, gloves, restricted visitor policies during outbreaks — all exist because the evidence shows they meaningfully reduce transmission. It's one of those areas where small, consistent actions have outsized impact.
What does post-operative care look like?

After surgery, you'll be taken to a recovery area where nurses will closely monitor your vital signs as the anaesthesia wears off. Depending on your procedure, you might have an IV, a surgical dressing, drains, or a catheter in place. Pain management will be a priority — your team will assess your pain regularly and provide medication as needed. Once stable, you'll return to your room. Recovery instructions will cover wound care, activity restrictions, diet, and medication. Nurses will continue regular checks throughout your stay. If your pain spikes, you feel nauseous, notice unexpected drainage, or something doesn't feel right, alert your nurse immediately.
Nobody at school understands what I'm going through.

You're probably right — most of your classmates haven't had this experience, and that can feel incredibly isolating. It's hard when people say things like 'at least you get to miss school' and have no idea what you're actually dealing with. Connecting with people who do understand can help. Upopolis is a secure social network for hospital patients aged 8–18 where you can talk with other young people across Canada who get it. The hospital also has group programs and a psychology service. You don't have to educate everyone around you or justify your experience. Finding even one person who understands can make a real difference.
They keep waking me up to check my vitals. I just want to sleep.

I completely get how annoying that is. You finally fall asleep and then someone's there with a blood pressure cuff. The reason they do it is to catch any changes early, which can be critical for your safety — but that doesn't make it less disruptive. You can ask your nurse if the overnight check schedule can be adjusted at all, or if any checks can be combined so you get longer stretches of uninterrupted sleep. Earplugs, an eye mask, and a consistent wind-down routine can also help you fall back asleep faster after checks. Your need for rest is important, and your team knows that.
What should I expect from the Paediatric Emergency Department?

When you arrive at the Paediatric ED, you'll pass through the weapons detection system at the entrance — it's quick and non-invasive. You'll then be seen by a triage nurse who will assess your symptoms and assign a priority level. Depending on the severity, you may be seen immediately or have a wait. One caregiver is expected to stay with you at all times. There are no sleeping accommodations in the ED, but staff will try to provide a reclining or fold-out chair with pillows and blankets. The environment can be busy and noisy, with lots of activity. Bring something to pass the time — your phone, headphones, a book. If your condition changes while waiting, let staff know immediately.
